The Elder of Jūzhōu was a prodigy from Shǔ. He possessed extraordinary talent and was skilled at composing literary works; his speech was invariably startling. One day, suddenly...
He abandoned his secular studies and traveled to various regions to study the Supreme Vehicle. Later, within the Miaoxi Studio, he attained definitive realization of the Great Matter.
He galloped ahead, leaving the dust behind him like the moon among a flock of stars. His late father, Prince Wenwei, passed away before the cauldron of the immortal crane.
Upon seeing him once, his joy moved the hairs on his brows and eyelashes. From that time forth, their literary paths and spiritual bonds were harmonized.

They wandered leisurely among the mountains and waters of East Lake; beyond the misty clouds, sands, and birds, their minds were deeply at ease. He built a pure monastery at the center of an island in the southern suburb to settle him there, honoring his virtue.

He planted ten thousand orange trees around the residence, and thus he styled himself accordingly. Every time [the Master] passed through the courtyard and heard his lectures, [he was filled with admiration].

When he attained clarity, his mind and eyes were fully enlightened. At that time, his brothers also delighted in following his instructions, refining themselves through his guidance, hoping to establish themselves at some point.
Consequently, they rose early and retired late, fearing they could not exhaustively master his arts.

The former Buddha Vipaśyin resided in the city of Bandhumatī; sitting beneath a Pāṭala tree, he preached the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering thirty thousand people.
There were forty-eight thousand people. There were two who possessed the power of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*):
first, Khaṇḍa; second, Tiṣya. The attendant was Aśokaśrī. The verse for transmitting the Dharma says: "The body arises from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is originally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, having no place of abiding."
Śikhin Buddha resided in the city of Prabhāsa. He sat beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree and preached the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering two hundred and fifty thousand people.
His two disciples with supernormal powers were Ābhū and Vappa; his attendant was Ananta, son of Kṣāntivādin. He transmitted the Dharma verse.

He said: "The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; the creation of all unwholesome karmas is likewise an illusion. The body is like a mass of foam, and the mind is like the wind;
they are illusory manifestations without root and without real nature."
Vipaśyin Buddha resided in the city of Anupama.
Seated beneath a śāla tree, he preached the Dharma in two assemblies, delivering one hundred and thirty thousand people.
His two disciples with supernormal powers were Pūrṇa and Uttara. His attendant was Śāntiputra Subuddhi. The verse of the transmission of the Dharma says:

One borrows the four great elements to form a body; the mind is originally without birth, arising only because of external objects. If the preceding object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist.
Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and then perish.

Kāśyapa Buddha resided in the city of Āmrapālī. Sitting beneath a śirīṣa tree, he preached the Dharma in a single assembly, delivering forty thousand people across. He had two disciples with supernormal powers:
first, Sani; second, Vīra. His attendant was Sujāta, and his successor was Jina. The verse for transmitting the Dharma says: "Behold the body..."

The absence of substantiality is the Buddha-body; realizing that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha’s illusion. When one realizes that the nature of body and mind is empty, how does such a person differ from the Buddha?
The Buddha Kanakamuni resided in the city of Śuddhavatī.
Seated beneath an udumbara tree, he delivered a single assembly of teachings, delivering thirty thousand people across the threshold of liberation.
The two disciples of supernatural power were Śūrpaka and Uttara; their attendant was Aniruddha, the son of the Teacher. The verse of the Dharma transmission says:
"The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; If there were truly a knowing, there would be no other Buddha. The wise are able to know that the nature of offenses is empty;
They remain composed and unafraid of birth and death."
Kāśyapa Buddha resided in the city of Vārāṇasī. Seated beneath a nyagrodha tree, he preached the Dharma in a single assembly, delivering twenty thousand people across.
His two disciples with supernormal powers were Tiṣya and Bharadvāja; his attendant was Saumya, son of Jita. He transmitted the verse of the Dharma as follows:
The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished. This very body and mind are born of illusion;
within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
Baotan said: "Throughout past and present, whenever the attachment to the Dharma is forgotten, it is entirely because this illusory samādhi has manifested before one.
The Buddhas of the past attained awakening through this samādhi, maintained the teachings through this samādhi, and took birth through this samādhi."
Such is the realization of the Way, from beginning to end and first to last; to hold this as a single voucher is the family dharma of the Buddha.
During his single lifetime of preaching the Dharma, which was like the sands of the Ganges, even the palaces of the bodhisattvas and nāgas could not contain its full extent.
At the moment of transmission and reception, one ultimately arrives at wordlessness. How exquisite, unified, concise, and rigorous it is!
Now, among the seventeen hundred heirs of wisdom transmitted in the Lamp Records, there are those who have personally conceived the embryo of the sages of all times within the Primordial Buddha;
of these, one hundred and sixty-eight contain words that revolve like pearls and turn like jade—how magnificent! One must not fail to recognize this.
Later generations regard this as mere illusory, stale words. Is such not lacking in the world? They ignore and discard it, no more than one would treat it as something placed in a corner.

It is like a person who, after several generations, produces a son worth ten thousand pieces of gold, yet ultimately fails to realize that his ancestral forefather was a humble farmer who practiced hidden virtue. Alas! It is like an illusion, like emptiness, like the wind.
It is like a mass of foam. These very faces and eyes that appear now are what all Buddhas have realized.
One should know that illusion has no intrinsic nature; illusion is free from conceptual discrimination; illusion has no interior, exterior, or middle; illusion is cut off from coming and going;
illusion is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; illusion has no objective realm. Illusion is the Buddhas, and the Buddhas are illusion. Therefore, the Buddha...
To realize the wisdom of all-knowledge is precisely the Samādhi of the Illusory Nature of All Dharmas.
All dharmas likewise realize this samādhi, manifesting and radiating it day and night to show it to others: the crane is white and the crow is black;
the pine is straight and the thorn is crooked. How could the Dharma deceive you? Yet people do not understand skillful means; their various views burn fiercely like a mountain fire.
The great earth and rivers deceive themselves; form and emptiness, light and darkness deceive themselves; good and evil, acceptance and rejection deceive themselves;
the holy and the mundane, defilement and purity deceive themselves. Deceived once within the mind, illusory karma is accomplished—how then could there be any such thing as an illusory realm?
I have often lamented that scholars of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras in recent times recklessly criticize the verses spoken by the Seven Buddhas.
Upon seeing the translator, it was as if one had been granted a magnificent mansion by a heavenly king yet was unable to dwell within it;
instead, one questioned who the architect was, for how could one feel pity for those left orphaned and suffering in the cold?

The *Śākyamuni-buddha-sarvopasaṃhāra-sūtra* states: "On the eighth night of the twelfth month, when the morning star appeared, the Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
He then rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and went to the Deer Park, where he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five companions, including Kauṇḍinya."
Turning the Wheel of Dharma, he expounded upon the fruits of the Path. He preached the Dharma for forty-nine years in this world. Later, he addressed his disciple Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I entrust to you my pure Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa—the subtle and sublime True Dharma that is the reality of formlessness.
You must protect and uphold it well. He further commanded Ānanda to serve as his deputy in propagating and transforming others, ensuring that [the teaching] would not perish.
[He] cut off [the connection]. A verse says: "The Dharma is originally no-dharma; no-dharma is also dharma. Now, when the no-dharma is transmitted, how has dharma ever been dharma?
He further addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "I shall entrust this golden-threaded saṃghāṭī robe to you.
Transmit it to Maitreya, the Buddha who will appear in the position of the successor. Do not let it decay."
Baotán said: "For those who study the Way, the value lies in gaining entry; for those who transmit the Way, the concern lies in handing it over.
This is a universal affliction of teachers and disciples throughout ancient and modern times. The Elder Śākyamuni said:
'In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, innumerable, nayuta kalpas have already passed. Such is the original nature of this Great Dharma."
Thus it is. At the mountain of Right Enlightenment (Sageṇa), when the morning star appeared, he attained awakening with sudden clarity;

he and all sentient beings of the great earth simultaneously attained Buddhahood. This is the realization of the truth of these words. Therefore, the Tathāgata attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi) in all places;
he attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment within the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings; he attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment upon lumps of clay and particles of dust.
"One attains equal and perfect enlightenment within boiling cauldrons and glowing coals; one attains equal and perfect enlightenment amidst the afflictions of joy;
one attains equal and perfect enlightenment under a blow from a staff; one attains equal and perfect enlightenment under a shout of 'Ho!

Is it not then the case that such a one is called a Buddha who attained enlightenment not through the initial resolve? The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat upon the path for ten kalpas..."

In such a state, the Buddha-dharma does not manifest before one, and one cannot attain the Way of Buddhahood. Is it not, then, appropriate to call this "a Buddha who has not yet attained final perfect enlightenment"?
Generally speaking, attaining Buddhahood is not difficult; rather, it is the ability to fully carry out the Buddha’s work that is difficult.
For this reason, it is called the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. Only a Buddha possesses it inherently, yet it can also be transmitted and bestowed upon others.

It is like the crown prince of a Cakravartin king receiving his office: the king personally pours the waters of the four great oceans over his head in a rite that no other person is capable of performing.
This tradition has been passed down from one generation to another for thousands of millions of generations; therefore, the Way must not fail to be examined with care.

Among the twenty-eight patriarchs of India, the First Patriarch, Venerable Kāśyapa, was at the Piṇḍola Cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; beholding a sublime radiance, he immediately entered samādhi. With purity...
With his divine eye, he beheld the World-Honored One entering parinirvāṇa by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River.
He then addressed his disciples, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa! How swift was it! He immediately went to the space between the twin trees and wailed in grief and longing.
The Buddha manifested his two upturned feet within the golden coffin. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "The Buddha has already been cremated; the diamond-like śarīra is not mine."
Regarding such matters, the disciples of the Tathāgata should not enter parinirvāṇa; those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) should attend the council.
At the time of the council at the Piṃpala Cave, Ānanda was unable to join the assembly because his outflows (*āsrava*) were not yet exhausted.

Later, having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he was thereby permitted to enter. The Patriarch said: "Ānanda possessed vast learning (*bahuśruta*), mastery of the dhāraṇīs, and great wisdom; he constantly followed the Tathāgata."
"His holy life (*brahmacarya*) is pure. The Buddha-dharma he has heard is like water passed from one vessel to another, with nothing left behind.
He is praised by the Buddha as being foremost in intelligence and quick-wittedness; it is fitting that he be requested to compile the treasury of the Dharma.

The great assembly remained silent. The Elder addressed Ānanda, saying: "You should now proclaim the Sūtra-piṭaka. Having heard these words, Ānanda accepted them with faith and, observing the minds of the assembly, [proceeded].
He spoke in verse, saying: "O bhikṣus and your retinues, Without the Buddha, you lack adornment, Just as in the empty sky, The multitude of stars is without the moon.
Having spoken this verse, he prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha and ascended the Dharma seat, speaking these words: "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was dwelling in such-and-such a place, preaching such-and-such a sūtra and teaching. ... [and so on] until the humans, devas, and others paid their respects."
So it was done. At that time, the Patriarch asked the bhikṣus, "Is what Ānanda has said free from error?
They all replied, "It does not differ from what the World-Honored One has taught. The Patriarch then addressed Ānanda, saying, "In this year, I shall not remain long.
Now I entrust the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to you; guard it well. Listen to my verse: 'Dharma after dharma is the original Dharma; there is no...'"
"The Dharma has no non-Dharma. Why, within a single Dharma, is there both Dharma and non-Dharma?

Baotan said: "On Vulture Peak, those who attained the Way at different times were as numerous as a marketplace. For what reason was this single matter of the 'separate transmission outside the teachings' entrusted exclusively to Kāśyapa?
Although I appeared later than Vulture Peak, I shall weigh the relative importance of these matters among the hundreds of thousands of people."
"All these are suspended from my hand. Kāśyapa was likely a Confucian scholar from the state of Lu. Observing his practice of the Buddha, he had long heard the Way;

he even reached the point where the faculty of mental intention was permanently extinguished, and his perfect, clear understanding no longer depended on mental thought. Thus, he simultaneously heard what he had never heard before.
It was simply because the teacher and disciple shared the same realization and their spiritual eyes were in mutual accord; in ordinary times, they silently granted each other permission.
The interval between the giver and the receiver must be no wider than a hair’s breadth. Thus, Kāśyapa was the Buddha’s pupil;
his mind was the aperture, and his crown was the marrow. His breaking into a smile upon the picking up of the flower was indeed the second meaning.

Nevertheless, this gesture could not have been omitted, for it was truly intended for both humans and devas to witness together, so that they might know where the Great Dharma was entrusted. Furthermore, it was for...

This serves as the transmission of the fundamental source for future generations. Just as a fire the size of a single bean is certain to spread and consume a vast plain, so too did the descendants of later generations illuminate the world with its remaining radiance;
this was truly the achievement of two successive generations. This book does not record the incident of the "Holding the Flower.
Some claim that the event is found in the *Dharmatrāta-dharmagupta-śāstra* (Fufa zang zhuan) and the *Zongmen tongyao*.

Consequently, it has been said: "The World-Honored One held up the flowers offered by the devas to show them to people," or "The World-Honored One gazed upon the great assembly with his blue-lotus eyes.

Neither of these accounts is found here. I fear that those who hold heterodox views or propagate false doctrines might point to this as the actual place where he raised his eyes and plucked the flower, mistakenly taking the cry of a crane for the song of a nightingale.
Let those who understand discern this.

The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was tested at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and, having been proven victorious, attained the Way and came to the council. He heard that Kāśyapa had passed away.

Regarding the story of the *kṣetra*-staff: it was truly transcendent. When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa in the middle of the Ganges River, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.
Within the Snowy Mountains, five hundred sages beheld this auspicious omen and traveled through the air to arrive.

They prostrated at the Patriarch’s feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and said: "We shall realize the Buddha-dharma under you, O Elder; we pray that you will deign to grant us [instruction]."
"Great Compassionate One, deliver us. The Patriarch accepted the invitation in silence and immediately transformed the Ganges River entirely into golden ground.
He preached the Dharma for the assembly of rishis and further thought, "Those whom I previously delivered should now gather here.
In a brief moment, five hundred arhats descended from the sky; he granted them the going forth and full ordination. Among that assembly was Śroṇa.
The one named Vasu resided in the womb for sixty years. His grandfather, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, told him:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Great Eye of the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; when Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption, he then entrusted it to me.

I now entrust it to you; you must listen to these verses: 'Originally there was a dharma to be entrusted; having completed the entrustment, I say there is no dharma. Each person must awaken to this for themselves.'"
"Upon awakening, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Baotan said: "The 'Investigation of the Mind in Seven Places' and the 'Discernment of Seeing through the Eight Returns' in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* were specifically established for Ānanda.
When he had not yet entered the Buddha-dharma, he was like a wild colt that would not accept the bridle; the World-Honored One, like King Liang..."

Zao Fu’s hands were skilled at controlling [the horse]; when it strode majestically through the nine thoroughfares, chewing upon its golden bit, it immediately possessed the air of one of the twelve celestial stables. For the most part, it was born from the waters of Wawa.
To compile the deeds of the true sages, *bahuśruta* (great learning) and *dhāraṇī* (retention) serve as the lock and key to a single treasury; the eye of wisdom and clear intelligence are...
They are the divining stalks and tortoise shells of the Great Dharma; they are neither Mañjuśrī, nor Kāśyapa, nor Ānanda.

Even those foremost in supernatural powers are insufficient to speak of this. From now on, once my final report is submitted, the Tathāgata’s burden of ten thousand *jin* will surely look upon me with disdain.
Reflecting on the hardships of my lifelong pursuit of the Way, I have encountered the Buddha’s reproaches and entreated him with fervent sorrow and tears.
As for those who weep with tears of sorrow, it is not merely reaching this point that constitutes the limit; even to bare one’s shoulder and carry the burden would not be considered excessive.

Yet scholars of later generations, before their feet have even steadied themselves within the teachings, claim they have already exhausted the Way of the former masters. How brilliant! How extraordinary!
The Third Patriarch, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, turned the wheel of the Dharma. At the Blue Forest in the kingdom of Mathurā, he subdued two fire-dragons.
He then traveled to the kingdom of Tāmraliptī and obtained Upagupta. He asked him, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old. The Patriarch said, "You..."

[The Master] said, "My body is seventeen years old; my nature is seventeen years old. [Bodhidharma] asked, "Master, your hair has turned white. Is it because your hair is white that your mind is white?
The Patriarch replied, "I am simply one whose hair is white, not one whose mind is white. Bodhidharma said, "My body is seventeen years old, but my nature is not seventeen years old.
The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, then told him: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the unsurpassed, true Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa..."
[The transmission has been] handed down from master to disciple until it reached me. Now I entrust it to you; do not let it be severed. A verse says:
Neither dharma nor mind, Neither mind nor dharma. When speaking of this mind-dharma, This dharma is not a mind-dharma.

The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, subdued the strongholds of various māras and converted more beings than anyone else; whenever he gained a single disciple, he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber.
The room was eighteen cubits long and twelve cubits wide, filled to capacity. Finally, the elder Xiangzhong arrived, seeking ordination.
The Patriarch asked him, “Do you leave home with your body, or do you leave home with your mind? He replied, “I have come to leave home; it is not for the sake of body or mind.
The Patriarch said, “If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that leaves home? He replied, “As for one who leaves home, there is no self.”
Because of "I," there is no self; because there is no self, the mind neither arises nor ceases. That the mind neither arises nor ceases is the eternal Way. The Buddhas are also eternal.
The mind has no form or appearance, and its essence is likewise so. The Patriarch said: "You shall attain great enlightenment and the mind will naturally be realized.
You should observe the precepts and propagate the Way. Your father dreamed of a golden sun when you were born; you may be named Diṭṭhaka (Tiduojiā). Thus spoke the Tathāgata."
The Great Dharma-eye has been transmitted in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: "The mind is, from the beginning, the original mind;

The original mind is not a dharma that exists. If there were a dharma that existed, there would be an original mind; But since it is neither mind nor a fundamental dharma, [there is nothing to grasp]."
Baotan said: "A thousand people pushing against a door are not equal to one person pulling it open.

One can imagine that the tally of those filling the hall does not even count among the assembly of incense-offering devotees. What the ancients called "realizing the fruit" was as humble as the soil of the great earth;
those who "attained the Way" were as precious as jade from other mountains. This speaks to the fact that those who attain the Way are always few, while those who realize the fruit are many.

The fruits [of the teaching] are indeed abundant. Some may doubt that our ancestors shared the same Buddha-land, considering it as difficult to find even one person as it is to obtain a piece of jade;
yet why is the transmission in the Eastern Land so voluminous and widespread? This is for no other reason than that the capacities of those in the East are superior.
Nevertheless, when viewed from the perspective of its mountains, rivers, and terrain, then Zhendan—

Among those in Jambudvīpa, he was the most eminent. Therefore, Dharmatrāta, clearly perceiving the beginning and end of the teaching, took it upon his single shoulder and traveled ten thousand *li* without delay to arrive here; six generations later, the Dharma began to flourish in full vigor.

Its vastness and profundity have already fallen short of those of antiquity; yet its brilliance surpasses them. The Way is transmitted through vessels, and while the vessels differ according to the times, the Dharma remains as it was.
In later generations, the apertures of worldly passions are daily excavated, and the windows of intellectual views are increasingly opened.
To seek that which is like the single word of the *Gandhahastin* assembly, one must take it as the treasury of the true Dharma-eye.
It cannot be obtained.

When the Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Tīṭibha, arrived in Central India, there were eight thousand great ṛṣis in that country, with Micchaka at their head; leading the multitude, they gazed upon him.
The Ritual Code says: "In the past, we were born together with the same father, Brahmā. I encountered the seer Asita, who bestowed upon me the methods of the immortals;
my teacher met a disciple of the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha), who practiced *dhyāna*. Since then, our lineages have followed divergent paths for six kalpas. The Patriarch said:
"That you have been separated for successive kalpas is indeed no empty boast. Now you may abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox. Mīḍhaka said: "In the past..."
The immortal bestowed upon me this prophecy: "Six kalpas hence, you shall meet a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
Meeting him now, I pray that you grant me ordination. At first, the assembly of immortals gave rise to conceit; [the Master] then displayed his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Thereupon, they both resolved to leave the household life. He then addressed Micchaka, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye to Kāśyapa."
[The transmission] has been passed down through successive generations until it reached me. Now I entrust it to you; let it flow forth naturally. He then spoke this verse:
"The mind that penetrates the fundamental Dharma Has neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; Without mind, there is also no dharma."

When the Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka, arrived in the kingdom of Northern India, he saw auspicious golden clouds above the city battlements and sighed, saying, "This is the breath of a person on the Path;
there must be a Great Being who shall become my Dharma heir. Entering the marketplace, he saw a man holding a vessel of wine in his hand.
He asked in opposition, "From what direction do you come, Master? Where do you intend to go? The Patriarch said, "I come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere.
[The monk] asked, "Do you recognize the object in my hand? The Patriarch said, "This is a vessel for contact that carries purity."
He said, "Master, do you still recognize me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not recognize you. If I were to recognize you, it would not be my true self.

Try calling out your name, and I shall show you your original cause. He spoke a verse, saying: "From immeasurable kalpas until my birth in this land, my original surname was Bharadvāja, and my given name was Vāsukī.
The Patriarch said, "My teacher says that the World-Honored One traveled through Northern India and spoke [this verse]:..."
Ānanda said, "Three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a sage named Vasu-mitra who shall be the seventh patriarch.
He placed his bowl down, paid homage, and stood by the Master’s side; recounting their past karmic causes and receiving a prediction, it accorded with the Master’s own words.

Thereupon, [the Master] granted him tonsure and the full precepts, and addressed him, saying: 'The transmission of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye has come down for a long time; now it is entrusted to you.'"

Do not allow it to be interrupted. The verse says: Where there is no mind, nothing can be attained; what is spoken of cannot be called a dharma. If one realizes that the mind is not the mind, only then does one understand the mind and its mental factors.

The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, arrived at the kingdom of Kāmala and extensively promoted the Buddha’s work. Suddenly, before his Dharma seat, a wise man appeared who declared, "My name is Buddhanandi;
I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "O Benevolent One, if it is a 'debate,' it is not the 'meaning'; if it is the 'meaning,' it is not a 'debate'."

It does not matter. If one were to deliberate upon the meaning of the doctrine, it would ultimately not be a discussion of the true meaning. Nandika realized that his teacher’s meaning was superior, and his mind immediately submitted with reverence.
He said, "I wish to seek the Way and partake of the flavor of the nectar. Thereupon, [the Master] conferred the full precepts upon him. He further told him:

"The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it yourself. He spoke in verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests equality..."
The Dharma of space: when one realizes space, there is neither "is" nor "is not.
Baotan said: "Realization and awakening are two matters. When the mind of birth and death is severed, that is awakening. To revive again after having been severed is realization."
This is realization. Vimalakīrti said: "Nor does one realize by extinguishing sensation; this is realization.
The Dharma-transmission verses are the very lifeblood of all the patriarchs; those who possess the eye of discernment should take them to heart. There is no dharma and no mind.
"Mindless and dharma-less"—in broad outline, this is merely a few words spoken by people who see nothing but withered austerity and thinness, utterly lacking any essential flavor, like chewing wax.

Yet they fail to realize that it is like a thorn hidden within cotton: if one were to throw it directly at one's face, there would be the calamity of having one's chest pierced and one's head shattered.
Apart from this, what could possibly serve as a statement of realization?
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānandi, arrived at the city of Tiqia in the kingdom of Vishaḷā. Seeing a white light ascending from the house of the layman Viśāla, he said to his disciples:
"In this household there shall be a sage who speaks no words and does not travel the four crossroads; he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna.
Having finished speaking, the elder came forth to pay his respects and asked, "What do you require?
The Patriarch said, "I seek an attendant. The elder said, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra; he is already fifty years old and has never spoken or walked. The Patriarch said, "As you say..."
[The Master] said, "Truly my disciple. Maitreya (Mìduō) immediately rose and prostrated, saying: "Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin?
The Buddhas are not my Way; who is the ultimate Way? The Patriarch replied: "That which you speak of is more intimate than the mind."
"Parents cannot be compared [to this]. Your practice accords with the Way; it is identical to the mind of all Buddhas. To seek an external Buddha with form is not like you.
If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate. Having heard this, Maitreya immediately took seven steps, then left the household life and received the full precepts.
He further addressed him, saying: "I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s Eye of the True Dharma."
I entrust this treasury to you; do not let it be severed. A verse says: "Space has neither interior nor exterior; the nature of mind is likewise so.
If one realizes space, one penetrates the principle of True Suchness (tathatā)."
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, arrived in Central India.
There was an elder named Gandhachattra who brought his son to pay homage to the Patriarch and said, "This son remained in the womb for sixty years;
therefore, he is named Duṣprasaha (Difficult to Be Born). He once encountered an immortal who told me that this child is no ordinary person and shall become a Dharma [teacher]."

“Vessel! Now that you have met the Venerable One, I wish for you to leave the household life and change your name to Xié (Pārśva). The Venerable One then shaved his head and conferred the precepts upon him.

A radiant light illuminated his seat, and he was moved by the manifestation of thirty-seven grains of *śarīra* before him. From then on, he practiced with diligence, forgetting all weariness. Subsequently, the Master said to him:
“The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you. You must cherish and protect it. He spoke this verse: “True...”
Principle is fundamentally nameless; it is through names that its principle is revealed. One receives and attains the true Dharma, which is neither real nor false.

The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Yakṣa, arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra and rested beneath a tree. Pointing to the ground with his right hand, he said to the assembly, "This ground shall turn into gold."
"The World-Honored One shall have a sage enter this assembly. As soon as he finished speaking, the ground turned the color of gold.

A householder named Pūrṇayaśas stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Yaśas replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The Patriarch asked, "Where do you dwell?
He replied, "My mind does not abide anywhere. The Patriarch asked, "Are you then not settled? He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise so. The Patriarch [said], "..."
[The Master] said: "Are you not the Buddhas? [He] replied: "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]. The Patriarch spoke a verse, saying: "This ground turns to the color of gold;
Foreknowing the arrival of the Sage, He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, And having perfected the Awakening Flower. Śāṇakavāsin also spoke a verse, saying:
"The Teacher sits upon the golden ground, Constantly expounding the meaning of reality. Turning his light back to illuminate me, Causing me to enter samādhi. The Patriarch...
He immediately conferred the full precepts upon him and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you.

Contemplate it well. He spoke in verse: "The true essence is naturally true; Based on this truth, there is a principle to be explained. Having realized the dharma of true truth, There is neither practice nor cessation."
Baotan said: "To sit for fifty years without stepping down or speaking, neither sleeping nor waking—this I know might still be possible within the realm of indistinct, inarticulate sounds.
But as for leaping down from the meditation seat, walking seven paces east and west, and letting out a great lion’s roar—that is something impossible to achieve. Such was the Elder Śākyamuni."
Now, this second person has resided in the womb for sixty years.
I know that he takes the Dharma as his body, emptiness as his seat, patience as his palace, loving-kindness as his father, compassion as his mother, conduct as his companion, and vows as his birth.
Even within the womb of Māyā, it was nothing more than this. To speak otherwise would be called "stalling. Thus it was said in ancient times.
People must recognize this person; he possesses his own orthodox Dharma-eye.
When the eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Punyayasas, arrived at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa came forward to meet him and asked: "I wish to know the Buddha. What..."
“This is it. The Patriarch said, “If you wish to recognize the Buddha, that which you do not recognize is he. He asked, “Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know that this is him?
The Patriarch said, “Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know that this is not him? The other said, “This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, “It is.”
"That is the meaning of 'wood' (dāru)," [the Master] said. "What is the meaning of 'saw' (krakaca)? [Mātr̥ceṭa] asked. "It is to come forth together with the Master," he replied.

"What is the meaning of 'wood'? [Mātr̥ceṭa] asked. "You have been cut by me," the Master said. At these words, Mātr̥ceṭa attained sudden enlightenment. He prostrated himself and requested ordination, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata gave this prophecy:
'Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a worthy one named Mātr̥ceṭa in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who shall destroy...'"
He subdued heterodox paths and delivered immeasurable people. To continue and transmit my transformation, now is precisely the time; I must entrust the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury to you.
He then spoke this verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; Brightness and darkness are never separate from one another.
Now I entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation; It is neither one, nor is it two."

The Twelfth Patriarch, Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma. An old man fell to the ground; the Patriarch said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person;
he shall manifest extraordinary signs. As soon as he had finished speaking, the man vanished and reappeared from the earth as a golden figure, who then transformed once more.
He recited verses for the noble one in the guise of a young woman; he then transformed into a golden dragon, manifesting his majestic spiritual power;

and he further transformed into a tiny insect, hiding beneath the seat to steal the Dharma. The Noble One subdued each of these manifestations one by one. They then returned to their original forms and apologized.
The Patriarch asked, "What is your name? How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is Kambala. My followers..."

[The monk] replied, "It is extremely vast. The Patriarch asked, "How would you transform it through the full extent of your supernatural powers? He replied, "I could transform a great ocean; that would be a very small matter.
The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*)? He replied, "What is meant by the 'ocean of nature'? I have never known it.

The Patriarch then explained the ocean of nature for him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it; the three samādhis and the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are all manifested from it."
Upon his appearance, he heard that [Nanyue] was seeking ordination together with his followers. The Patriarch summoned five hundred arhats to bestow full precepts upon him.
He further addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to my verse: 'Veiling and manifesting are the fundamental Dharma;
Brightness and darkness are originally not two. Now I entrust to you the Dharma of realization, Neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned.'"
The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, arrived at Western India.
Prince Meghasvabhāva welcomed him to a stone cave. After traveling several *li*, they encountered a great python coiling around his body;
[the patriarch] conferred the Three Refuges upon it, and it departed. As they were about to reach the cave, there was an old man who had previously been that very python.
Having prostrated before him in thanks, he asked, "Are there any other people on this mountain? He replied, "Ten *li* away, there is a tree that provides shade for five hundred great dragons;
the king of those trees is named Nāgārjuna. He constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of dragons.

When the Patriarch arrived, the King of Trees came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is desolate and solitary, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons. Great Virtue, you who are most honored, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet here? The Patriarch—

The Master said, "I am not a sovereign; I have come to visit a worthy one. The other thought silently to himself, "Has this teacher not received the secret instructions, perfected his nature, and clarified the eye of the Way?
Is he not a Great Sage who continues the True Vehicle? The Patriarch said, "Though you speak with your mind, I know it with my own."
"Simply prepare for renunciation; why worry about not becoming a sage? Upon hearing this instruction, he expressed his gratitude and, together with five hundred followers, received full ordination.
The Master further told him: "I now entrust the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury to you. You must protect and cherish it yourself. He spoke in verse: "The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest;
It is said that one attains the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). One who awakens to this hidden and manifest Dharma Is no longer a fool."
Nor is it wisdom. The Fourteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Nāgārjuna, arrived in South India.
The people of that country mostly believed in the efficacy of meritorious deeds and did not believe in Buddha-nature. Thereupon, from his seat—
He manifested a body of sovereign mastery like the full moon disk; the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and did not perceive the physical form of the Teacher.
Among that assembly was an elder named Kanadeva, who asked the crowd, "Do you recognize this sign? They all replied, "We have never seen such a sight before; how could we discern it?
Kanadeva said, "The Venerable One has manifested the essential nature of a Buddha to show us. [They asked,] "How do you know this?"
Because the form of the signless samādhi is like the full moon, and the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.

Having finished speaking, the wheel-mark vanished and he returned to his original seat. He spoke a verse, saying: "The body manifests the form of the full moon to represent the essence of all Buddhas;
the preaching of Dharma has no fixed shape, used to discern that which is neither sound nor form. Upon hearing this, the assembly suddenly attained the realization of non-arising. All...
He sought full ordination. Previously, there were over five thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths who practiced great magical arts and all revered their ancestral traditions;

he immediately transformed them and led them back to the orthodox path. He composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, which he bequeathed to the world.
He then addressed the chief attendant, Kāṇadeva, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you. He spoke in verse:
"To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, I have now explained the logic of liberation. Regarding these dharmas, the mind finds no realization; there is neither anger nor joy."
Baotán said: "Aśvaghoṣa composed the Mahāyāna-śāstra based on one hundred lakṣas [of verses], which Nāgārjuna then commented upon.
Furthermore, he composed various treatises such as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra to bequeath them to the world. How wondrous and profound they are!"
To carry a red banner and drag one’s *saṃghāṭī* robe while entering among the hosts of Māra and non-Buddhists—how grand and unrestrained this is!
That a single person could act so differently at different times: is there perhaps a subtle mystery within the grand and unrestrained, or is there grand unrestraint within the subtle mystery?
Such is the nature of the Dharma. The Mahāyāna is the medicine for treating the mental illnesses of sentient beings.
Those who have lost their minds, upon seeing this, fall into a state of frantic delusion.
Some even slander the Patriarchs, claiming they did not transcend the net of the scriptural teachings; such madness is beyond redemption.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kanadeva, cast a needle into the water of a bowl as a sign to awaken the potential of Nāgārjuna; at that moment, the form of a lunar disc appeared.

The Patriarch took this to signify the manifestation of the Buddha’s essential nature, representing that the teaching of the Dharma transcends both sound and form. Having done so, he arrived in the kingdom of Viḷāsa, where there was an elder named Brahma...
Vimalatejas then sent his second son, Rāhulabhadra, to enter the monastic order as an attendant.

Upon reaching the city of Śrāvastī, he heard that various non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas) had long intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma. Thereupon, holding a tall banner, he went into the midst of the non-Buddhist assembly and refuted them with unimpeded eloquence;
consequently, they were converted and submitted. He then addressed the leader Rāhulabhadra, saying: "The True Dharma..."
I entrust this Eye-Casket to you. Listen to my verse: "For the sake of one who transmits the Dharma, I have explained the principle of liberation;
yet in reality, there is no realization of the Dharma—neither end nor beginning."
Baotan said: "The śrāvaka perceives the nature as one sees the moon at night; the bodhisattva perceives the nature as one sees the sun by day.
He further said: "The bodhisattva sees the Buddha-nature with his eyes; alas, sentient beings are unable to see it."
When Nāgārjuna manifested the form of a lunar disc, the Venerable One regarded it as the manifestation of the Buddha’s essential nature;
this too was the Venerable One’s own vision. As the saying goes: "The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom."
It is like a person who speaks of fire all day long without ever burning their own mouth. Nevertheless, as benefit and harm are so pressing in these末代 (final) times, one cannot help but discern them.
I fear that those of a certain class who are muddled and agitated may find themselves unable to overcome their habitual tendencies.
Thus, one gives rise to the perception of a lunar disc, regarding it as a place of cool refreshment and rest;

yet fearing that those who are like withered wood or cold ashes might have no use for such perception, one then gives rise to the mental image of a lunar disc, regarding it as a source from which radiance emanates.
Both are brought about by deluded conceptualization. This is illustrated by the story of Mazu and his three disciples gazing at the moon.
Changsha and Yangshan were observing the moon. Their mutual recognition was like that of ancient sages who, like those who pursue foul odors, do not loathe what they loathe.
Furthermore, they produced such phrases as "the clouds disperse, the sky widens, and the moon emerges from the coral," taking them as definitive pointers.
This deceives and misleads students, causing them to fall into great darkness; with a single snap of the fingers, one's entire life is cast away.
This is a perverse path. In recent times, those of this kind are still numerous; therefore, I, a fool, cannot remain silent.

When the Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, arrived at the city of Śrāvastī, he saw Saṃghanandin sitting in meditative absorption. He waited for him to emerge from samādhi and then questioned him.

[The Master] asked: "Is your body concentrated, or is your mind concentrated? He replied: "Both my body and my mind are concentrated. The Patriarch said: "If both body and mind are concentrated, how can there be entering and exiting [of breath]? He replied:
"Although there is entering and exiting, it does not lose the characteristic of concentration. It is like gold in a well; the essence of the gold remains eternally still."

The Patriarch said: "If the gold is in the well, or if the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself has neither motion nor stillness; how can there be coming and going? [The monk] said: "If you speak of the motion and stillness of the gold, what thing is it that comes and goes?
Granting that the gold comes and goes, the gold itself is not motion or stillness. The Patriarch said: "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that has come out?
If the gold has come out of the well, what is the thing that remains in the well? [The monk] said: "If the gold has come out of the well, then that which remains in the well is [the gold]."

"It is not gold. If gold were in the well, then that which emerges would not be the object. The Patriarch said, "This interpretation is not correct. [The monk] said, "That interpretation is not established.

The Patriarch said, "This interpretation must fall away. [The monk] said, "That interpretation is not established. The Patriarch said, "Since that interpretation is not established, my interpretation is established.
[The monk] said, "Although my interpretation is established, the Dharma is not mine. The Patriarch said, "My interpretation is already established; I have no self."
"Therefore, it is said: 'Because I am without self. What further meaning does this establish? The Patriarch said, "Because I am without self, your own position is thereby established.
The Master asked, "In which sage did you find your teacher? From whom did you obtain this realization of non-self? The Patriarch replied, "My teacher was Kāṇadeva; from him I realized this non-self.
The Master said, "I prostrate to Teacher Kāṇadeva, who has emerged through you. Since you, O Master, are without self, I—"

Therefore, when he was about to take Sanghanandi as his teacher, the Patriarch said: "Since I have realized non-self, you must perceive my self. If you take me as your teacher, you will know that my self is not a self.
At these words, Nandika’s mind became suddenly clear and expansive. Thereupon, [the Patriarch] charged Sanghanandi with the Dharma-eye, saying in verse:
"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; Neither grasping nor abandoning. The Dharma has neither the mark of existence nor non-existence."
"How do the internal and external arise?
Baotan replied: "Observe how the two masters engage in question and answer, each reaching the ultimate limit. It is like fish swimming in the river and birds soaring in the clouds.
Whether entering or exiting, moving or still, beginning or end, it is all but a single word. Can it ever be exhausted by thought? (Quotation ends).
One reaches the realm of the inconceivable, where even the inconceivable is exhausted. At the point of exhaustion, nothing remains established;
only then is the Buddha-way truly accomplished. One is then separated from the Patriarch-Teacher by but a single interval.
The ultimate principle is as clear as this, yet those who are ignorant still harbor doubts. Wait for my arm to bend and extend but once—the Buddhas of antiquity have already passed away.
It has been a long time.

When the seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, a cool breeze suddenly swept over the people. The assembly felt an extraordinary sense of joy and contentment, yet they did not know its cause.
This was indeed so. He said to the assembly, "The wind of this Way and its Virtue shall surely have a sage to succeed to the ancestral seat.
As soon as he had finished speaking, a young boy carrying a round mirror appeared before him from the mountain hut. The Master asked him, "How old are you? The boy replied, "One hundred years."
The Patriarch said, “You are still young; why do you speak of a hundred years? He replied, “I do not understand principle; I am exactly a hundred years old.

The Patriarch asked, “Are you skilled in the pivot? He replied, “The Buddha said: ‘If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the pivot of the Buddhas, it would be better to live for a single day and attain decisive realization. The Patriarch asked, “What does that which is in your hand represent? He replied, “All [dharmas].”
The Buddha is the great perfect mirror; without flaw or obscuration within or without, two people may see it together, for their mind-eyes are alike.

He immediately left the household life and received the precepts, being named Kāśyapa. One day, as the wind blew against the copper bells at the corner of the hall, the Patriarch asked, "Is it the bell that rings, or is it the wind?
He replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bell that rings; it is my own heart that rings. The Patriarch said, "And what of the heart?"
"Who is it? [The Master asked]. "Because both are equally tranquil," [the disciple replied]. The Patriarch said, "Excellent! If it were not for you, who else could succeed to my Way?
He then transmitted the Dharma to him, saying in verse: "The ground of the mind is originally without birth; The ground arises from conditions. Condition and seed do not obstruct one another;
Flower and fruit are likewise so."
Baotán said: "The wind-bells were the vision of a novice; the wind and the banner were the device of an elder master.
As for the mind, who is it? It is because both are utterly still. This single phrase strikes to the very marrow of the Patriarchs.

Even if one were to cause the two monks of the wind and the banner to attain realization beneath these words, they would not necessarily possess the marks of such great men. For the most part, this is what was realized."
The more expansive the scope, the clearer the words; when what is seen is flickering and chaotic, the explanation becomes muddled and indistinct.
This is like the difference between a clear blue sky and the sun versus clouds, fog, and a dark moon: the difficulty or ease of the path is inherently not hard to discern.
Yet, many scholars enter the treacherous while remaining ignorant of the easy; this is a common human failing. However, from—
From Dajian Huineng, the lineage was transmitted once to Nanyue and Qingyuan; it was transmitted a second time to Shitou and Mazu, both of whom adhered to the principle of simplicity and ease.
When it reached the five schools, which split apart like the constellations, they employed both the difficult and the easy methods.

In later generations, there was an increasing tendency toward profundity and severity, like those who manipulate texts and distort the law, causing the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to sink day by day.
Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who, in their honest deliberations, have mistakenly taken the meaning of "simplicity" (pingyi) to imply "ease" (pangyi).
Therefore, I have repeatedly engaged in debate and analysis to correct this misrepresentation. As the saying goes: "A deviation of a hair's breadth leads to an error of a thousand li."
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, led his disciples to the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna).
Upon seeing a certain atmosphere emanating from a Brahmin’s house, he was about to enter it when the householder Kumāralāta asked, "Who are these followers?
The patriarch replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. When he heard the name of the Buddha, [he was moved].

His spirit was struck with awe, and he immediately closed his door. After a long while, the Patriarch knocked on the door. Luoduo said, "There is no one in this house. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that answers 'no'?
Upon hearing these words, he realized the visitor was an extraordinary person; he then opened the bolt and invited him inside. The Patriarch said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy:
'A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mozhī (Yuezhi) to succeed [the Dharma]...'"

He flourished the profound transformation. Now you have encountered me; you should respond to this auspicious fortune. Rāhula developed the wisdom of his past lives, left the household life, and received full ordination.
The verse of entrustment says: "Where there is a seed and the ground of the mind, causes and conditions can cause it to sprout. When these conditions do not obstruct one another,"
When arising arises, there is no arising.
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, traveled to the kingdom of Central India. There was a Mahāsattva named Jayanta who asked: "In my family, my parents have always..."
He placed his faith in the Triple Gem, yet he was constantly afflicted by illness; his endeavors were unsuccessful.

His neighbor had long practiced the ways of a *caṇḍāla*, yet his body remained ever vigorous and healthy, and whatever he undertook met with success. "How can he be so fortunate while I am so solitary? he wondered. The Master said, "Why should you doubt this?
Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil has its presiding authority. When ordinary people see the benevolent die young and the violent live long, or the rebellious meet with good fortune,"
"This principle is ominous; it would mean that cause and effect perish and merit and retribution are empty.

Little do you realize that shadow and echo follow one another, with not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy, and that this remains undiminished even after thousands of millions of kalpas. Upon hearing these words, Jayata was suddenly relieved of his doubts. The Patriarch said:

Although you have already placed faith in the three types of karma, you have not yet clearly understood that karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*), delusion exists because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*), and non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*).
The mind is fundamentally pure; it is without birth or extinction, without creation or action, and without retribution.
There is no victory or defeat; it is utterly tranquil and profoundly luminous. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas.
All that is good or evil, conditioned or unconditioned, is like an illusion or a dream. Having heard this, Śāṇakavāsin awakened his latent wisdom and spoke this verse of entrustment:
"In the ultimate nature, there is originally no arising; It is spoken only to counter those who seek [a self]. Since within the Dharma there is nothing..."
"Yes, I have attained it. "What do you mean by 'decided' or 'not decided'? The Patriarch spoke again: "This is the phrase of the Tathāgata Sublime Sound regarding the purity of seeing one's nature.
You should propagate it."
Baotan said: "Śāṇakavāsin’s wisdom was vast and profound. How could he not have known that the retribution for good and evil follows one like a shadow follows a form?
However, within this process there are distinctions of degree and sequence—matters that ordinary people must understand.
The Bodhisattva posed these questions to resolve his doubts, and the Venerable One analyzed them with such clarity that they were manifest from branch to root."
From the leaves back to the roots, and from sentient beings up to the Buddhas, it does not exceed a few words.

Yet, within these words lies the matter of the transmission of the Dharma-eye. Having spoken the verse, he said: "These are the words of the Tathāgata Subhūṣaṇasvara regarding the purity of seeing one's nature.
How could I intentionally leak this secret cause? You should know that the Patriarchs never utter idle words."

The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the teachings of the sudden school (*tun-jiao*). There was a scholar named Śubhavyūha, also known as Sarvagāmin.

He always ate only one meal a day and did not lie down to sleep; he prostrated before the Buddha six times each day. The Patriarch asked the assembly, "Can the dhūta ascetic practices and the brahmacarya lead one to Buddhahood?

They replied, "Through diligent effort, one can attain it. The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he undergoes ascetic practices for kalpas, they are all rooted in falsehood.
The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct does the Venerable One possess that you should disparage our teacher? The Patriarch said:
I do not seek the Way, yet I am not deluded. I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, yet I do not eat at improper times. I am not contented, yet I have no covetous desires.
"A mind that has no expectations is called the Way. Having heard this, Bianxing gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and recollected events from seven *kalpas* ago.

He then made a vow, seeking the wondrous Way, and requested: "Please grant me instruction. The Patriarch said: "You have long planted the roots of virtue; you shall succeed to my lineage. And he spoke in verse:
"When words fall away, one accords with the non-arising [of phenomena], Identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If one can understand it thus, One will penetrate all phenomena."
The principle is concluded.
Baotan said: "I do not seek the Way, nor am I inverted; even to my lack of contentment, I do not harbor greedy desires.
By this, one may see that our Master is truly majestic. Only after one has definitively attained wisdom and realization can one [truly understand him]."
To discuss this with you: it is not so. Otherwise, it would be like a drunkard who, when supported on the east side, leans to the west;

when raised from the west, he falls to the east. Seeking the Way and knowing contentment are two extremes. Some abandon these two extremes and grasp at the "Middle," claiming thereby that they have attained it.
This is just like someone running away from their shadow while walking in the midday sun—the more they run, the more the phantom grows. Such is the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

In the absence of a self, there are no two extremes. Nor is there anything gained or not gained. Simply remain in a state of equanimity and vast openness, polishing yourself through the years and months;
then the solid fortress of birth and death will collapse of its own accord without being attacked. The World-Honored One said: "O Bhikṣus, practicing the Way is like the method of tuning a lute.
If the strings are too tight, the sound is cut off; if the strings are too loose, there is no sound. The Venerable One likewise [said].
He taught his disciples in this manner; there was certainly a reason for it. Thus, the world has the saying that the worldly conditions are like sparks from stone or flashes of lightning.
Did my late master not know this? He said, "If one establishes a standard based on frugality, its corruption will still lead to greed;
if one establishes a standard based on greed, what will the subsequent corruption be like? Was this not a profound concern for the degenerate age?
The twenty-first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, traveled from Rājagṛha to the kingdom of Nādikā. The king there was named Nitya-vaśavartin. He had two sons:
the elder was named Mahāla, and the younger was named Maṇḍala. They asked the patriarch, "How does the climate and customs of Rājagṛha differ from those here?"
The Patriarch said, "In that land, three Buddhas have appeared in the world, and two masters have traveled there to transform beings. The King asked, "Who are these two masters?
The Patriarch replied, "The Buddha prophesied that five hundred years after his passing, a Great Being endowed with supernormal powers would leave the household life to succeed to the holy position;
this is none other than your second son, Maṇḍara. Although my virtue is meager, I dare to take on one of those roles. The King said, "It is truly as you say."
The Venerable One said, "Renounce your second son to become a śramaṇa. The Patriarch replied, "Excellent! Your Majesty is able to follow the Buddha’s intent.
He immediately conferred full ordination upon him and transmitted the Dharma verse, saying: "Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded; why do you not realize this?
To penetrate the Dharma within it—neither now nor of old."
The twenty-second patriarch, the Venerable Maṇḍara, arrived in Western India.
The king there was named Deva; he remarked, "A Most Holy One is difficult to encounter, yet worldly pleasures are not enduring.
He immediately passed the throne to his crown prince, entered the monastic order under the Patriarch, and in seven days realized the fruit of the Fourth Path. The Patriarch comforted him deeply.
Huì said, "In order to deliver people here, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the bhikṣu Helena in the kingdom of Mozhī, saying:
'You are there in that land teaching the flock of cranes; as you are about to realize the fruit of the Way, you should know this for yourself.
When he saw the extraordinary fragrance forming into tassels, he knew his teacher had arrived. The king and Helena made offerings to him and asked: 'By what conditions have I come to this?'"
A flock of cranes followed him in response. The Patriarch said, "In the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu who attended an assembly at the Dragon Palace.
Your disciples wished to follow you, but you observed that none among them were fit to partake in that sublime offering.

The disciples said, "The Master taught that those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma. Now, since this is not the case, what holiness can there be? Thereupon, he caused them all to go together.

He went to the assembly. Because his merit was meager, he had been born among the feathered tribes (birds). Moved by your kindness, he has come to follow you. He said, "I pray that the Venerable One will use skillful means to deliver me.
The Patriarch said, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure; I now entrust it to you. You shall transform beings yourself until the end of time.
He spoke a verse: "The mind turns according to the myriad objects; In the place where it turns, there is profound mystery. If you recognize it as it follows the current..."
"By nature, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
Baotan said: "Since the seal was cast at Vulture Peak and bestowed upon Kāśyapa, it has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, never daring to be shown lightly to others.
This seal is like a linked chain; it is seen only occasionally in the land deeds and contracts of one's ancestors."

Reaching this state, the seal extends to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, reaching as far as the Floating Banner King Realm (*Sumeru-rāja-loka-dhātu*) without leaving a single fragment behind.
Though the myriad phenomena are subtle and minute, this seal is not large; though empty space is vast and expansive, this seal is not small. It transcends the Buddhas and patriarchs.
Applying it sideways or upside down, insights emerge one after another; throughout antiquity and the present, there has been but one such person. How great is this Seal!
From Kāśyapa to the Sixth Patriarch in China, there have been thirty-three transmissions in total, comprising thirty-three verses.

Verse after verse, they were entrusted to one another so that their transmission was never lost. Every person has, from the beginning, clarified this for themselves to seal their own original mind, like ascending a pagoda, stepping higher and higher with each step.
Therefore, I have manifested its essential meaning both before and after, so that you may know that dharmas have no fixed nature;
they are like a pearl on a plate or a ball on a slope—how could they leave behind any shadow?
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hakkana, arrived in Central India.
Because his disciple Longzi (Nāgaputra) had died young, he had an elder brother named Shizi (Siṃha), who was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory.
He served a Brahmin. When his teacher had passed away and his younger brother had also died, he returned to the Venerable One and asked, "I wish to seek the Way;
how should I apply my mind? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, do not apply your mind.
He asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the work of a Buddha? The Patriarch said, "If you have any application, it is not merit. If you have no doing..."
"This is itself the work of the Buddha. As the sutra says: "The merit I have performed is free from the notion of 'mine'.

Having heard this, Śiṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha. At that moment, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked him, "What kind of phenomenon is that? Śiṃha replied:
I saw a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth; furthermore, there were five paths of black vapor crossing horizontally across its midst.

The Patriarch asked, "What is the omen of this? He replied, "It cannot be known. The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India that will afflict you.
Once I have passed away, I now [entrust] the Eye of the True Dharma..."
I entrust this treasury to you; guard and uphold it well. The verse says: When one recognizes the nature of mind, it may be called inconceivable;
yet when it is clearly realized, there is nothing to be attained, and at the moment of attainment, one does not speak of "knowing."
The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃha, arrived in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

He refuted the five schools: the attachment to signs, the abandonment of signs, the view of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the view of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and the school of non-speaking.
Now, seeing that you, O Benevolent One, belong to the class of those who do not possess the jewel, he encountered an elder who led forth his son and asked: "As for this child..."
His name was Sita. As soon as he was born, his left hand remained in a fist. His grandfather looked at him and said, "Give me back my pearl.
The boy suddenly opened his hand and presented the pearl. Everyone was struck with wonder. The grandfather said, "In my previous life, I was a monk who went to the Western Sea to make offerings."
"The pearl I bestowed upon you as an offering must now be returned to me; this is but natural. The King, due to their prior connection, granted him permission to leave the household life.

The Patriarch said, "My Master prophesied that I would encounter hardship before long. I shall now transmit to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the *saṃghāṭī* robe, so that they may universally benefit all future generations.
He spoke in verse: "When the true teaching of knowledge and vision is realized, knowledge and vision are themselves..."
As for this mind, one should know and see it as it arises; that knowing and seeing is right here and now. Having finished speaking, he was sent to travel and transform others in other lands.
Because his departure would have been difficult to avoid, the Patriarch remained in Kaśmīra. At that time, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners in the country: one was Māmuta.
Second was Duoluoche (Droṇa), who, wishing to cause a disturbance through illusory arts, donned monastic robes and secretly entered the royal palace. He plotted, saying:
"If this matter fails, the guilt shall fall upon the Buddha. Since the sorcery was committed by him, the calamity shall follow in his wake. When the plot failed, the King was enraged.
When he had finished destroying the monastery, he took up his sword before the Master and said, "Have you realized the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied, "I have realized them.
He asked, "Are you free from birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I am free. He said, "Since you are free from birth and death, you may give me your head. The Patriarch said:
"The body is not mine; why begrudge my head? The King brandished his sword and severed Nandīśvara’s head. White milk surged forth several fathoms high, and the King’s arm fell off of its own accord.
Baotan said: "Calamities and hardships are truly the bellows of those who possess the Way. By the wind-power of their great vows, they are stirred into life."

A dead furnace boils and surges with inauspicious gold; yet by remaining still, it causes calamity to dissolve before it has sprouted, and by acting, it brings peace to calamity once it has arrived—only our Honored One, the Lion, is without reproach.
While he was still on the stage of a student, he questioned his teacher regarding the baleful vapor of a white rainbow, and he lingered long as if dwelling in a state of detached composure.

In his native land, he feared only being late; yet when he encountered the cruel flames of the heretics and obtained the *maṇi* jewel, he pressed it to his head and sealed his heart as if in the urgency of treading through water or fire. Having fulfilled the affairs of his father, he then lingered and met his death.
That even in later generations there are still those who slander and wound him—how tragic! [Written by] the monk Shenqing of Beishan in the Tang Dynasty.
In his writings, he disparaged [the lineage], stating that those who followed Śāṇavāsa were all collateral branches and not the orthodox transmission.

A monk of the Yong’an Monastery during the present dynasty, Qisong, loathed these words; he composed the *Dingzutú* (Chart for Determining the Patriarchs) and the *Chuánfǎzhèngzōngjì* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma) and submitted them to the throne.
Emperor Renzong issued an imperial decree for its inclusion in the Tripitaka; thus, the encounter with the Buddha-dharma reached a most flourishing state.

Now that this definitive treatise has been established, I, though ignorant, still have something to say. The Venerable One’s verse states: "When right speech and knowledge-vision arise, knowledge-vision is itself the mind.
When the mind is present, it is knowledge-vision; knowledge-vision is right here and now. This very gāthā is naturally [profound].
Having verified that both head and tail are correct, how could the principles of Bodhidharma and Daosheng be anything less than as vastly different as heaven and abyss?
Thus spoke the twenty-fifth patriarch, the Venerable Vasubandhu.
The Patriarch arrived in Central India, where the king was named Buddhajaya. He paid him profound respect, while the heretic Anātman-gaurava (Wuwozun) was ill.
The Patriarch went to seek a debate on doctrine but did not prevail. Furthermore, before the king, the heretic said to the Patriarch, "I understand the discourse of silence;

it does not require verbal expression. The Patriarch asked, "Who shall determine victory and defeat? He replied, "We do not contend over victory or defeat; we merely seek the meaning. The Patriarch said:
"What do you take to be the meaning? he asked. He replied, "The absence of mind (*acitta*) is the meaning. The Master said, "Since you have no mind, how can you obtain the meaning?
He replied, "When I speak of the absence of mind, it should be called the 'non-meaning' (*anartha*). The Patriarch said, "You say that the absence of mind should be called the non-meaning;

I say that the non-mind (*acitta*) is the meaning and not the name. He asked, "If it is the meaning and not the name, who is able to discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "Your name is not [the meaning]."
"What is the name for this 'meaning'? he asked. [The Master] replied, "To distinguish what is not meaning is called 'namelessness.

He asked again, "If names are already not names and meanings are also not meanings, who is it that distinguishes, and what is there to be distinguished? Thus they exchanged questions and answers fifty-nine times.
The non-Buddhist was silenced and submitted with faith. The Patriarch suddenly turned to face north, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying, "My teacher, the Honored One Siṃha."
Meeting with such hardship today is truly lamentable. Taking his leave of the king, he traveled south to the Heavenly Mountains (*Nanten*), where he lived in seclusion within the mountain valleys.

The king of that land was named Tiande (*Tian-de*). His second son was gentle and mild-mannered, yet had suffered from illness since childhood. The Patriarch explained the principles of cause and effect (*yin-guo*) for him, and the king immediately resolved his doubts.

A master of incantations (*zhoushu-shi*) harbored malice toward the Patriarch; he secretly placed [poisonous] medicine and food within [the offerings], but the Patriarch, knowing this, consumed it intentionally. Consequently, the sorcerer himself was the one who suffered the retribution.

Huò (Huo). He entered the monastic order under Nanzhu. Six years later, Crown Prince De-shèng ascended the throne; however, he again placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas), which brought calamity upon Nanzhu.
When Crown Prince Bùrúmìduō (Bhṛkuṭī) offered counsel and was imprisoned, he questioned Nanzhu, saying: "In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive teachings have long been absent.
What school is it that you, Master, profess? Nanzhu replied: "In Your Majesty’s kingdom, there has indeed been no false dharma since ancient times. That which I have attained—"
"Thus, the Dharma Seal was personally transmitted from the Great Being Drāhyaka (Yinguang) through twenty-four successive generations down to the Venerable Siṃha, who then transmitted it to me.
The King said, "If the Bhikṣu Siṃha could not escape execution, how could he have transmitted the Dharma to future generations?"

He said, "When my teacher’s life was still in peril, he secretly entrusted me with the robe and the dharma-verse. When the King sought them out to burn them, the firewood was consumed while they remained as before.

The King repented and apologized, paying his respects by saying, 'Since it is now clear that you, Lion, are the true successor, I hereby pardon the Crown Prince and permit him to leave the household life.'"
The Patriarch asked, "What should you do? He replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not engage in any other affairs.

The Patriarch asked, "What affairs will you not engage in? He replied, "I shall not engage in worldly affairs. The Patriarch asked, "What affairs should you engage in? He replied, "I should engage in the Buddha's work (*buddhakārya*).

The Patriarch said, "Since the Crown Prince and the various sages have manifested their traces here, you may now receive full ordination. He then bestowed upon him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma: "The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision; In the objective realm, there is nothing [to be seen]."
"This is right; this is wrong. I have now awakened to the true nature: there is neither the Way nor principle. Maitreya asked again, "Should the Dharma robe be transmitted?
The Patriarch said, "This robe was for the sake of difficulty; it was used as a provisional means of verification. Your person is free from such difficulties, so the robe is unnecessary.
Transform those throughout the ten directions, and people will naturally have faith and turn toward you."
Baotan said: "From this point on, the hardships of the Buddha-dharma shall cease; from this point on, the robe of faith of the Patriarchs shall be transmitted.

Since the transmission between master and disciple was so clear, and since Central India and Southern India were so close, yet there were still those who harbored doubts at that time—were it not for the spiritual efficacy of Prajñā and the radiant light of the robe of faith, how could there be such excellence today?"
Alas! When I, a fool, observe the hardships and perils endured by the Patriarchs, for whose sake were these truly undertaken?
