Yet later generations fail to reflect upon this, boldly indulging in self-deception without a hair’s breadth of true understanding; they take such experiences as final proof and treat the Buddhas and Patriarchs as rare commodities to be sold to the age.
Beginners and those newly entering the path point to them as their own teachers, failing to realize that such actions are utterly inappropriate.
"In the time of my ancestors, what could have been hoped for? The former Buddhas denounced them as people of overweening pride;
I did not expect to witness this with my own eyes."—Thus spoke the twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Amṛtodana.
When the Patriarch arrived in Eastern India, the king and the non-Buddhist elder, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha, both beheld a white vapor piercing the heavens.
The king asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Brahmin, ignorant of the truth, replied to the king, "It is a sign that Māra is approaching.

He then consulted his followers, saying, "The Upatiṣya (Maitreya) is about to enter the capital; who among us can defeat him? His followers said, "Each of us possesses incantations capable of shaking heaven and earth."
"Entering fire or water—what cause for concern? When the Patriarch arrived, he saw black vapors rising from the palace walls and remarked, "This is but a minor obstacle.
He proceeded directly before the King. The King asked, "Master, why have you come? He replied, "To deliver sentient beings. The King asked, "By what method do you deliver them?

He replied, "I deliver each according to their kind. The Brahmin grew enraged and conjured a great mountain atop the Patriarch’s head. The Patriarch immediately pointed at the mountain, which was then transferred back onto the Brahmin’s own head. Thereupon...
He surrendered himself. The Patriarch, pitying his ignorance and delusion, pointed him out to transform him and preached the Dharma for him.

As the Patriarch was leaving with the King in the same carriage, he suddenly saw a youth adorned with necklaces who had no family name or surname. The youth bowed his head before him. The Patriarch asked, "Do you remember past events?
He replied, "I recall that in a distant kalpa, I lived together with you, Master. You expounded the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and I turned [the wheel of] the profound..."
This profound *sūtra*—the events of today are surely in accord with past causes. The Patriarch said to the King:
"This youth is no other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. This sage will later produce two individuals:
one shall transform South India, and the other’s karmic conditions lie in China. Thus, on account of these past causes, he is named Prajñātāra. I, now—"
I entrust to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. A verse says: The treasury of the mind-ground of true nature has neither head nor tail;
responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called "wisdom."
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, arrived in South India.
There he encountered King Ghandhāra, whose veneration and magnanimity were beyond compare; the king bestowed upon him a priceless jewel.
The king had three sons, the youngest of whom was a bodhisattva. Desiring to test what [the prince] had attained, the patriarch asked about the gift of the jewel.
The three princes asked, "Is there anything more excellent than this, O Perfectly Enlightened One? They all replied, "Among treasures, nothing surpasses it.
[The King said,] "Were it not for the power of the Venerable One’s Way, who could have received it? The youngest prince, the Bodhisattva Bodhidharma, said, "This is but a worldly treasure;
it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. This is but a worldly light; it is not sufficient..."
Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme. This worldly illumination is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all forms of clarity, the clarity of the mind is supreme.
This radiance of the jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must depend upon the light of wisdom to be discerned.
Once it has been discerned, one knows it to be a jewel. Once it is known to be a jewel, its preciousness is clarified. If one clarifies it...
The baby does not possess the treasure by itself; if one examines the pearl, the pearl does not possess the treasure by itself.

Since the pearl does not possess the treasure by itself, it must rely upon the treasure of wisdom to clarify the treasure of the Dharma. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, his treasure immediately manifests.

It is the same for sentient beings: when they possess the treasure of the mind of the Way, it likewise appears. The Patriarch asked: "Among all things, what thing is without form? He replied: "Among all things, that which is not..."
He gave rise to the signless. Again he asked: "Among all things, which is the highest? He replied: "Among all things, the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) is the highest.
He asked: "Among all things, which is the greatest? He replied: "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the greatest."
The Patriarch knew he was his Dharma heir; once he had left the household life, he entrusted him with the Eye of the Dharma, saying: "The mind-ground gives birth to all seeds;
through conditions, the principle is further realized. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower blooms, the world arises."
Baotan said: "The forty-seven patriarchs of the Western Heaven were all holy masters. Their roots and ground were stable and firm, as seen in their conduct;
their eloquence and wisdom were swift and brilliant, as seen in their speech and demeanor.

Many have seen their teachers carrying the Way and sought them out by observing their vital energy (*qi*), like searching through one's own old garments to retrieve what was stored therein, or like inheriting the ancestral occupation of generations past."
The common people of the marketplace say that for sages to follow one another in succession is how easy it is!

However, when Huaiyin said to the Han Gaozu, "Your Majesty is skilled at commanding commanders," I would say: how could every person be like Xiao He, Cao Shen, or Han Xin to be employed by an Emperor?
Thus we know that the Great Dharma, flowing eastward, was intended primarily for commoners to share.

It is like a lowly servant or slave who, upon being called to duty, realizes that there will surely come a day when he is enfeoffed as a marquis. Only our Patriarchal Teacher was not far removed from the Buddha.
His preaching of the Dharma according to the capacities of his audience was, for the most part, no different from the words of the Buddha or the Bodhisattvas.
However, his Chan encompasses all its various forms; even if later descendants each obtain but one aspect, it is sufficient to establish a school.

Whether it be "the swift flame passing through fire" or "running across a rushing torrent or leaping over a blade," there is nothing that does not manifest its signs herein. Let students recognize this.

When the Great Master Daruma refuted the six schools, a teacher of the School with Characteristics (Sāṃmitīya) came forward and asked: "What is called the 'true mark' (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all dharmas? The Venerable Sāramati replied: "Regarding..."
"Among all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), that which does not mutually interact with other phenomena is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The Master asked, "If all phenomena do not mutually interact, then when one clarifies the true mark, what would it be fixed as? He replied, "Within all phenomena, there is truly no fixed state.
If phenomena were fixed, how could they be called 'true'? The Master said, "The fact that phenomena are not fixed is precisely what clarifies the true mark. You, however, are currently not fixed."
"How can this be attained? He replied, "My words are not fixed; I do not speak of various characteristics. When I speak of various characteristics, their meaning is likewise so.

The Master said, "Your words are not fixed, yet they should constitute the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because they are both fixed and not fixed, they are not the true characteristic. He replied:
If that which is fixed is not fixed, it is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). Since one knows the self is non-existent, it is neither fixed nor changing.
The Master said: "If you are now unchanging, how can you be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away is the same in its meaning.

[The student] said: "Because 'unchanging' must exist or not exist; therefore, by means of change, the true mark establishes its meaning. The Master said: "The true mark is unchanging; if it changes, it is not [the true mark]."
"True. "Among existence and non-existence, what is called the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*)? Sariputra understood the noble teacher’s profound intent;
pointing his finger at the sky, he said, "This is the mark of existence in the world, yet it is also capable of being empty. Will this body of mine ever become like this?"

The Master said: "If one understands true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one sees that which is non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*). If one comprehends that which is non-characteristic, then form (*rūpa*) is likewise so.
One should not recognize the essence of form within form, nor be obstructed by existence within that which is non-characteristic. If one can understand in this way, this is called true reality.
When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it with faith.

The Master of the Formless School arrived and asked, "To what do you base your claim that there is no form? Among the assembly was a wise man named Pratītya who replied, "I am called 'formless' because my mind does not manifest.
The Master said, "If your mind does not manifest, by what means would you clarify it?"

[The student] said: "I clarify that in the mind of non-characteristic (*animitta*) there is neither grasping nor rejecting; even at the time of this clarification, there is no one who clarifies. The Master said:

"In all that exists or does not exist, the mind neither grasps nor rejects, and furthermore, there is no one who clarifies because there is no 'non-existence' to be clarified. [The student] said: "Even when entering the Buddha-samādhi, there is nothing to be attained;
how much more so, since it is without characteristic, could one wish to know it? The Master said: "Since you do not even know the characteristic, who can speak of it?"

"Existence and non-existence—since even these cannot be apprehended, what can be called samādhi? He replied, "I speak of not realizing realization; because there is nothing to be realized, I call it samādhi.
The Master asked, "If it is not samādhi, what should it be named? Since you have not realized anything, nor are you realizing anything, what is there to realize?
Having heard this, Pratibhānu immediately awakened to his original mind. He repented his past errors and was again granted a prediction of enlightenment.
He said to him: "You shall attain the Way; you will realize it before long. There is a Māra in this country; you shall subdue him before long.
Having spoken, he suddenly vanished. This is the school of Samādhi and Prajñā.

When the Master arrived, he asked, "In your practice of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), are these one or two? Among the assembly was one named Pūrṇata, who said, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two.
The Master said, "If they are neither one nor two, how can they be called concentration and wisdom? He replied, "In the state of concentration, it is not concentration;
in the sphere of wisdom, it is not wisdom. One is not one, and two is not two. The Master said, "At that moment, it is both one and not one."
"Is it both two and not-two? Since it is neither fixed nor wisdom, by what means could it be defined as fixed or wisdom?

He replied, "It is through the non-one and non-two that fixedness and wisdom can be known; it is likewise with that which is neither fixed nor wisdom. The Master said, "Since wisdom is not fixedness, how can it be known?
In the state of neither one nor two, what is fixedness and what is wisdom? When Pūrṇata heard this, his doubts were completely dissolved like ice melting away.
The Master Wude was asked: "You speak of 'no-attainment. What is attained through no-attainment? Since there is nothing to be attained, there is also no attainment of attainment.
A person named Baojing from that assembly said: "What I call the attainment of no-attainment is not a non-attainment; it is the attainment that should be called the attainment of attainment."

"Non-attainment is attainment. The Master said, "Since attainment is already non-attainment, even attainment is not attainment. Since it is called 'attaining attainment,' what is there to be attained?
[The student] said, "Seeing that attainment is non-attainment, this non-attainment is itself attainment. If one sees non-attainment, this is called attaining attainment.

The Master said, "Since attainment is already non-attainment, attaining attainment is non-attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, how can there be an attaining of attainment? Baojing heard this.
Knowing that his doubts and delusions were suddenly dispelled, the Master of the School of Quiescence came and asked:
"What is meant by 'quiescence'? Within this Dharma, what is it that is stilled and what is it that is pacified? There was a householder there who...
[The student] said: "This mind being unmoving is called 'tranquility' (寂); being unstained by phenomena is called 'stillness' (靜). The Master said:

"If the original mind were not already tranquil, it would require tranquility and stillness as a support. Since it is originally tranquil, what need is there for tranquility and stillness? [The student] said: "All phenomena are originally empty;

because they are empty of emptiness, one speaks of 'tranquility and stillness' with respect to that emptiness of emptiness. The Master said: "Once even emptiness is empty, all phenomena [are revealed]."
It is likewise so. In quiescence and signlessness, what is there to be stilled and what is there to be pacified? Having heard this, the elder attained sudden and clear awakening.
The Master of Precepts and Conduct then asked him: "What is called 'precept' (śīla) and what is called 'conduct' (caryā)? Are these precept and conduct one or two?"

Among that assembly there was a worthy one who said: "One and two, two and one—all these are produced from that [source]. To rely on the teaching without defilement is what is called 'conduct of precepts'.
The Master said: "Your statement that 'relying on the teaching' implies there is defilement; since both 'one' and 'two' are violated, how can you say one relies on the teaching?"
"These two are contrary and fail to reach practice. Since there is neither internal nor external clarity, what can be called precept?
He replied: 'I have already fully understood that there is both internal and external; having attained such thorough penetration, this is itself the practice of precept.

If one speaks of contrariety, it is both right and wrong. When speech reaches purity, that is the precept and that is the practice. The Master asked: 'If it is both right and wrong, how can you say it is pure? Since—"
Having attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), what need was there to discuss internal or external [teachings]? Upon hearing this, the worthy ones immediately felt ashamed and submitted.

Subsequently, the six schools all vowed to take refuge. From this, his transformation spread throughout Southern India and his fame resounded across the Five Indias; scholars from near and far turned toward him in unison, following his influence.
Baotan said: "The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are separated from the Buddha by but one interval. Their power is like that of the Buddha; their discourse is like that of the Buddha;
they manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) like the Buddha. It is only because they perceive dharmas as existing apart from the mind that they cannot become Buddhas.

Long ago, on the day the Tathāgata first departed from the city of Vaiśālī, he entered Mount Taṇḍita, Mount Gajaśīrṣa, and other mountains to associate with the non-Buddhists, even going so far as to..."
For years he subsisted on hemp and wheat, traversing every one of the ninety-six schools of the Red-Flaged sects;
this is what is meant by the saying that one cannot obtain the tiger’s cub without entering the tiger’s den.

Once he had attained the Way and begun preaching the Dharma, those externalists still maintained their fortresses of Mara and Buddha, frequently seizing the Buddha by the neck and strangling him. I witnessed it with my own eyes.
Beholding the imposing army, he remained as composed as ever, speaking with ease and laughter; yet there were those who sought to offer their apologies by presenting severed heads.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various masters encountered those who were burdened by errors and followed the beat of the drum, treating them with contempt, while others acted like dogs toward the Heavenly Way (*tian*).
Now my ancestor Bodhidharma personally bore the authentic seal of Prajñātāra, and [the lineage of] the Golden...
The sharp edge of the sword blazes in one’s hand. As it is said: "If you test a minor official, the official perishes; if you test a dog, the dog perishes. Is this not of the same nature?
Now, observe the six schools, such as the Mahāyāna-samaya-parivarta and others; they hold divergent views, split into factions, and each clings to their own understanding.
If even the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas are thus unlike [the ultimate truth], how much more so when compared to our Buddhas and Patriarchs?
Is he an adversary? He once attempted to invert his arguments and obscure the names of his masters in order to test those in the present age who possess correct views;
yet it was not necessarily the case that the teachers of the Eastern Land were truly superior to the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heaven.
When the Great Master Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch of the Chan school in China,
arrived at Jinling, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty summoned him and asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master replied:
"Vast and empty, there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Master replied, "I do not know.

The Emperor was not in accord with him, so he eventually traveled to Luoyang and stayed at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. He sat facing a wall, and no one could fathom his intent; at the time, he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin.
Soon after, the monk Shen Guang came to seek instruction, but the Master sat upright without offering any words of exhortation. Shen Guang stood beneath the courtyard eaves.
At dawn, the accumulated snow reached their waists. The Master, moved by compassion, asked him, “You have stood in the snow for so long; what do you seek?
Dazhuangguang wept with sorrowful tears and said, “I only pray that, out of your compassion, you will open the gate of ambrosia to widely deliver all beings.

The Master said, “The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort over vast eons to practice what is difficult to practice. How could it be attained with a light heart, through small virtue or small wisdom?”
With a mind of pride, he hoped to attain the True Vehicle. After Huiguang heard this, he took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Master.
The Master then asked, "Can the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas be heard? Huiguang replied, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
[The Master] said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you. [Huiguang] said, "I search for it..."
"The mind cannot be apprehended. The Master said, "I have finished granting you peace of mind. He further recorded this, saying:
"If you simply cease all external conditions and let the internal mind be free from error—making the mind like a wall—you may enter the Way.

Later, when nine years had passed and he was about to return to the Western Heaven (India), he addressed his disciples, saying, "The time has come. Each of you should speak of what you have attained. Daofu replied:
"As I see it," he said, "one does not cling to words nor depart from words, yet takes them as the means for the Way.
The Master said, "You have obtained my skin. Niti Zongchi said, "What I now perceive is like Ānanda perceiving the land of Akṣobhya Buddha:
seen once, never to be seen again. The Master said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates are not..."
“There is. Yet, in my state of realization, not a single dharma can be apprehended. The Master said, “You have attained my bones.
Huike stepped forward, prostrated three times, and stood in his place. The Master said, “You have attained my marrow.

The Master further addressed him, saying, “The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa, and through successive transmission it has come down to me. You must protect and uphold it.”
I bestow upon you this *kāṣāya* robe as a token of my faith in the Dharma. That which is transmitted internally is the Dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*) to seal the fundamental mind;

that which is transmitted externally is the *kāṣāya* robe to establish the essential teaching. In future ages, when the world becomes turbid, there will be a division between the Chinese and the Indian traditions.

Since it will be difficult for [the truth] to arise later, you should produce this robe as proof to clarify your transformation. A verse says: "I have come to this land from the beginning, To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings."
"One flower opens and five petals unfold; the fruit ripens spontaneously.

Baotan said: "When our Patriarch entered China, there were initially no auspicious signs such as the radiance of light or the shaking of the earth, nor was there the benefit of rain falling like clouds from the Dharma, nor any matter of conforming to worldly standards. At that time, people looked toward him..."
However, it is not merely a matter of referring to him as a "wall-contemplating" (*bhittidhyāyin*) Brahmin;
when he raises his empty fist to seek real efficacy, he possesses the strength of Wu-huo and the courage of Meng-ben. Even a hundred Mātanga and Dharmaratna could not compare to him.
Having traveled to Liang for but a short time, he departed because he had offended the sovereign’s “sensitive scales,” yet even then he could not find leisure to offer consolation.
However, Emperor Wu of Liang was able to pose the question regarding the archery target, yet he could not endure the arrow that struck the center of the pheasant-feather;
he was able to exert the strength of others to draw the bow, yet he could not perform the act of biting the arrowhead. This is truly pitiable, like a man who studies archery.
It was only after a long time that he finally entered [the Way]. Did the blue-eyed barbarian not know this? From then on, Shaolin itself became the archery range for his person.
A separate record states that [Bodhidharma] said to Shen Guang: "You need only externally cease all conditions and internally ensure your mind is free from error."
Thus, he taught them by means of the compass within their own bodies and the square-ruler in their hands; with a mind like a blank wall, they were able to enter the Way.
This was called being able to hit the mark every hundred times one shoots. After nine years, father and son attained mutual understanding and hand and mind became mutually forgotten.
I know not whether the divine light shot toward Shaolin, or whether Shaolin shot toward the divine light.
Archery is a single art, yet it can strike the hide, the flesh, the bone, or even the marrow;
it depends entirely upon how great one's strength is. Those who hit the hide are many; those who hit the flesh are few;
those who hit the bone are not two or three in a hundred or a thousand; and those who hit the marrow are but one in ten thousand.

The Second Patriarch, Grand Master Huìkě, traveled north to the Qi dynasty. There was a lay practitioner whose name and lineage were unknown; he came to pay his respects and asked, "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment.
I beg the Master to grant me absolution. The Master said, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I will grant you absolution. The lay practitioner...

After a long silence, he said, "I have searched for my transgression, but it is utterly unfindable. The Master said, "I have finished repenting your transgressions for you. You should dwell in reliance upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The monk asked, "Now that I see the Master, I already know what the Sangha is. But I do not yet understand what is called the Buddha and the Dharma. The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha;
this very mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. The monk said, "Only today do I truly know."
"The nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma; there is no duality.
The Great Master regarded him with deep esteem and immediately shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him. After two years had passed, the Great Master said to him:
Bodhidharma came from afar from Zhugan (India) and secretly entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to me.

I now transmit it to you, together with Bodhidharma’s robe of faith. You must protect and preserve it so that its lineage is never severed. A verse says: "Originally there was ground due to conditions;
From the ground, seeds and flowers grew. Originally there were no seeds; Thus, flowers have never grown."
Baotán said: "In the time of Bodhidharma, there were already disciples who followed alternative paths; Dàfù and the others are examples of this.
Observe the Second Patriarch’s three prostrations and his standing in his place—how does this compare to what the previous three sons each presented as their realization?
As Gautama once said: 'For example, the great ocean does not reject even small streams, down to those of mosquitoes and gadflies.'"
Furthermore, when asuras drink from its waters, they all obtain full satisfaction; this is what is meant by the "outflowing branches.
It refers to the bestowing of the Way according to individual capacities. How could the Patriarchs not have desired for everyone to be like the Master Daokai?

Yet, since the spiritual faculties and dispositions of beings are such as these, what can be done? As time progresses, the peripheral currents will likely no longer be the authentic transmission, much like those outflowing branches.

The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, was visited by the novice Daoxin, who was fourteen years old. He came to pay his respects and said, "I pray that the Master will, out of compassion, grant me the Dharma-gate of peace and bliss.
The Master asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Master said, "Why then do you seek liberation?"

Touhu attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. He served [his master] diligently for nine years. Later, he received full ordination in Jizhou and attended upon his master with even greater reverence.
The Master repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle matters; knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma, saying in verse:
"The seeds of flowers, though dependent on the earth, From the earth they grow and produce flowers. If no one sows the seeds, Neither flowers nor earth will ever come to life."

The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, arrived in Jizhou during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty. He encountered a band of rebels who had besieged the city for seventy days without lifting the siege; the multitude was filled with terror.
The Master instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the rebel host perceived what seemed to be divine soldiers within the battlements.
They appeared and disappeared, and then said to one another, "There must be an extraordinary person within the city; we cannot attack it. They gradually withdrew.
A day later, they went toward Huangmei County and encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and extraordinary, unlike those of ordinary children.
The Master asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.
The Master asked, "What is it? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Master asked, "Do you have no surname? He replied, "Because nature is empty.

The Master silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and sent an attendant to his home to request that he be allowed to leave the household life. Because of past affinities, his parents had no objection whatsoever.

Feeling a sense of trepidation, he finally renounced his home and entered the monastic life, continuing until the transmission of the Dharma and the entrustment of the robe. The verse says: "The nature of a flower-seed has the capacity for growth;
Depending on the soil, the flower grows. When the great conditions unite with faith, Birth after birth shall lead to non-birth."
Baotan said: "A physician can cure a person's illness but cannot bestow peace and harmony upon them; only Qin Yue-ren could do so, and he is truly what is called a 'virtuous physician.
The *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on the Mind of Faith) contains the essential teachings of the Third Patriarch.
It dispels both the sickness of the Buddha and the sickness of the patriarchs, and the ground of great peace and great rest is entirely contained within it."

Among these, the Fourth Patriarch was one who had already reached his destination; he attained it as if eating a meal of ambrosia, whereby he ultimately did not die, and thereafter established it as a bridge and raft for others.
As for those who have not yet reached their destination, it is like obtaining a chariot equipped with a south-pointing compass.
There will no longer be the affliction of losing one's way. A complete verse can bring the Great Matter to completion;
even half a verse can resolve the affairs of a lifetime. Let students take this to heart. —Master Wuzu Daman.
The Master was residing at Mount Pótóu. During the Xiánhéng era, a layman surnamed Lú and named Huínéng came from Qízhōu to pay his respects.
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From south of the Ling Mountains. The Master said, "What do you seek? He replied, "I only seek to become a Buddha.
The Master said, "People of the south have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha? He replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but the Buddha..."
"How could such be his nature? The Master, knowing he was an extraordinary person, rebuked him, saying, "Go and work in the fodder shed.

He bowed at the Master's feet and withdrew, then entered the area between the pestle and mortar. For eight months he served with diligence. When the Master knew the time had come for him to receive the Dharma, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; one must not merely memorize my words and take that as their own task. Each of you..."
He then composed a verse according to his own inspiration. If the words and meaning were in perfect accord with the Dharma, he would bestow both the robe and the Dharma upon him.

Among the seven hundred eminent monks in the assembly, Shenxiu was the preeminent leader whom all revered. He inscribed a verse on the wall, saying: "The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is a stand for a bright mirror.
At all times diligently wipe and polish it, Lest dust and grime should gather upon it. Because of this, the Master...

While walking in meditation, Neng suddenly saw it and recognized it as having been composed by Master Xiu. He praised it, saying: "Those of future generations who rely on this for practice will also attain supreme fruits.
He then had everyone recite it. When Neng heard of this while at the grain-hulling shed, he said to his fellow students, "It is beautiful indeed, yet it is not yet complete.
A student scolded him, saying, "How could a commoner like you know anything? Do not utter such groundless words. Neng replied, "If you do not [understand],..."
Xinxie said, "I wish to harmonize this with a single verse. His fellow students did not answer, but looked at one another and smiled.
When night fell, Xinxie personally took up a candle and had a youth add the following lines beneath Xu’s verse: "Bodhi is originally not a tree; The bright mirror is also not a stand.
From the beginning, there has been nothing at all; How could it be stained by dust? When the Master saw this, he asked, "Who wrote this? It is not yet..."
Upon seeing his nature, the assembly heard the Master’s words and consequently did not look back. When night fell, they secretly sent someone to summon Huineng to enter the room.
He declared: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is for the sake of one great matter. According to the capacities of beings—whether great or small—they are guided accordingly.
Thus, there have arisen the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the teachings of sudden and gradual as various gateways to the Dharma.

Nevertheless, the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *Dharmaparyāya*—the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma (*dharmadharmacakṣur-garbha*)—was entrusted to the foremost disciple, Kāśyapa, and passed down through twenty-eight successive generations."
From the time the World-Honored One reached this land with the Dharma, it was transmitted through the Great Master and has come down to me.
Now I entrust both the robe and the Dharma to you. Guard and uphold them well so that they shall not be severed. Listen to my verse:
"When sentient beings come to plant seeds, The fruit arises from the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, That which lacks nature does not arise. (Repeat.)
Qing said, "The Dharma has now been received; to whom shall the robe be given? The Master said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet know or believe him.

He transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma. Now that faith is matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with your person and will no longer be transmitted."
Baotan said: "The Five Patriarchs of China were also ordinary people of common ground. Yet, in a single day, they were able to accomplish the deeds of sages;
they did not calculate gain or loss, nor did they look to advantage or harm. Are they not truly fierce and heroic great men?
Some say that the Patriarchs all came from among the worthy and holy ones, which would leave no room for ordinary people. I have often read..."
In the *Biographies of the First and Second Patriarchs of the Dharma*, one sees a most detailed account of the two masters’ lives and the hardships they endured in transmitting the Way.
Privately, I rejoiced and said: "From this day forward, it is clear that my ancestors did not descend from heaven [as mere spirits].
From the Third Patriarch downward, there was already the air of a tradition from the Western Land. Had it not been for Shaolin..."
As for the act of severing one's own arm, later generations would surely draw their swords in suspicion; how could there be such a thing today?
Generally speaking, when a person builds a household through great hardship, the Creator will surely reward them with brilliant descendants to expand their legacy;
this is an inevitable principle. Yet, when observing the moments of transmission between the Buddhas and patriarchs, if it were not for...
Difficult matters are such that while others may be capable of reaching them, one’s own person may not necessarily succeed;

it is like a great mountain falling before one, unaware until it is already crushed. Thus we know that only after possessing the strength of a hundred *jin* can one carry our burden of a hundred *jin*.
To gallop a thousand *li* at a single stroke without looking back—this is truly the "sweat-blooded" steed of our own house.
The Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Dayi, succeeded the Dharma of Chan Master Farong of Jinling.
The Master resided in a rock cave to the north of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou; there was the marvel of hundreds of birds bringing him flowers.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric signs from afar and knew there was a person of extraordinary character.
He went to search for him and heard a monk say, "Ten *li* from the mountain there is Lanrong; when he sees people, he neither rises nor joins his palms.

The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw the Master sitting upright and composed, never once looking around. The Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am contemplating the mind."

The Patriarch said, "Observe: what is this person? What is this mind? The Master had no reply; he then rose, joined his palms in salutation, and asked, "Where does the Venerable One dwell in seclusion?
The Patriarch said, "This poor monk has no fixed abode; sometimes I go east, sometimes west. The Master said:
"Do you still know Chan Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked. "Why do you ask about him? the Master replied. "I have long admired his virtue and hope to pay him a visit.
The Patriarch said, "I am he. The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you.
"Is there another place for us to rest? the Master asked. He led the Patriarch to a small hermitage, where they saw only tigers, wolves, and other such beasts.
The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of intimidation. The Master said, "There is still this remaining. The Patriarch asked, "What did you see just now? The Master was speechless.
After a short while, the Patriarch sat upon a rock and wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛). Upon seeing it, the Master stood in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining.
The Master, not yet understanding, bowed his head and requested an explanation of the essential truth. The Patriarch said, "A hundred..."
The thousand dharma-gates all return to the single square inch of the mind. The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the heart.
All gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and spontaneously complete;

they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty and still. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no bodhi to attain.
It may be sought. The nature of humans and non-humans is equal. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.
Such a Dharma as this you have now attained; there is nothing lacking. How is it different from that of the Buddha? There is no other separate Dharma.
You need only let your mind be free and at ease; do not perform contemplative practices, nor clarify the mind, nor give rise to greed or delusion, nor harbor anxiety or worry.

Vast and unobstructed, moving freely in all directions, neither performing any good nor committing any evil—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever meets the eye and whatever one encounters is entirely the wondrous function of the Buddha. Because there is joy and no sorrow, it is called "Buddha. The Master said:

"Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha and what is the mind? The Patriarch said, "If it is not the mind, one does not inquire about the Buddha; if one inquires about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind.
The Master asked, "If one does not engage in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), how does one counteract when objects arise?

The Patriarch said, "The conditions of objects have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind. If the mind does not insist on assigning names, from where would deluded sentiments arise?"
Arise! Once deluded emotions no longer arise, the true mind will naturally possess universal knowledge. You need only follow the mind with freedom; there is no further need for antidotes.
This is precisely what is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, which is without change or variation. I received from Master Can the Dharma-gate of Sudden Enlightenment.

"I now entrust this to you. You must now receive my words with earnest attention and remain solely on this mountain. There shall be five men who attain realization and will carry forward your profound transformation.
Subsequently, the Master carried one *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, departing in the morning and returning by evening;
he provided for the monks for three years without fail, regardless of cold or heat.
Baotán said: "Before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch, the hundred birds brought flowers as offerings; after he saw the Fourth Patriarch, the hundred birds did not come.
There have been many such proclamations throughout ancient and modern times, but only Nanquan said:
'Even if they do not come, it is still one hair's breadth inferior to Old Wang. This is precisely the sphere of the Great Physician. Thus it is with the Buddha-dharma.
The matters at stake are of the utmost gravity. By means of a different species, one comes to know the Ox-head [tradition];
how could this possibly be inferior to the various factions of later generations? Now, the Way has both a direct transmission and collateral branches.

The direct transmission is like a biological son who serves as the successor to his father; the collateral branches are like younger offspring. That parents love their younger children is a sentiment shared by all human beings.
Yet he addressed them with gentle words and received them with kindness and tolerance; even when instructing them, he never did so exhaustively.
His treatment of those following his father must certainly have been different from this: he exhorted and tempered them so they would know the duties of ruler and subject, father and son;
he cautioned and refined them so they would know the bonds of brother and friend. Thus he entrusted his instructions to the younger generation.
One should ensure that [the child] knows his lineage and family background, hoping that he may establish himself; only then does one cease this method of instructing a son.
This is what is appropriate for a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). If a good spiritual friend possesses the affection of a cow licking its calf, [then this is the way].
Thus, the true lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs was as precarious as a dangling tassel. Niu Tou was truly a person of great merit;
that he would transmit the lamp for six generations had already been foretold in the prophetic records. Subsequently, his radiance became even more magnificent than that of his master.
How could this have been due to the strength of my own Lanrong, who lived eighty *li* from the mountain and carried one *shuo* and eight *dou* of rice back and forth daily?
Chan Master Fǎróng’s Dharma successor was Chan Master Zhìyán.

While the Master was in meditative absorption within a mountain ravine, he encountered a sudden flood; yet he remained serene and unmoving, and the waters receded of their own accord. There was once...
Two of his fellow soldiers heard that the Master was living in seclusion within the mountain valleys. They went to seek him out and said to him, "General, are you mad?

Why do you dwell here? He replied, "I am mad and wish to awaken; you are mad and are now fully possessed by it. Those who crave sensual beauty and licentious sounds, and who greedily pursue honor and prosperity, will transmigrate through birth and death—by what means can they emerge from this on their own?
The two men were moved to realization, sighed deeply, and departed. (Recorded during the Zhenguan era.)
He returned to Jianye and entered Mount Niushou to pay his respects to Master Daorong, seeking clarification on the Great Matter. Subsequently, the Patriarch said to him:
"I received the true transmission from the Great Master Xinxing; what I have attained, I have entirely forgotten.

Even if there were a dharma that surpassed nirvana, I would still say it is like a dream or an illusion. A single speck of dust flying can obscure the sky; a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth."
"You have now transcended these views; what more need I say? The guidance of this mountain gate shall be entrusted to you.
The Master received this command to serve as the second patriarch and subsequently transmitted the True Dharma to Chan Master Fang.
Master Fang of Shisanhui was originally a teacher of the sutras and śāstras with profound clarity. Later, he entered Niutou Mountain to visit Master Yan and inquire about secret resolutions.

Master Yan observed that his faculties were capable of receiving the True Dharma and consequently bestowed upon him the Mind Seal. The Master attained sudden and complete realization; thereupon, he...
Ten years after he emerged from the forest thickets, he addressed the assembly, saying: "I wish to travel elsewhere to benefit sentient beings according to their capacities;
you should remain at peace. He then entrusted the True Dharma to Master Chi Chan.

The Fourth Patriarch, Dharma-holder Chan Master Hongren, attained the opening of his mind upon hearing the Dharma under the seat of Master Huiming at Huangmei. He further encountered Master Fang, who granted him formal certification (*inka*).
He subsequently succeeded to the ancestral lineage of Niutou. When Huiming passed away, he said to his disciple Xuangze, "You shall further transmit my Dharma."
There were ten such individuals. The first was Fachi of Jinling. Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to Master Wei.

Five generations later, when Master Zhwei heard that Master Wenchi had appeared in the world, he went to pay his respects and receive the True Dharma. Disciples flocked to him from all directions. Among them—
Huizhong arrived and said, "The Master of the Mountain has come! At this, [Nanyue] was immediately enlightened.

Nanyue presented him with a verse, saying: "Do not fixate on thoughts; thoughts form the river of birth and death. One revolves within the ocean of the six realms, unable to see the end of these long waves.

Huizhong replied with a verse: "Thoughts and perceptions have always been illusory; their nature is itself without beginning or end. If one grasps the meaning within this, the long waves shall naturally subside."
[The Master] stopped. The Master said, "My original nature is void and non-existent; it is due to delusion that the notions of self and other arise.
How can one cease these deluded sentiments? Return and sit in the place of emptiness. Zhong said, "If voidness is the true reality, where do self and other exist?
There is no need to cease deluded sentiments; one simply boards the Prajñā boat. Thereupon, he was entrusted with the Dharma to transform and guide others.
The Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Huizhong, while on a pilgrimage to the Wei Commandery at Jujie Monastery, saw a *lingxiao* vine that had withered during the summer.
When people wished to cut it down, he said to them, "When I return, this vine will have grown back. Upon his return, it was indeed just as he had said; he then transmitted [the Dharma] to him.

His dharma teachings were concluded. Throughout his life, he possessed only a single robe and a single cauldron. He always maintained two granaries for offerings of grain to the sangha, which three tigers guarded.

His spiritual wonders were manifold, and those whom he delivered were also very numerous. Addressing the assembly, he said: "When both person and dharmas are purified, good and evil are both forgotten."
"The straightforward mind is reality; it is the site of enlightenment.
Baotan remarked: "The Dharma taught by Niutou, in its general substance, did not deviate from what his teacher had transmitted to him."
The first verse says: "Precisely when the mind is applied, precisely there is no application of mind; this is most refined and absolute.
Yet, in the end, it is not as essential as the state where deluded emotions do not arise at all, and the true mind is allowed to know universally.
Upon receiving Master Yinkan’s single phrase, was this not the Buddha-work of his final years? Thereafter, for five generations of father and sons...
It is traditionally said that they were merely able to support and establish the orthodox lineage of Niutou.

Among those three generations of masters, Rong and Wei, there were still several who branched out from the side yet resembled those of the direct transmission; An Guo, Tianzhu, Jingshan, and Niaoke were such individuals.
It is like the pungent fumes of a submerged path by the seashore; it lacks even a single grain of the fragrant scent of its ancestral source.
It did not come from the Heaven of Delightful Transformations (Nirmāṇarati) in the Yāma realm; it would not be easy to reach such a state otherwise.
Chan Master Zhiwei succeeded Chan Master Xuanting of Anguo Monastery in Xuanzhou. Once,
while [Xuanti] was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in Chang’an, a monk came and asked the Fifth Patriarch, “What is the meaning of ‘true nature dependent origination’?”

The Patriarch remained silent. At that time, as the monk was standing in attendance, the Master said to him, "Virtuous One, at the very moment you give rise to a single thought of inquiry, that is the dependent origination of true nature.
Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Someone asked, "From what did the Southern School establish itself? The Master replied:
The Mind-essence school makes no distinction between North and South.
Once, a monk asked Chan Master Chonghui of Mount Tianzhu in Shuzhou, "What is the realm of Mount Tianzhu? He replied, "The heights of Mount Zhubu make the sun difficult to see; the jade mirror..."
Before the Peak, it is easy for people to understand. A question was asked: "Before Bodhidharma had not yet arrived, was there still the Buddha-dharma?
He said, "Setting aside for a moment the time before his arrival, what is the matter right now? [The monk] said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master for instruction.

He said, "Ten thousand ages of eternal sky; one morning’s wind and moon. After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? As for your own portion, what does it have to do with Bodhidharma’s coming?"
"What will you do with the future? He has come from that house much like a fortune-teller. Seeing that you do not understand, he pierces through it for you.
As soon as the lines of the divination appear, good or bad fortune lies within your own lot; look at everything yourself. A monk asked, "What is one who understands divination?
He said, "The moment you step out the door, you have already missed it. The monk asked, "What is the house of Tianzhu? He said, "It is where you are right now."
The wind said: "At times white clouds come to close the door; there is no more wind or moonlight, yet the four mountains flow.
Chan Master Daoqin of Jingshan in Hangzhou was once asked by a monk, "What is the Way? The Master replied, "A carp on the mountain; duckweed at the bottom of the water. Mazu.
He sent someone to deliver a letter. Upon opening the seal, he saw a circle with a single stroke drawn inside it; he returned the letter unopened.
When National Teacher Zhong heard of this, he remarked, "Master Qin is still being deluded by Master Ma. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s intent?
The Master said, "Your question is improper. The monk asked, "How can one be proper? The Master replied, "Wait until after my passing, and I shall tell you. This was Master Ma.
The Patriarch [Nanyue Huairang] instructed Zhizang, asking, "In the twelve periods of the day, what do you take as the object?
The Master said, "Wait until you have returned, and then there will be news. Zhizang said, "I am returning right now. The Master said, "When you deliver my message, you must ask about Caoxi yourself.
Emperor Daizong summoned him to the inner court. One day, seeing the Emperor stand up, the Master also stood up. The Emperor asked, "Why do you rise, Master? The Master replied:
"Benefactor, how could you have seen this poor monk while he was engaged in the four deportments?
Master Daolin of Niaoke in Hangzhou, having been shown the verses on True and False by the Master of the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*, Fuli, was instructed to practice *dhyāna*. The Master then asked:"

The Master asked, "How do you first observe? How do you apply your mind? Nanquan prostrated three times and remained silent for a long time without speaking; the Master then performed three prostrations and withdrew.

Emperor Daizong summoned Guoqing to the imperial court, whereupon the Master went to pay his respects and was granted the True Dharma. He subsequently took up residence in the fork of a tree, which became known as Bird’s Nest (Chuko).
A disciple named Huatong took his leave to depart, and the Master asked him, "Where are you going now? He replied, "To study in various quarters."
The Buddhist Dharma is departing. The Master said, "If it is the Buddhist Dharma, I too have a small portion of it here. [Hui]tong asked, "What is the Master’s Buddhist Dharma?
The Master picked up some cloth-pelts from his body and blew upon them; Huitong was immediately enlightened.
When Bai Juyi came to pay his respects and asked, "The place where the Chan Master resides is very precarious," the Master replied, "The Prefect’s situation is even more precarious."

Baizhang said, "I am a disciple whose position is to stabilize mountains and rivers; what danger could there be? The Master said, "When firewood and fire intersect, the nature of consciousness does not cease;
is this not dangerous? He asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good."
The Fifth Patriarch was the one who branched out into the Northern School in his lifetime; this was Zen Master Shenxiu.

Regarding him, Tripiṭaka Master Yeśas recorded: "The profound principle arises from the earth of艮 (Gen); the honored and the lovely are both honored. He stands shoulder to shoulder with the Three [Sages]."

The nine clans [of his kin] were involved. A single hair from beneath his foot was [offered]. When the Master arrived at Dongshan Temple on Shuangfeng in Qizhou, he encountered the Great Master Wuzu Ren, who took seated meditation as his primary practice.
[Huineng] sighed in admiration and submission, saying, "This is truly my teacher.

He vowed to undergo rigorous discipline, employing himself in tasks such as gathering firewood and drawing water. The Patriarch said, "I have often ordained many people, yet in terms of awakening and understanding, none has reached you."

He attained the Dharma while residing at Dangyang Mountain in Jiangling. During the reign of Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty, she issued an imperial decree for him to attend the Inner Dao-chamber (Nei-daochang).

Among the princes, dukes, and high officials, there were none who did not submit to his influence upon merely hearing of his reputation. When Zhongzong ascended the throne, he treated him with even greater honor.

The great minister Zhang Yue once inquired about the essentials of the Dharma and observed the etiquette of a disciple. The Master spoke a verse which said: "All Buddha-dharmas are from one's own mind."
"Originally present, yet seeking it outwardly with the mind; abandoning his father and fleeing.
Baotán said: "In evaluating people, one must not be so categorical. When Master Fāngxiù was at Huángméi..."
He had not yet fully exhausted the intent of his teacher; thus, there arose the saying, "The body is like the Bodhi tree, the mind is like a bright mirror stand.
Later generations consequently harbored doubts about him. However, by the time his Way flourished, those he gathered were also exceedingly numerous.
When it came to the moment of spiritual awakening, they were no less than their teacher; the disciples of Jiangmo Zang were all outstanding and transcendent. There was one of great—
The state of transcending ordinary men has been difficult for all time. He once sent his disciple to Caoxi, instructing him, saying:
"He has attained teacherless wisdom and profoundly realized the Supreme Vehicle; I am not his equal. Go there to resolve your doubts.
When you return in the future, you must explain it to me. Was this not perhaps a manifestation of the power of Huangmei? As the *Cantong qi* says:
"Human faculties may be sharp or dull, but the Way has no Southern or Northern patriarchs. How truly profound these words!
When National Teacher Huian of Mount Song was being served by Tanran and Huairang, the two came to inquire of him, saying, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The Master said, "Why do you not ask about your own mind? He asked, "What is my own mind? The Master said, "Observe the secret functioning.
He asked, "What is the secret functioning? The Master indicated it by opening and closing his eyes. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment beneath these words.
No longer seeking elsewhere, he declined the opportunity for a formal succession and departed for Caoxi. When Empress Wu summoned him, he arrived at the imperial carriage.
The Emperor treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher and accorded him the same respect as Zen Master Shenxiu.
Empress Wu asked the Master his age, and he replied, "I do not remember. The Emperor said, "Why do you not remember? The Master said, "The body of birth and death is like a revolving cycle."
Since the cycle has neither beginning nor end, what need is there for recording? Moreover, within this continuous flow, there is no interval;
to perceive the arising and ceasing of bubbles is merely deluded thought. From the initial consciousness until the cessation of the moving signs, it is exactly like this.
How could one possibly record it by year or month?
Baotan said: "I read the biography of Lao'an and saw that his status as a successor of the orthodox lineage was very clear.

For what reason, then, was he recorded as a collateral branch of the Fifth Patriarch? I harbored this doubt in my heart. Upon examining the year he met the Fifth Patriarch, it was during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.
Zhenguan was the reign title of Emperor Taizong; at that time, the Fourth Patriarch was still alive. This continued until the Xinsi year of the Yonghui era..."
He entered nirvana at the beginning of the Hai (Xihai) year, which was the second year of the Gaozong era. The Fifth Patriarch saw the Fourth Patriarch during the Wude era;
from Wude to Zhenguan, only ten years had passed. Now, it is said that Seng'an saw the Fifth Patriarch during the Zhenguan era;
at that time, the Sixth Patriarch did not yet exist. It was only during the Xianheng era that the Sixth Patriarch first met the Fifth Patriarch.
The Patriarch [Hongren] passed away forty-five years after the Zhenguan era.
Anhua was ordained in the second year of the Shenlong era, and the Sixth Patriarch entered nirvana in the second year of the Xian Tian era. Only nine years had passed from Shenlong to Xian Tian;
at that time, the Venerable An was already one hundred and nineteen years old. Thus, it must be that the Venerable An met the Fourth Patriarch.

Within the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch, both Ming and Xiu were equally renowned; yet, although Master An was a venerable elder of an entire generation, he alone was not recorded [as receiving the robe].

Furthermore, if one considers the receipt of the robe as the mark of the orthodox transmission, then those without the robe would all be non-orthodox—this is greatly contrary to the intent of the Patriarchs.
In my humble opinion, it is only after the robe has been transmitted that the person worthy of the True Lineage is found.
How could this be discarded? Consider, for instance, the Dharma-gate taught by the Fourth Patriarch to Lan’an;
one may verify from the teachings he received from the Patriarch that they emerged as collateral branches.

As for the capacities employed by Master Lǎo’ān and the disciples he transformed—such as Rénxiǎn, Pòqǒng, Duòyuán, Guīzhōng, and other masters—all of them realized the non-arising of dharmas and excelled in eloquent exposition.
This is no small matter; how could it be treated with such casualness? Therefore, I cannot but clarify this point.
If the sequence of the *Lamp Records* has already been established, I dare not lightly alter it.

Chan Master Daoming of Mount Meng in Yuanzhou was a grandson of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty. After the fall of the state, he lived among the common people; because he was a descendant of royalty who had once held official rank, he was known as a "General.
He relied upon the Fifth Patriarch but attained no realization. Hearing that the Patriarch had secretly entrusted the robe and the Dharma to Lu Xishan, he went to seek him out.
He led ten like-minded companions to track him down and pursue him as far as Mount Dayu. The Master had already seen them; the others had not yet arrived.
When Layman Lu saw the Master rushing toward him, he immediately cast his robe and bowl onto a flat rock and said, "This robe represents the seal of faith;
can it be contested by force? You may take it as you please. The Master then attempted to lift it, but it remained as immovable as a mountain. He stood there, hesitating and awestruck.
Liu said, "I have come seeking the Dharma, not for robes. I pray that the Practitioner will grant me instruction.

The Patriarch said, "At this very moment, when you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—what is that which is the Original Face of Master Ming? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment;
sweat poured from his entire body, and he prostrated himself several times. He then asked, "Beyond these secret words and secret meanings..."
"Is there yet another secret place? The Patriarch said, "If you reflect back upon your own original face, the secret is right with you.
If I were to explain it to you, it would no longer be a secret."

Baotán said: "Ming fled southward; was it not because the time had come? The Fifth Patriarch’s prediction stated that the life of the one who receives the robe is as precarious as a strand of silk hanging from a beam;
at the head of Mount Dayu, he nearly could not escape. Ming was a descendant of the Wang clan and bore the title of General.
Now, here he comes, prostrating himself with his face flushed and his feet swollen—this is not merely an attempt to seize the robe, but seems destined to..."
They ate its flesh. It was like an old man from Min sending a *gu* poison;
when a traveler on the road hesitated before lifting it, the *gu* poison would manifest, so that one blow would kill him, while a second blow would revive him—just like testing a sword on a hair.
"My art is efficacious. Good friends have indeed attained realization and awakening; yet, as for those who have never encountered a true person in their entire lives, what is their ailment?
It is often that they exert too much effort and yet fail to reach the mark. The Old Man of Baoying said:
"Those in various quarters possess only the eye of the simultaneous pecking and hatching, but they do not possess the function of the simultaneous pecking and hatching."
A monk asked, "What is the simultaneous application of the peck and the tap? He replied, "The master does not peck or tap;
when pecking and tapping coincide, one misses it. How profound this is!
Chan Master Shenxiu of Hebei was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Kuangfang of Mount Wutai;
the latter established the Northern School. Chan Master [Shen]xiu asked, "What is it like after the white clouds have dispersed? The Master replied, "It is not obscured. Furthermore...
Question: "After arriving here, what should one do? Xiu said, "A single branch of right view produces five leaves.
Xiu silently granted him permission, and he went to dwell at Hanling in Shangdang.

After Chan Master Zhi of Mount Tiao in Hezhong Prefecture finished his lectures, he went to Mount Wudang, where he met Chan Master Xiu and received his seal of approval. The local governor, Wei Wensheng, invited him to reside at Xin'an Monastery.
The governor then asked, "What shall I do from this day forward? The Master replied, "The sun rises from the Mongsu."
When the light shone upon the tree, there was no shadow at all. At first, the Prefect could not understand this; he bowed with joined palms and withdrew.
After a short while, he attained enlightenment and felt a sense of liberation. He maintained a relationship with the Master for twenty years.
Chan Master Jiangmo Zang of Yanzhou left home at the age of seven.

At that time, there were many malevolent spirits in the wilds who deluded people; the Master, with his solitary form, subdued them and never showed even the slightest fear, thereby earning the name "Subduer of Demons" (Jiangmo).
He followed the North School, and when Master Xiu questioned him, he said: "Your name is 'Subduer of Demons. Regarding this..."
Wushan Mu said, "I have taken offense at you and have instead become a demonic heretic. The Master said, "There are Buddhas and there are demons.
Xiu said, "If you are a demon, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm. The Master said, "Even a Buddha is empty; what realm could there be?
Xiu recorded this in writing, saying, "You have a karmic affinity with Xiaoxiao’s wilderness," and subsequently entered Mount Tai, where his spiritual transformation flourished greatly.
