He manifested the form of a bodhisattva, the form of a deva, or a human; at times he emitted light, and at other times produced sounds. His disciples could not fathom these phenomena, yet after ten years had passed, they heard nothing more.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "A rustic man may employ many arts to dazzle and delude people, but it takes only for this old monk to remain unseen, and his tricks are exhausted."

Chan Master Quanzhi of Mount Liangshan in Huainan initially gathered disciples and established the Dharma at Changshou Temple in his home province. When the provincial governor, Wei Wenqing, asked him, "What will be the future prosperity or decline of the Buddha-dharma?
the Master replied, "The reality of true suchness has neither past nor present; it leaves no tracks and no footprints."
Conditioned phenomena are subject to the flux of the four marks; the Dharma is bound to encounter obstruction and distress, as Your Lordship may observe.
The former National Teacher Huian of Mount Song was a successor to Chan Master Renjian of Fuxian Monastery in Luojing.
This was Master Teng-Teng. During the Tianche era of the Tang dynasty, Empress Wu issued an imperial decree for him to enter the palace and appear before her in the hall.

He gazed up at the Empress for a long time and asked, "Do you understand? The Empress replied, "I do not. The Master said, "I, this old monk, observe the precept of silence," and having finished speaking, he departed.
On the following day, he presented nineteen short songs. When the Empress read them, she praised him highly.
Regarding the Venerable Puzao Duo of Mount Song:
there was once a shrine on a ridge of Mount Song that was extremely efficacious. Within its hall stood a single hearth, to which offerings were made by people from near and far without ceasing.
In the fifth watch, many living beings were being slaughtered. One day, the Master led his attendant monks into the temple and struck it three times with his staff, shouting:
"You are originally composed of clay and tiles; from where does the sacred come? From where does the spirit arise? He struck it another three times, and the hearth collapsed.
A moment later, a figure in green robes and a tall crown appeared before the Master and bowed. The Master asked, "Who are you?"

The spirit said, "I am originally the deity of this temple. Having long endured the retribution of my karma, today I have had the fortune to hear the Master preach the Dharma of non-arising and have attained liberation from this place.
I have come specifically to express my gratitude. The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature; it is not something I have forcefully spoken of for you. The spirit bowed twice and vanished.
An attendant monk said, "I have been by the Master’s side for a long time, yet I have never received such an instruction. [The Master replied,] "It was the god of the hearth."
"What have you attained that you have achieved such deliverance? The Master said, "I have no special principle; I simply told him: 'You are originally composed of clay and tiles.
From where does the sacred come? From where does the numinous arise? The attendant monk remained silent. The Master asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not.

The Master asked, "Why do you not understand the nature that is inherently present? The attendant monk prostrated himself. The Master said: *Note: This passage is from the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, a collection of Zen records compiled in the early 13th century.*
"Break it! Fall into it!

Zen Master Yuangui of Mount Song visited National Teacher Huian and attained sudden enlightenment regarding the profound essence. He subsequently chose to dwell at Pangwu on the mountain. One day, there was a marvel.

A man arrived wearing a formal cap and trousers with pleated leggings; his attendants were extremely numerous. He advanced with light steps and composed, measured gait, announcing that he came to pay his respects to the Great Master.
The Master, observing that the man’s appearance was extraordinary and far from ordinary, addressed him, saying: "Welcome, O benevolent one! For what purpose have you come?"
The spirit said, "Does the Master recognize me? The Master replied, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all as one—how could I make distinctions?
The spirit said, "I am this mountain deity, capable of bringing life and death to others. How can you, Master, view me as one with everyone else?
The Master said, "I do not give birth to you, so how could you bring death to me? I regard my body as equal to empty space; I regard myself [as equal to all]."
"I give it to you. Can you destroy emptiness and give it to me? If you could indeed destroy emptiness and destroy yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished;
yet even that you cannot do. Being thus, how could you cause my birth and death? The spirit bowed his head and said:
"I am also clever and upright compared to other deities; how could I have known that you, Master, possess such vast wisdom and eloquence?
I pray that you will bestow upon me the true precepts, so that I may cross over this world. The Master said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them.

Why is this? Because there is no precept apart from the precept; what further precept could there be? The deity said, "This is indeed the principle. What I had heard was obscure and dim; I merely sought—"

The Master’s Precepts: "I am your disciple; you, Master, shall provide a seat, hold the incense burner, and set out the ritual table to confer upon me the Five Precepts regarding alcohol, meat, sexual misconduct, killing, and theft.
The Master said: "As for the aforementioned Buddha-precepts, do not harbor a mind of rigid attachment."
To take the mind as a thing while having no thought of the body—thus, though born before heaven and earth, one does not become a "spiritual essence" (*jing*);
though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become "old. It reaches even to the non-existence of "you" and the non-existence of "self.

Without "you," who would speak the words of admonition? The Spirit said: "My supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are second only to the Buddha's. The Master said: "Of your ten supernatural powers, five you can exercise and five you cannot."
The Buddha, however, has ten propositions: seven he can do, and three he cannot. Shen [the Emperor] suddenly rose from his seat, knelt, and asked, "May I hear them?
The Master said, "Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn back, making the Seven Luminaries travel east while you go west? He replied, "I cannot.
The Master said, "Can you seize the Earthly Deities, melting the Five Sacred Peaks and congealing the Four Seas? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "This is..."
This refers to the five things [the Buddha] cannot do. The Buddha can empty all phenomena of their marks and achieve the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively comprehend the events of billions of kalpas, yet he cannot transform and guide those who lack the karmic affinity.
He can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot bring the realm of sentient beings to an end. These are called the three things [the Buddha] cannot do. Fixed karma...
Nor is it enduring; even the absence of conditions is termed a single period. The realm of sentient beings has fundamentally neither increase nor decrease.
From antiquity, not a single person has been able to master the phenomena of existence (*dharmas*). That phenomena have no master is called the non-existence of phenomena (*adharma*).

That there is no phenomenon and no master is called the absence of mind (*acitta*). As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); he is merely able to penetrate all things through the absence of mind.

"It is the natural order of things," the spirit said. "I am indeed shallow and ignorant, and have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As for the precepts you have conferred upon me, I shall faithfully practice them.

Now, I wish to repay your kindness by displaying my minor supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), so that five types of people—those who have already resolved [to attain enlightenment], those who have newly resolved, those who lack faith, those who will surely gain faith, and others—may behold my spiritual traces with their own eyes, and come to know that there are Buddhas and spirits, and that there is a capacity [for transformation]."
“There are things that cannot be done. There are those that are natural and those that are not. The Master said, “It is unconditioned (wuwei). It is unconditioned.
The Spirit said, “The Buddha also commands spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, rebel against the Buddha? I pray that you will grant me your instruction as you wish.
The Master, having no choice, spoke: “The grounds of Dongyan Temple are overgrown and treeless. To the north there is a mountain ridge, yet the north is not [the place].”
The Master screened him from view and asked, "Can you move the northern tree to the eastern ridge? The spirit replied, "I have received your command.
However, there will surely be a great commotion during the darkness of night; I pray that the Master does not be alarmed. He prostrated himself and withdrew.

As the Master saw him off at the gate, mists, vapors, and clouds intermingled in profusion, while banners and streamers and tinkling bells appeared and vanished, soaring through the air. That very evening, a violent wind indeed arose with great speed.
Thunder crashed, clouds rumbled, and lightning flashed; the buildings shook and the nesting birds clamored. The Master said to the assembly, "Do not be afraid;
the deity has made a pact with me. At dawn, when it was clear and bright, all the pines on the northern cliff had been moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows.
Baotan said: A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) does not merely possess right knowledge and views and clearly recognize the Buddha-nature;
one must know that consciousness serves as the precursor for both the mundane and the supramundane.

If a spiritual friend lacks clarity of consciousness despite being fully endowed with virtue and conduct, it will not only fail to satisfy the hearts of students, but will be especially detrimental to the interests of the Buddha-dharma. Therefore—
From this, the slander that the external is important while the internal is trivial arose. Humans may still be deceived, but the divine cannot be deceived.
I observed that from the single phrase "the spirit of Mount Yue faces north toward Mount Song," I already knew the supreme dignity of Mount Song.

Only after the spirit had offered his sincere devotion did he preach the Dharma for him; he established the fixed laws of the precepts, which Mount Song then put into practice. It was just as [described in the scriptures].
It is like a pearl rolling on a platter or a platter rolling a pearl; appearing and disappearing, piercing through without obstruction, it accords perfectly with the Buddha’s intent.
Furthermore, he was adept at responding to capacities by carrying out his fundamental task from beginning to end—this is precisely what a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) ought to do.
His spirit was inherently intelligent and upright, and his discernment surpassed that of others; yet, when it came to that which he could not [master], he was unable to proceed.
He then responded directly with the truth, and his expressions of gratitude for the virtue [of his benefactor] reached three times. Mount Song refused him as if rejecting a bribe.
With such a level of discernment and resolve, how could he not be one whom gods and men look up to and admire?

In later generations, those who, out of delusion regarding merit, greedily seek favor and honor, do not even care for their own persons—how much less for the Buddha-dharma, and how much less for the spirits?
Therefore, I say that a good friend (kalyāṇamitra) must prioritize discernment;
those with resolve must not fail to study this.
The former Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song succeeded the Dharma of Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain.
Having received the Dharma, he immediately entered Mount Taiyī, where students filled his quarters. During the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty, Emperor Wénzōng...

He was fond of clams. Coastal officials would present them to him, which caused people much hardship. One day, among his imperial provisions, there was one that had been split open but did not close back up.
The Emperor considered this a marvel and immediately burned incense and prayed to it; it then opened. Suddenly, the form of a Bodhisattva appeared, complete with all its Brahma-like features.
He placed it in a casket made of gold-dusted sandalwood, covered it with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Temple, ordering the assembly to enshrine it.

The monks prostrated themselves in worship. Thereupon, the Emperor questioned his ministers, "What auspicious omen is this? Some replied, "The Chan Master Weizheng of Dayi Mountain has a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma and is widely learned and of powerful memory;
it would be appropriate to issue an imperial decree to question him. The Emperor then issued the decree. When the Master arrived, he replied:
"Your servant has heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause; this is merely to awaken Your Majesty’s faith. The Master continued, "The Sūtra says:

'To those who should be saved by means of this body, he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said, "I have seen the Bodhisattva's body, but I have not yet heard him preach the Dharma.
The Master asked, "Does Your Majesty regard this manifestation as permanent or impermanent? Do you believe it is real or unreal? The Emperor replied, "It is extraordinary!"

"I have deep faith in these matters," the Emperor said. The Master replied, "I have already finished hearing the exposition of the Dharma. At that time, the Master’s response was given eleven *ke* (approximately one hour and forty-eight minutes) after nightfall.
The Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased.
Baotan said: "Under great doubt, there must be great faith; this is why the Transformation Bodhisattva was able to awaken Master Wen’s faith in the Dharma.
Once this faith is aroused, the true Buddha appears before one. The Buddha does not know himself; it is only through faith that he knows the Dharma.
He does not see himself; it is only through realization that he sees. Master Zheng was one who had thoroughly realized this Dharma."

Therefore, to awaken such clarity in the sovereign, if the Honored One of Literature (Emperor Xuanzong) had, during the eleventh watch after midnight at the Yanying Hall, achieved even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) of reflective illumination, this would surely have become a merit of inexhaustible radiance.
Alas, it ended merely with the Emperor’s singular pleasure. Indeed, the Dharma of the Buddha and the worldly dharma are one and the same path.
Its arrival was gradual, yet its application required resolute decisiveness; once an opportunity is lost, it will not come again.
In my humble view, Wen Zong’s employment of Tang was not far removed from hearing the Way under Zheng Gong.
The Fifth Patriarch, Chan Master Daman, was a dharma successor of the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Huineng, the Great Mirror.
Before noon, while he was selling firewood in the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reaching the passage: "One should abide nowhere..."

A mind of awakening arose within him, and with a start he experienced a profound realization. He traveled directly to Mount Dongshan at Huangmei, where the Fifth Patriarch saw him and recognized his potential.

He was assigned to work in the fodder barn. Not long after, when the head disciple, Master Xiù, inscribed the verse "The body is like the Bodhi tree" upon the corridor wall, the Master took up a candle and had a youth write beside it: "The Bodhi is originally not a tree; the bright mirror..."
Nor is it a stand; originally there was not a single thing. Why allow it to be defiled by dust?

In the deep of night, the Patriarch summoned the Master into his room and secretly transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma, instructing him to conceal them within his bosom and travel to the region between Sihui and Jishi. At the beginning of the Yifeng era, he arrived at Nanhai.
He encountered Master Yinzong at Faxing Temple while he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Master was staying in the corridors;
there, as the wind blew the banner atop the flagpole, he heard two monks debating. One said, "The banner moves," and the other said, "The wind moves.
They argued back and forth several times without reaching a resolution. The Master asked, "May a layman be permitted to join this high discourse? The monk replied, "Please, try."
He asked him to explain what he had seen. The Master said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. It is your own mind, O worthy one, that moves.
Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Yinzong stood up in awe and wonder, asking, "The practitioner is certainly no ordinary person.
Who is your teacher? The monk recounted everything he had received without any concealment. Yinzong then performed the rites of a disciple and requested to receive the transmission of Chan.
Thereupon, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Yinzong is but an ordinary person in every respect; yet today he has encountered a Great Being in flesh and bone.

He then pointed out Layman Lu and requested that he bring forth the robe of faith, so that all might gaze upon and pay homage to it. On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, he gathered men of renowned virtue to serve as preceptors for his tonsure and full ordination.
There, beneath the Bodhi tree, he opened the Dharma-gate of Dongshan, as if in accordance with a long-standing karmic affinity.
In the autumn of the following year, he took leave to return to his former retreat at Baolin Monastery.

Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou, requested that he turn the Wheel of Dharma at Dafan Monastery and receive from him the Precepts of the Non-Substantial Mind-Ground. His disciples recorded these teachings, titling them the *Platform Sutra*, which became widely circulated throughout the world.
Later, he returned to Caoxi, where the great rain of the Dharma was bestowed and students gathered like clouds. During the Shenlong era, an imperial edict was issued.
The Emperor said: "I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to reside within the palace so that, during the intervals between the myriad affairs of state, I may investigate the True Vehicle.
Both masters declined, saying, 'In the south there is Master Neng; he received the robe and dharma of Great Master Ren in secret. You should go to him and inquire.
Now I have dispatched the inner attendant Xue Jian with this imperial decree to invite you. We pray that you will hasten to the capital. The Master ascended [the carriage].
The memorial states: "My wild nature is like ice and frost; I wish to spend my final years at the foot of the forest," and so forth.
Later, a monk asked Linji, "When the practitioner in the stone chamber was treading the pestle, why did he forget to move his foot? Linji replied, "He was submerged in a deep pit."
Baotán said: "The robe and bowl transmitted by seven hundred eminent monks at Huangmei were obtained by a miller.
Master Xiù was the foremost among scholars, yet a single four-line verse was bestowed upon one who could not read.
From this we know that the Buddha-dharma cannot be contended for by force, nor can it be seized through power. Old Lú fell [into the pit]..."
A boulder as large as several *shuo* sank into a deep pit; only Linji of later generations knew of it.
It was just like the Asura King who dragged the great cities of the triple world and the ocean of afflictions, yet did not realize the extent of his own power.
Holding a torch of fire, he requested someone to write upon the wall; this was to draw forth the arm of Master Xiu and bind it to Huangmei.
At that time, only Huangmei knew of it, just as when the *chuangzi* crossbow fired in a dream at Danyuan, the force of its discharge was not known by the dreamer himself.
Bodhidharma said: "I observe that the Divine Land of China possesses the spirit of the Mahāyāna. Beyond this—
Crossing the seas and deserts to seek the Dharma for the sake of others—this is like one lamp transmitting its light to another lamp, no less than a single hair pulling a weight of a thousand *jin*.
When this is reached, there is the principle that all people throughout the great earth are universally invited to attain Buddhahood;
this is the moment when the trigger of the bed-stool crossbow in the hands of the Asuras is used with perfect smoothness. Even Bodhidharma never once left behind his single shoe.
They departed for the West. Even the masters of Huangmei never once adjusted their robes or remained in silent stillness.
It has been barely six hundred years since the Sixth Patriarch passed away, yet the power of a drawn strong bow can no longer pierce Lu Gao silk. Alas!
It is tragic that his descendants cannot personally behold such a man; they know only that he did not use the Dharma of the Mind to slaughter the world, for future generations.
May students also hope to attain this? Chan Master Dajian,
the Sixth Patriarch, succeeded to the Dharma from Chan Master Zhidao of Guangzhou.

The Master visited the Sixth Patriarch and said, “I, a student, have recently left the household life and have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for barely more than ten years, yet I have not clarified its meaning.

I pray that the Honored Monk will grant me instruction. The Patriarch asked, “What is it that you have not understood? He replied, “Regarding the passage: ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss’—this is where I am in doubt. The Patriarch said, “How do you interpret this?”
"How do you doubt this? [The Master] replied, "All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The form-body is impermanent, having birth and cessation; the dharma-body is impermanent, without cognition, and without awareness. As the Sūtra says, 'When birth and cessation have ceased, nirvana is bliss.
I do not yet understand which body attains nirvana and which body experiences bliss. If it is the form-body..."
When the physical body perishes, the four great elements disperse; it is entirely suffering, and suffering cannot be called pleasure.
If the Dharma-body were in a state of quiescent extinction, it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones—who then would experience pleasure?

Furthermore, the Dharma-nature is the essence of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing. The one essence and five functions mean that arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, it proceeds from the essence.
When functioning arises, it withdraws its function back into the essence upon cessation. If rebirth were permitted, then the class of sentient beings would neither cease nor be extinguished;
if rebirth were not permitted, they would forever return to quiescent extinction and become identical to insentient things.
Thus, all dharmas would be suppressed by nirvana and would not even be able to arise—what joy could there be in that? —The Patriarch.
He said: "You are a disciple of the Śākya; why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism to discuss the Supreme Vehicle?
According to your understanding, you claim that apart from the physical body there is a separate Dharma-body, and that one seeks nirvana by departing from birth and death.

Furthermore, you infer that because Nirvana is eternal and blissful, there must be a physical body that experiences it. This is nothing but clinging to birth and death and being addicted to worldly pleasures. You—
Now you should know: for all those deluded beings who mistake the composite of the five aggregates for their own self-nature and discriminate all phenomena as external objects;
who cherish life and loathe death, drifting through the flux of every thought-moment;

who do not realize that things are like dreams and illusions, falsely undergoing saṃsāra, and who instead of the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa perceive it as a form of suffering—the Buddha, out of compassion, [teaches them].
For this reason, he demonstrates the true bliss of nirvāṇa: for a moment there is no mark of arising; for a moment there is no mark of cessation.

Since there is further no arising or cessation to be extinguished, this is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śamatha*). At the time of its manifestation, there is also no measure of manifestation;
this is what is called bliss. One should always delight in this bliss. There is neither one who experiences it nor one who does not experience it. How could there be...?
This is already the designation for "one essence and five functions"; how much more so when one further claims that *nirvāṇa* suppresses and subdues all dharmas so that they never arise again?
This is indeed to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse: The unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa*, Perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating.
Ordinary fools call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation. Those seeking the two vehicles regard it as non-action.

All these belong to the conceptualizations of the emotional mind—the very root of the sixty-two views. They are merely false and provisional names conceived by deluded thoughts; how could they be the true meaning?
Only those of superior capacity penetrate the state beyond grasping or rejecting; for they know the phenomena of the five aggregates as well as the "self" within those aggregates.
To them, the external manifestations of sounds and forms—each and every characteristic of sound—are equal to dreams and illusions, such that neither ordinary nor holy views arise.

One does not form the conceptualization of nirvana; the two extremes and the three periods of time are severed. One constantly employs the functions of the sense faculties, yet does not give rise to the thought of such employment.

One discriminates all phenomena, yet does not give rise to the thought of discrimination. Even when the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and winds strike mountains together in collision, [the mind remains unmoved].
"The bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—such is the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*. I now speak these words by force; you should now abandon your false views.
Do not follow the literal meaning of my words; I permit you only a partial understanding. Upon hearing this verse, the teacher leaped for joy, prostrated himself, and withdrew.
Baotan said: Chan is the Buddha’s mind; the sutras are the Buddha’s words. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra* contains the "Chapter on the Mind of the Buddha’s Words";

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* contains the meaning of opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* contains the principle of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
All are but one Way. It is like a lute, a zither, or a harp: though they possess exquisite sounds, if there is no...
The "wondrous finger" can ultimately never produce [the sound]; the finger is indeed the wondrous sound, and speech is indeed the Buddha-mind.
To take the wondrous sound as the finger and speech as the Buddha-mind—is this not perverse? The ancients forgot the relationship between sound and finger;
their minds were in suspended resonance with their speech. As Zhaozhou said: "All people are made use of by Bodhi; I, the old monk, make use of them."
Once one has attained Bodhi, one is able to mold earth into gold and mold gold into earth;
all of this is the natural function of my own mind, requiring no other artifice.
After Chan Master Yinzong of Faxing Temple in Guangzhou had traveled to Qichun to pay his respects to Great Master Ren, he subsequently lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Guangzhou’s Faxing Temple.
It was only upon meeting the Great Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, that he first awakened to the profound principle.

He took Huineng as his Dharma-transmitting teacher and further compiled the sayings of eminent masters from various quarters spanning the Liang to the Tang dynasties, composing the *Xinyao ji* (Collection of the Essence of Mind), which became widely circulated throughout the world.
Baotán said: The Elder Zhēnjìng remarked that when Dharma Master Yìnzōng asked Layman Lú, "What instructions, essential points, and transmissions did you receive from Huángméi?
Lú replied, "That which he transmitted to me concerned only the realization of nature to attain Buddhahood;
it did not speak of dhyāna-concentration, liberation, non-thought, or non-action. Yìnzōng asked, "Why did he not speak of these?"
"Dhyāna, samādhi, liberation, non-thought, and non-action. Lu said, "Moreover, these are dualistic dharmas;
they are not the Buddha-dharma of non-duality. Zong asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma of non-duality?
Lu said, "For instance, when you, sir, lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature—this is called the Buddha-dharma of non-duality. Zhenjing said:

That was merely cleverness; the Way of Chan had already reached its midpoint. Nowadays, the monastic communities discuss nothing but meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimukti*), non-thought (*amanyana*), and non-action (*avikṛta*). Yet, tell me: which is it? That of the Sixth Patriarch, or that of today? How profound these words are!
It has been eighty finger-snap moments since Zhenjing departed. As for meditative concentration and liberation in later generations—

There is no thought, no action, and likewise no hearing. Those who are able to excavate the past and present, to bring forth and let names and phrases emerge, and who grasp the "dead snake" with such certainty that it becomes a "living scorpion"—they alone possess the True Eye (samyag-dṛṣṭi) to transmit and bestow it upon one another.

In this age, there is no one of great knowledge and vision to distinguish between the correct and the heterodox; even if such a person were to exist, they would find it difficult to prevail against the "unified chorus of Chu," where the masses all join in as one.
"Alas! When the Buddha-dharma reaches this point, can one not feel heartache?
Master Xingsi of Qingyuan Mountain in Jizhou went to Caoxi to pay his respects and asked: 'What should one apply oneself to so as not to fall into stages? The Patriarch said: 'You..."
"What have you done? The Master replied, "I have not even practiced the Noble Truths; what levels or stages could there be?
The Patriarch regarded him with deep esteem, remarking, "In seeing the atmosphere of Shaolin, I see the Second Patriarch. Later, he resided at Qingyuan Jingju Temple.
When the Sixth Patriarch was about to pass away, the novice Xiqian—this is Shitou—asked, "After the Master has passed on, Xiqian..."

"To whom should one turn for refuge? The Master said, "Seek and contemplate. When the Master passed away, [Nanyue] moved to a quiet place and sat upright, remaining silent and forgetting his own existence.
His senior disciple said, "Your teacher has already departed; what is the purpose of sitting here in vain? He replied, "I am contemplating because I have received my teacher's final instructions.
The senior disciple said, "You have an elder brother, Master Xingsi, who resides at Qingyuan in Jizhou. Because of this...
"The conditions lie there. Your teacher’s words were very direct; it is you who are deluded. When Huian heard this, he took his leave and went to Jingju.
The Master asked him, "From where have you come? He replied, "From Caoxi. The Master said, "What did you bring back from there?
He replied, "Even before arriving at Caoxi, I had not lost anything. The Master said, "If that is so, then what was the use of going to Caoxi? He replied, "If I had not gone..."
"Who would have known that Caoxi did not lose it? He asked again, "Does the Great Master of Caoxi recognize you, Reverend?
The Master said, "Do you recognize me now? He replied, "I recognize him, yet how could I truly recognize him? The Master said, "Though there may be many horns, a single unicorn is enough.
The Master then instructed him to take a letter to Reverend Letang of Nanyue. After delivering the letter, he was to return quickly with a small axe for you.

Zhuzi was staying at the mountain. Upon arriving there, before he had even presented his letter, [Nanyuan] asked him: "When one does not admire the various sages and does not prize one's own spiritual nature, what then?
Nanyuan said, "Your question is far too lofty, my son. Why do you not ask about things that are more down-to-earth?

Zhuzi replied, "I would rather undergo eternal sinking and delusion than seek liberation through the sages. Nanyuan then desisted, and Zhuzi returned. The Master (Baizhang) asked him: "Not long after you left, I sent..."
[The messenger] said, "The letter did not reach you. [Dongshan] asked, "The letter did not reach you, and the message was not delivered either? The master said, "How so?

He then recounted the previous conversation and concluded by saying, "When I left, I was granted the promise of the 'Ox-Handle Axe' (Caofuzi) by the Master; I now request it. The master then dangled down one of his feet.
Thereupon, he took his leave with formal bows. A monk from Mount Nanyue asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha?
The Master replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling? Baotian said: "When Qingyuan attained the Way, he possessed the full majesty of the Second Patriarch at Shaolin. At that time..."
It is now the late autumn season; yet the atmosphere of warmth and gentleness is most prevalent in the southeast.
Although his thoughts turned toward Jiangxi, his ancestral home was in Nanhai, which he regarded as the southeast of the Middle Kingdom.

While the Buddha-dharma does not take the climate or topography of a land as a matter of joy or sorrow, human beings are born endowed with the central harmony of Heaven and Earth; they receive this central harmony of Heaven and Earth.
It has never been the case that one cannot attain the central harmony of the Way. Qingyuan was the father and the patriarch;

his son, Shitou, manifested externally through the resonance of their shared spiritual energy. Their grandsons, Yaoshan and Yunyan, gave rise to the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Longtan and Deshan flowed forth from within the "price of rice in Luling. They had a father.
I do not believe that one who possesses the heroic spirit and majesty of our ancestors, and who has attained the central harmony of Heaven and Earth, could fail to become a sage,
a worthy, a stern father and teacher, or a model of the Dharma.

When Chan Master Huairang of Nanyue arrived at Caoxi, the Sixth Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What kind of thing is it that comes like this?
The Master was speechless. After eight years had passed, he suddenly attained realization and said to the Patriarch, "I have something..."

At the meeting place, the Patriarch asked, "How do you understand this? He replied, "To call it a single thing is not appropriate. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still anything to be cultivated or realized?
He replied, "There is indeed nothing that is not to be cultivated or realized; yet one must not allow oneself to be defiled.
The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is what all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. [This concludes the account of] West India..."
Multarāśmi prophesied: "From beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. The Master served him for fifteen years.
In the second year of the Xuantian era of the Tang dynasty, he resided at Prajñā Monastery on Mount Heng. Addressing his disciples, he said: "All myriad phenomena arise from the mind.
The mind is fundamentally unborn, and phenomena likewise have no abiding place. If one reaches this level ground, all actions will be unimpeded."
This is not for those of superior faculties; one must be cautious with one’s words. A monk asked, “When a mirror is used to cast an image, once the image is formed, where does the light go?
The Master said, “When you, Venerable Sir, had not yet left the household life, where did your physical form go?
The monk said, “Once it has been formed, why does it no longer reflect? The Master said, “Although it does not reflect, not a single point can deceive it.”
There was a monk named Daoyi who resided at the Chan Court Hermitage and constantly sat in meditation.
The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation? Daoyi replied, "I hope to become a Buddha.

The Master then took a brick and began polishing it on a stone in front of the hermitage. Daoyi asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "I am polishing it to make a mirror. Daoyi said, "How can polishing a brick..."
[The student] said, "I can make a mirror. The Master said, "By practicing *zazen*, how could one become a Buddha?
He immediately left his seat and asked, "How is it so? The Master said, "It is like an ox pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, do you strike the cart or do you strike the ox?
He further said, "In your practice of *zazen*, are you learning to sit as a Buddha? If you are learning *zazen*, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you are learning to sit..."
"Buddha. A Buddha is not a fixed phenomenon; regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as a Buddha, that is precisely killing the Buddha.
If you cling to the form of sitting, you have not realized its principle. Upon hearing this instruction, he was like one drinking the finest clarified butter (*amṛta*).
He immediately prostrated and asked, "How should I apply my mind to accord with the signless samādhi? The Master said, "You must study the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground."
"It is like a seed. I have preached the essentials of the Dharma, which is like the rain from heaven; you shall perceive the Way through the convergence of conditions.
He asked again, "The Way has no form or characteristics; how can it be seen? The Master said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way;
so too is the signless samādhi. He asked once more, "Is there arising and ceasing? The Master said, "If one regards it as..."

To claim that one perceives the Way by destroying the aggregates and dispersing them is erroneous. Listen to my verse: The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When it encounters moisture, they all sprout.
The flower of samādhi is formless; What is there to destroy, and what is there to establish?
Baotan said: "The realization of the vast and great cannot be accomplished in a single lifetime.

It is like Mount Sumeru, which, though formed by the accumulation of dust, at first appears no different from the surrounding Cakravāḍa mountains; yet when it rises on all four sides, it completely encompasses the Cakravāḍas.
Even the power of a hundred kalpas cannot reach it. This is for no other reason than the inherent nature of smallness and greatness. (Nan)
The Way of Mount [Heng] is simple and easy to perceive, clear and easy to understand.
Though those with a beginner’s mind may seem capable of entering deeply, once they extend a hand, there is a force that cannot be lightly exerted;
when they take a single martial step, there is a ground that cannot be casually trodden. If everyone were like Nanyue or like a colt, then the void would be completely filled.
All things empty are destined for those who possess the Way. Generally speaking, if one’s ancestors were brave and resolute, their descendants will suffer no affliction of decline or weakness.

Yet even when the Duke of Tai governed Qi and the Duke of Zhou governed Lu, they could not avoid the criticism that their lineages would eventually become increasingly powerful or increasingly feeble. How can one not be cautious?
Chan Master Xuangjue of Wenzhou went to Caoxi.
Upon his initial arrival, he shook his staff, carried his water jar, and circumambulated the Patriarch three times, then stood there motionless. The Patriarch said:

"A śramaṇa is one who possesses three thousand points of dignified demeanor and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you, Great Virtue, come as to give rise to such great conceit?
The Master said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising?
Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? The Master said, "Realizing it is non-arising; understanding it is fundamentally without swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is."
This was so. At that time, the great assembly was struck with amazement. The Master then performed his salutations with full ceremonial decorum and took his leave after a short while.
The Patriarch said, "Is your return too swift? The Master replied, "Since it is fundamentally not moving, how could there be swiftness? The Patriarch asked, "Who knows it is not moving?"
The Master said, "You yourself give rise to discrimination. The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising.
The Master said, "How can non-arising have any meaning? The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who is it that discriminates? The Master said, "Discrimination, too, is not a matter of meaning."
The Patriarch sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one night. At that time, he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yi-xiu-jue).

The following day, he returned to Yongjia, where he composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) in one chapter, along with the *Words on the Perfect Attainment of Awakening and Cultivation in the Chan School*, both of which circulate in the world to this day.

Furthermore, there are the *Ten Gates of Contemplating the Mind*: first, it speaks of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); second, it sets forth the essence of contemplation; third, it describes its characteristics.
1. It should [be understood that] the fourth [point] serves to warn against arrogance; 2. the fifth serves to admonish against negligence; 3. the sixth reiterates the essence of contemplation;

4. the seventh clarifies what is right and wrong; 5. the eighth simplifies the explanatory terminology; 6. the ninth shows how every encounter becomes contemplation; 7. and the tenth brings about a wondrous realization of the profound source, and so forth.
Baotán said: "Yǒngjiā wished to establish the fundamental tenets [of the school]; he could not help but come once to Cáoqī.

Once they met and their minds were in accord, he could not help but stay for one night before departing. When the path between teacher and disciple was fully realized, the teachings of the Buddha were forgotten.
Truly, he was like a dragon leaping from the gate of Longmén, or a solitary falcon among a flock of birds. His fellow disciples included Lǎng of Zuǒxī and others.
Yang Ce and his peers were all, in their own time, the very repositories of the sūtras and śāstras. While Daolang followed Zhiyi as his master, Yang Ce went to Caoxi.

"In every three steps there must be someone from whom I can learn"—this is what Yongjia meant. Yongjia’s realization of the Way was extraordinary and sublime, such that none before or since has equaled it.
That final word was something he had personally realized through his own efforts at Caoxi. As the ancients said:
Having attained awakening, one must necessarily encounter a person. If one does not encounter such a person, it truly becomes a mere empty exercise.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One contemplates the sequence of dharmas and discriminates them with wisdom; having definitively determined right and wrong, one does not violate the seal of the Dharma.

Is this not what is meant by Yongjia’s statement that "discrimination is also not of the mind"? The *Song of Enlightenment* is what the Western Regions call the *Sūtra of the Sage of Zhendan*. That is to say—
The final teaching of Caoxi is like rainwater from the heavens that meanders into the sea and returns to the heavens;
only those who ride the raft upon the tide can truly know this.
Chan Master Benjing of Sengong Mountain received the profound essence of Caoxi’s teaching and was affiliated with Wuxiang Temple on Mount Sengong.

During the Tianbao era of the Tang Dynasty, Emperor Xuanzong dispatched the imperial envoy Yang Guangting into the mountains to gather *changchun* (evergreen) vines. Upon reaching the Master’s chamber, he asked: "I, your disciple, admire the Way."
"It has been a long time. I only wish that you would grant me your instruction. The Master said, "The eminent scholars of the Chan school throughout the empire have all assembled in the capital.

When the imperial messenger returns to court, you will be able to consult them for a definitive resolution. As for this poor monk, he dwells by the mountains and beside the waters with no concerns to occupy his mind. Guangting bowed in tears.
The Master said, "Cease bowing to this poor monk. Does the Celestial Messenger come to seek the Buddha or to inquire about the Way?
The messenger replied, "Your disciple’s understanding is clouded and dull; I do not yet know the meaning of 'Buddha' and 'the Way'.

The Master said, "If you wish to seek the Buddha, the very mind is the Buddha. If you wish to realize the Way, no-mind is the Way. The messenger asked, "In what sense is the very mind the Buddha? The Master said, "The Buddha..."

One awakens through the mind; the mind is manifested by the Buddha. If one awakens to the absence of mind, even the Buddha does not exist. [The questioner] asked: "How is it that the absence of mind is the Way?
The Master said: "The Way is fundamentally without mind; the absence of mind is called the Way. If one realizes the absence of mind, then the absence of mind is itself the Way."

Guangting paid his respects and accepted [the teachings] with faith. Upon returning to the palace, he submitted a detailed report on what he had heard in the mountains. In the twelfth month, the Master was summoned to reside at Bailian Pavilion.
The following year, an imperial edict was issued for the eminent monks and great scholars of the Left and Right Monastic Quarters to expound upon Buddhist principles together with the Master.
He analyzed each point with flowing eloquence. Finally, Master An Chan asked, "If you say that all things are illusory, then illusion is the same as reality.
Since there is no distinction between reality and illusion, what exactly is it? The Master replied, "If one asks 'what,' then every thing is also illusory.
As the sutra says: 'There is nothing similar; there is no analogy. The path of language is cut off, like a bird flying through the sky. This is what I have shared with you, Master."
Several individuals questioned and debated this point; their arguments are numerous and have not been recorded here.
Baotan said: "The mind itself is the Buddha; the absence of mind is the Way. From the Buddhas to the patriarchs, all have appeared with no differing teachings.
No-mind is Buddha; this very mind is the Way. Buddhas and patriarchs have jointly realized that there is no dharma apart from this.
Therefore, within this state, they press out "stone-fire" and let go of "lightning-flash" to manifest no-mind;

Zhong asked the Master, "What is it like? The Master said, "It is like a dog. Zhong asked Nanquan, "What is it like?

The monk said, "Since he already possesses it, why is he not ill? Caoshan said, "Because he is alert and conscious.

He laughed and said, "A rat caught by a cat would be better off being renamed a cat.

[The Master] shot a flock of birds with a single arrow. [The monk] said, "Since both parties possess life, why shoot that flock?
The Patriarch said, "Since you know this to be so, why do you not shoot yourself? [The monk] said, "If you were to command me to shoot myself, there would truly be no place to apply my hand."
The Patriarch said, "This man's ignorance and afflictions, accumulated over vast kalpas, have today been suddenly stilled.

The Master immediately destroyed his bow and arrows, cut off his hair, and threw himself at the Patriarch’s feet to leave the household life. One day, while he was performing labor in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing?

He replied, "I am tending the ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you tend it? He replied, "Whenever it enters the grass, I pull it back by the nose. The Patriarch said, "You are truly [a practitioner]."
He was a cowherd. After he became the abbot, he would often receive visitors with bow and arrow. When Sanping arrived, the Master made a gesture of drawing his bow and said, "Watch the arrow!
Sanping made a gesture of dodging. The Master said, "In my life, I have drawn one bow and shot one arrow;
it has only managed to hit half a saint. The Master asked Xitang, "Can you catch empty space? Xitang said, "I can."
"Attained. The Master asked, "How do you catch it? Xitang pinched empty space with his hand once. The Master said, "How can you catch empty space in such a way?
Xitang then asked the Master, "How do you catch it, elder brother? The Master grabbed Xitang by the nose and pulled.
Xitang made a cry of pain and said, "You are pulling too hard! You are pulling my nostrils right off!"
The Master said, "You must grasp empty space in this very way before you will succeed. During the monks' period of inquiry, the Master asked, "Where has that which was just here gone?
A monk replied, "It is here. The Master asked, "Where is it? The monk snapped his fingers once. Another monk approached and bowed.
The Master asked, "Have you brought that thing back? The monk replied, "I have brought it back. The Master asked, "Where is it?"
[The monk asked: "In what place? [The Master] snapped his fingers three times. [The monk] asked: "How can one avoid birth and death? The Master said: "What need is there to avoid it?
[The monk] asked: "How then can one avoid it? The Master said: "This very thing does not undergo birth and death."
Baotan said: "Shigong pursued the deer, and Mazu caught the deer. The Patriarch said, 'This man's ignorance from kalpas past has been instantly extinguished.
These words possess a force as heavy as ten thousand *qun*. His lifelong tending of the ox was this very force;
his seizing of empty space was this very force. Therefore, Bodhidharma said, 'One attains it through the practice of affairs.'"
The Dharma possesses powerful strength. One who perceives the Dharma within their activities will not fail in any situation;
this is what is meant by Shigong. Thus, throughout his life, he drew his bow and set his arrow, claiming that he could only shoot half of a sage.
He did not know that Master Mashi had come in person. "Could one person suffice?

The Master said, "He-he. Yangshan then stood on the eastern side, then stood on the western side, and then stood in the center.
After he had finished receiving the precepts, he withdrew to stand behind. The Master asked, "Where did you obtain this samādhi?
Yangshan replied, "I learned it from the 'mold' at Caoxi. The Master asked, "Whom does Caoxi employ this samādhi to receive? Yangshan said:
Upon meeting Yexiu Jue, [Nanquan] asked, "Where did you obtain this samādhi, Master? The Master replied, "I learned it from Master Mazu.
[The monk] asked, "How does one realize one's nature? The Master said, "It is like a house with six windows."
Inside there was a monkey. When [the Master] called "Shanshan" from the east, Shanshan responded; he did so likewise from all six windows.
Yangshan bowed in thanks, rose, and said, "I have understood everything through the Honored One’s parable. However, there is one further matter."
"Just as the inner monkey is drowsy with sleep, how is it when the outer monkey wishes to meet him?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, took Yangshan’s hand, and danced, saying, "Shanshan, I have already met you.

once one enters the realm of expedients, one immediately encounters gain and loss. It is like the six windows calling out 'Mountain, Mountain'—in later generations..."

One day, while the Master was attending upon Mazu as they were walking, they saw a wild duck fly past. Mazu asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "A wild duck. Mazu said, [and continued].
“Where did you go? the Master asked. The Teacher replied, “I flew away. The Patriarch then twisted the Teacher’s nostrils, causing him to let out a cry of pain.

The Patriarch said, “When did you ever fly away? At these words, the Teacher attained realization. The next day, when the Patriarch ascended the hall and had just sat down, the Teacher stepped forward and rolled up the cushion before him.
The Patriarch immediately descended from his seat, and the Teacher followed him to the abbot’s quarters. The Patriarch asked, “From where have you come?”
The Master said, "I have come from the mountain. The Patriarch asked, "Did you encounter anyone on the way?
The Master said, "I did not encounter anyone. The Patriarch asked, "Why did you not encounter anyone? The Master said, "If I had encountered anyone, I would have reported it to the Master.
The Patriarch said, "From where did you receive this news? The Master said, "It is my fault. The Patriarch said, "On the contrary, it is my own fault."
