The Master said, "I ask the Master to withdraw his feet. Mazu said, "Once extended, they are not retracted. The Master said, "Once advanced, they are not withdrawn."

He did not retreat; instead, he pushed the cart over him, crushing his exposed foot. The Patriarch returned to the Dharma Hall, grasping an axe and saying, "Come out, you who just now crushed the old monk’s foot!
The Master then stepped forward before the Patriarch and extended his neck. The Patriarch then set down the axe.
Later, when the Master arrived at Nanquan and saw the assembly of monks in session, Nanquan pointed to a water pitcher and said, "The copper pitcher is an object. Within the pitcher..."
"There is water. You must not touch the vessel. Bring the water to the old monk. The Master then took the clean pitcher and poured it out before Nanquan.
Nanquan then desisted. While at Xiangzhou, he was presiding over the Hall of Broken Dignity;
wearing only his undergarments by the iron mallet, he said, "If you can speak, I shall not strike you. At that time, the assembly remained silent. The Master then struck him once.

The Master took his leave of Mazu and headed for Shitou; the details of their conversation are recorded in the *Mazu Chapter*. During winter, the Master resided at Mount Heng, and during summer, he stayed at Qingliang.
In the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled to Mount Wutai; on his way, he passed through Huaisi, where Wu Yuanji had mobilized troops to rebel and defy royal authority.
When the imperial army and the rebels were locked in combat and neither side had yet emerged victorious, the Master said, "I shall go there."

To resolve their distress, he tossed his *śikya* staff into the air and passed through it with his body flying. The officers and soldiers of both armies looked up at this event, which fulfilled the dream of Fu Yu;
their hearts to fight were instantly stilled. Once the Master had manifested such supernatural wonders, he feared they would lead the masses into delusion.
He then entered the Vajra Cave, and before manifesting his final nirvana, he asked the assembly: "In various regions, I have often seen those who pass away while sitting or lying down."
"Is there anyone who has manifested parinirvāṇa while standing upright? The assembly replied, "There is. The Master asked, "Is there anyone who has manifested parinirvāṇa while standing on his head?
The assembly replied, "No one has yet done so. Thereupon, the Master manifested parinirvāṇa while standing on his head; he remained perfectly erect, his robes falling naturally over his body.
Baotan said: "If one claims that Yinfeng was a sage, then he twice encountered the 'slippery path' of Shitou.
If one claims that Yinfeng was not a sage, then there remains the extraordinary account of his single staff soaring into the air and the imperial army ceasing its battle.
Thus we know that the Way of the Patriarchs cannot be fathomed or deliberated by ordinary sages. From this point on, [Yinfeng] could neither control his father Mazu nor his elder brother Nanyue."

He was like a spring from which no one dared to question him; though he came and went, breaking conventional decorum and performing the affairs of a minor forest monastery, he was a sage who had attained the Way—a tiger with wings.
When he stood on his head to transform others, his robes remained upright and tall, perfectly conforming to his body.
Someone once asked Huitang about this, and Master Huitang said, "When you stand in your ordinary state, your robes likewise [conform to your body]."
"Does this accord with your own nature? It is not that I say a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is encountered only once every few hundred years;
how extraordinary! Master Wujou!"
The Master was visited by the two senior monks, Xuán and Shào, who had come from Jiangxi to seek instruction. The Master asked, "Where did you two masters of Chan set out from?
Xuán replied, "Jiangxi. The Master took up his staff and struck him. Xuán said, "I have long known that the Master possesses such a vital pivot of teaching.
The Master said, "Since you do not understand, come forward, monk behind me. As Shào prepared to step forward, the Master—
He then struck him and said, "I know for certain that there is no difference between the same pit and its soil. Go to the hall. Baotan said:
"Wujou used the fodder of his own station to receive the two senior monks; this is what is proper for a true teacher of goodness (Sanskrit:
*kalyāṇamitra*). It is like a horned eagle catching a rabbit: with a single snatch from the bellows-like fist, the rabbit leaves no trace behind. People today..."
Nowadays, Chan masters and followers of the Buddha-dharma engage in a chaotic fray with their students;

though they possess long spears and great halberds, they set them aside and do not employ them, instead attacking one another with nothing but shards and rubble. An onlooker cannot help but laugh at this. To seek the preservation of the seeds of Buddhahood so that they are never severed is impossible under such conditions.

Chan Master Dashan of Shishuang in Tanzhou was asked by a monk, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "The rooster crows in spring; the dog barks on the Mid-Autumn festival.
The Master ascended the hall and said, "Everyone, come forth! Come forth! The old monk has a vital teaching to give. After a hundred years..."
"I will not trouble you. The assembly said, "We request that the Master speak. The Master said, "It does not require even a single pile of fire.
Dongshan asked, "A young boy before the altar was very capable; where has he gone now that we no longer see him? The Master said:
"One cannot rest upon the flames; one must return to the world of cool clarity.
Baotan said: "The rooster crowing on a spring day, the dog barking on a mid-autumn night—this is the matter within the fierce flames of Shishuang."
It is called a raging fire. To aim at it is to be consumed; to approach it is to be scorched. Fire can burn others but cannot burn itself.
Yet within the flames themselves, there is inherently a world of coolness; only fire knows this, though in truth it does not know it.
When I speak thus, it is precisely a matter of the shadows and light at the edge of that raging fire.
Chan Master Shenzang of Maitou Peak in Cizhou addressed the assembly, saying:
"To know while being without knowing is not the same as being without knowing; yet it is called 'being without knowing. Nanquan said, "Only by following the Master’s words can one attain half of it.
Huangbo remarked, "It was not that Nanquan was stripping away [the meaning]; he intended to complete the previous statement."
Baotan said: "The single word 'knowing' is a source of calamity. Even with all the power of Shenzang, one could not turn this calamity into fortune;
it has resulted in Nanquan and Huangbo being regarded as people who rejoice in misfortune.
Had I been born several years later, and studied the *I Ching* at the age of fifty, I might have avoided great error. This is a matter within Shenzang's own sphere; it is 'knowing.'"
"The Spring and Autumn Annals praise me; the Spring and Autumn Annals condemn me. This is the matter concerning Nanquan.
"Since I obtained Zilu, evil words have not entered my ears. This is the matter concerning Huangbo.
"Worldly speech and the means of livelihood are all non-contradictory with the true mark (*dharmatā*). These words cannot be dismissed as mere rhetoric.

Master Liang of Xishan in Hongzhou had abandoned the study of the sutras and śāstras. Upon visiting Mazu, Mazu asked him, "I have heard it said that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras;
is this true? Liang replied, "I dare not say so. Mazu asked, "With what do you lecture? Liang replied, "I lecture with the mind. Mazu said, "The mind..."
It was like a troupe of performers; the Master’s mind was like a master of ceremonies who competed with them to see who could explain and expound best.

Huilang raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot be explained, perhaps empty space can? The Patriarch replied, "Indeed, it is empty space that can explain. The Master shook out his sleeves and departed.
The Patriarch then called out, "Dharma Master! The Master turned his head. The Patriarch said, "From birth until old age, you have been nothing but this."
The Master [Huilang] attained great enlightenment. He then prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "Why does this dull-witted monk prostrate?
Huilang returned and told the assembly, "I used to claim that no one could equal me in the exegesis of the sutras and śāstras.
Today, having been questioned by Master Ma, my lifelong efforts have melted away like ice. Thereafter, he retired to Mount Xi, and no further news of him was heard.
Baotán said: "The manner in which Master Mā (Mazu) received Master Liàng was of a distinct character, entirely different from how he received his eighty-odd other disciples.
Liàng’s seclusion in the Western Mountains was also a matter of his very nature. Yet, once gone, he did not return;
the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs values the transmission of one lamp from one lamp—this was Liàng’s intent. Master Mā’s...
The gatekeeper was no less a guest to him; thus, he ultimately fulfilled his aspirations. To this day, those living in the Western Mountains frequently see him.
During the Zhenghe era, there was a scholar surnamed Xiong whose name has been lost; his family had long resided in Poyang.

While traveling among the various mountains of Hongzhou, his path led past Cuoyan. At that time, the Elder Simun, who was a native of that region, sent two laborers to carry him in a sedan chair to the abode of Kongsang.
As they passed through dense forests and secluded valleys, he suddenly beheld a monk whose appearance was ancient and whose spirit was pure;
with bushy eyebrows and a snow-white head, clad in garments woven from leaves, he sat upon a flat rock like a figure depicted in a mural.

Regarding the image of Fotucheng, Xiong suspected he was an extraordinary person. He thought to himself that Master Liang had been living in seclusion in the Western Mountains and feared this might be him.
Feeling hesitant and respectful, he asked, "Could this be Master Liang? The monk pointed his hand toward the east;
Xiong turned his head to follow the direction of the hand, but the monk had vanished. At that time, a light rain had recently cleared, and Xiong stroked the place where the monk had sat.
The stone was still warm. He looked around in hesitation and sighed, saying, "My past affinities were not profound; meeting [you] is as if not meeting at all."
Dharma-heir of Master Dayang was Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi. Once,
while Master Yi was engaged in seated meditation, the Master said, "Master Yi, recently a certain class of Chan masters point toward the present moment."
The Master said, "I have taught people enough. One who takes up the affairs before one's eyes to act for others—do you still understand the state when the literary patterns have not yet manifested?
He replied, "I wish to pose a question here to ask the Master; I do not know if it would be permitted. The Master said:
The Master replied, "You have already understood; do not speak of 'yes' or 'no. The man said, "Do you recognize what is right before you?
The Master asked, "How would you recognize what is right before you? The man said, "In any case, it is subject to scrutiny. The Master asked, "By whom? The man said, "By me.
The Master then gave him a shout. The man stepped back and stood there. The Master said, "You only know how to look forward; you do not know how to look behind."
Later, Yi said, "Adding frost upon snow. The Master said, "Neither side gains any advantage.
Baotan remarked, "This refers to a time before any signs of literary expression appeared.

Nowadays, people push themselves into a vast, shimmering void and willingly settle into the midst of silent, dark obscurity, even going so far as to bestow names upon it, calling it 'before King Vairocana' or 'the edge of the empty kalpa.'"
Little do they realize that this is precisely within the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain.

As for what is called "when the patterns have not yet manifested," even sixty kalpas of three lifetimes would not have been enough to dream of it. He said, "I intend to pose a question here to ask the Master;
I do not know if I may. Yang said, "My answer to you is already finished; do not ask whether you may or may not. This is what is called—
Is it possible to engage with the present matter? When its patterns have not yet manifested, one must see it only after attaining definitive awakening.
Once seen, both the seeing and the awakening must be cast away; only then does it become one and the same as the Great Sun. Master Yi used this very matter for Chan practice.
People today are not masters who can ride the tide; I urge you not to enter the surging waves. The surging waves are heartless and will destroy your life.

The Chan Master Niu-tou of Zhenzhou personally prepared rice to offer to the assembly of monks. Every time it was mealtime, he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the Sangha Hall, dance, and say, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat!
Then he would clap his hands and laugh loudly. He did this every day. One day, as the Master approached...
When Nanquan came, he leaned his staff crosswise across the pillars and sat before the Abbot. Nanquan then clapped his hands three times and returned to the hall.
After the master had dismissed the attendants and finished his affairs, he asked: "When guest and host meet, each has their proper etiquette.

Why did you, the Senior Monk (Zhangfang), act so discourteously? Nanquan said, "What are you talking about? As the Master was about to open his mouth, Nanquan struck him with his sitting mat, and the Master fell over.
Ji struck his meditation mat once more. The Master said, "Today you have missed your chance," and then returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Baotán said: "The mechanism of Niu-tou was like setting fire to dry grass with a favorable wind;

yet many people see only minor benefits and forget the great matter, so not a single person managed to enter his gate. They do not realize that once one has entered the gate, the host is truly skillful."
What plan was devised afterward? At that time, I regretted not having someone who could "sit upon the tiger's head and seize its tail" to contend with him by force,
thereby allowing the mechanism of the Golden Ox to escape alone into the Great Way,
so that it might stir the hearts of posterity like the gold of the people of Qin or the fire of Tian Dan.

Chan Master Dadi of Xinzhou had received the essential instructions from Jiangxi. He concealed his own name; whenever a student came to pose a question, he would only respond by striking the ground with his staff.
Thus, he was known at the time as "Master Dadi" (Staff-Striking). One day, a monk hid the staff away before questioning him. The Master [responded].
He merely opened his mouth wide. A monk asked a disciple, "Whenever someone asks a question, the Master simply strikes the ground; what is the meaning of this?
The disciple immediately took a piece of firewood from beneath the hearth and threw it into the cauldron.
Baotan said: "A sudden blow of the staff is like the crash of a bolt of lightning.
The thunder has no intention to strike, yet those who feel resentment happen to encounter it; thus, the thunder is able to unleash its full power. Beating the ground is much like this.
During the era when the Buddha-dharma was at its zenith, various quarters were vast in their discourse on Chan, and there were inevitably instances of both enmity and gratitude."
"Among those matters, I would rather bear the blame myself; I cannot bear to let another person down. The mechanism of a striking lightning bolt allows no time for concealment.
At that moment, even my disciples were somewhat clever yet largely ignorant."
Chan Master Shanjue of Hualin in Tanzhou constantly carried his mendicant’s staff.
At night, he would go out among the forest slopes; every seven paces he would shake his staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara once.
Jiashan Shanhui went to the hermitage and asked, "I have recently heard that you, Master, recite the name of Avalokiteśvara; is this true? The Master replied, "Yes.

Shanhui said, "If you are already mounted upon his head, how can you do so? The Master said, "If you come out from under the head, I will let you ride; if you do not come out from under the head, what is there to ride?"
A monk came to pay his respects. Just as he was unfolding his sitting mat, the Master said, "Slowly, slowly. The monk asked, "What do you see, Preceptor?
The Master said, "It is a pity that you have just struck and broken the bell. From this, the monk attained awakening.
One day, the Inspector Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Does the Master have any attendants? The Master replied, "There are one or two. Pei asked, "Where are they?"
"Where are you? The Master then called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng! At that moment, two tigers emerged from behind the hermitage.

Pí was struck with terror upon seeing them. The Master said to them, "There is a guest; now depart. The two tigers roared and left. Pí asked, "What kind of practice did you perform to evoke such a response?
After a long silence, the Master said, "Do you understand? Pí replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The mountain..."
The monk was constantly mindful of Avalokiteśvara.
Baotán said: "This old fellow is sandalwood at night and cow dung by day; even tigers and wolves would bow before such a wind—how much more so for a human being?
Jiashan wanted to ride upon the tiger's head, yet that monk immediately understood how to probe it.
The Tiger’s Den. This is a clear verification of what is called "reverting the power of contemplating Avalokiteśvara back upon the person themselves.
Master Zhen Shu of Mount Yangqi in Yuanzhou addressed the assembly, saying:
"The single source of all sentient beings is conventionally named 'Buddha. Though its substance is exhausted and its form dissolves, it does not perish. It is gold..."

The flow of simplicity disperses yet remains eternally present; in the ocean of nature, where there is no wind, golden ripples surge spontaneously. When the spiritual mind is free from dependence, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously illuminated.
One who realizes this principle traverses the sands of the world-realms without speaking, and without effort, their merit further deepens the mysterious transformation.
How could he turn his back on awakening and instead conform to worldly afflictions, falsely imprisoning himself within the aggregates and realms?
From the time the Master first ascended this mountain to dwell in seclusion, until the establishment of the monastery where he gathered disciples and expounded the Dharma for over forty years.
Baotán said: "When the ocean of nature is windless, golden ripples surge forth spontaneously; when the spiritual mind is free from dependence, the myriad phenomena are illuminated all at once.
This is the realm of the great beings Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. How could Zhēnshū have attained this on his own?
In the gate of Great Quiescence, even Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are ranked below it. Zhēnshū was merely a clever hand; how could he have contained such realization within himself?"
People today do not see where the benefits and defects of the ancients lie.
When Chan Master Shuilao of Hongzhou first visited Mazu, he asked, "What is the great meaning of the coming from the West? Mazu grabbed him by the chest and gave him a blow.
He stumbled and fell. Rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary!
The hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings are all found by recognizing their source upon a single hair-tip. He then prostrated himself.
After the Master had settled there, he once told the assembly: "Ever since I took one bite from Master Ma’s kick, I have laughed without ceasing until this very day.
A monk came to pay his respects; he drew a perfect circle and, with his hand, pinched it toward the Master’s body. The Master then pushed it away three times.
He also drew a single circle and pointed back at the monk. The monk then prostrated. The Master struck him, saying, "This man of empty pretenses!
The monk asked again, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa? The Master said, "Movement brings forth shadows; awareness gives rise to ice."
Question: "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master clapped his hands and laughed heartily. Such was generally his manner of receiving people.
Baotan said: "The ancients did not shoot their arrows in vain; they were unwilling to expend even the strength of a single hair lightly, let alone [other efforts]."
What hundredfold strength! Thus, when he strikes, there is no shot that does not hit the mark; when he hits the mark, there is no victim who does not fall.
When Mazu kicked Water-lao down, this was the power of those hundred bushels. Water-lao rose up and laughed heartily, saying:
"The myriad gates of Dharma and immeasurable subtle meanings all reside upon the tip of a single hair."
Once you have recognized the root source, you will naturally manifest your own hundred-bushel strength.
Later, when he addressed the assembly, he simply said: "Ever since I was kicked by Master Ma, I have laughed without ceasing until this very day.
This arrow, however, seems intent on piercing people. I do not know when, at the final stroke, one will finally uproot the foundation.
Master Fubei was visited by Ling Xingpo, who came to pay her respects and asked, "To whom do you entrust that phrase which cannot be spoken even with one's utmost effort?
The Master said, "Fubei has no superfluous words. Xingpo said, "Even before reaching Fubei, I could not help but harbor doubts. The Master said:

If you have another point of excellence, feel free to bring it forth. The old woman folded her hands and wept, saying, "Alas! To this already bitter suffering, you add further grievance. The Master remained silent.

The woman continued, "In speech you do not distinguish the biased from the correct; in principle you do not recognize the inverted from the upright. To act for others' sake in such a way brings only calamity."
Later, a monk recounted this to Nanquan. Nanquan said, "How bitter! Fubei has been broken once more by this old woman.
When the old woman heard this, she wept and said, "Master Wang still lacks a bit of skillful means. At that time, there was a Chan practitioner named Chengyi from Youzhou.
He then asked the old woman, "Why does Nanquan lack the essential pivot? The old woman wept and said, "How tragic! How painful! Chengyi was at a loss for what to do.
The old woman asked, "Do you understand? Chengyi stood there with his palms joined. The old woman said, "Dead Zen monks are as numerous as hemp and millet.
Later, Chengyi recounted this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "If I had seen that foul old woman..."
A questioner asked about the "mute-mouthed teaching. Chengyi said, "I do not understand; how does the Master question him? Zhaozhou struck him.
Chengyi said, "Why did you strike me instead? Zhaozhou said, "For a dead Zen monk like you, when would I wait to strike?
When the old woman heard this, she said, "Zhaozhou deserves to eat a blow from my staff. Upon hearing this, Zhaozhou wept and said, "It is fitting."
How tragic! When the old woman heard this, she sighed and said, "Zhaozhou’s eye of wisdom pierces through the four worlds.
Zhaozhou sent a messenger to ask her, "What is Zhaozhou’s eye? The old woman then raised her fist. Upon hearing this, Zhaozhou composed a verse and sent it to her, saying:
"When the occasion arises, he presents it face-to-face; Face-to-face, the occasion is swift. I tell you, Laywoman Lingxing, Why do you weep?"

Lost. Ba-da said: "The Master has already understood through the sound of weeping; having already understood, who else could know? At that time in the kingdom of Magadha, how many would have lost the opportune moment before their eyes?"
Baotan said: "Ling Xingpo must have been a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for countless lifetimes. Among those of the ancestral school (*zongmen*), there have been women who were heroic men;
she cannot be compared with such people. A single turning word from Jingbei has become a strategic masterpiece of all time.
Master Wang was one who planned his campaigns from within the tent; Ling Xingpo and Zhaozhou may indeed be considered her peers."
It was said that her horsemanship and archery were peerless. Once, while Cheng was covered all over with arrows, the old man Fang drew his bow and the old woman Ling released her shaft;
as her body was cast sideways and her horse turned, the two arrows met head-on.

When they were later verified, each had their own private mark, and those watching onlookers were struck with awe. In ancient times there were armies of women, yet these were not veteran generals of long standing.
It is not sufficient to account for her. Regarding the beginning and end of Master Lingxing’s life, nothing appears in the records;
only this single turning word from Fubei is preserved. It is a pity that we do not see more of her.
Chan Master Longshan of Tanzhou (also known as Yishan) asked a monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From where the elder resides. The Master said, "What words or phrases did the elder speak?
The monk said, "If he speaks, there are a thousand phrases and ten thousand words; if he does not speak, there is not even a single character. The Master said, "So it is."

The monk immediately released the cord and prostrated; the Master then struck him. When Dongshan and his senior companion, Master Mi, were traveling on pilgrimage and became lost, they arrived at the mountain.
The Master asked, "There is no path to this mountain; from where have you come, Venerable? Dongshan said, "From where did the Master enter?
The Master replied, "I am not a wandering traveler. Dongshan asked, "How long has the Master resided on this mountain?"
At that time, the Master said, "You have not yet passed through the years [of maturity]. Yunmen said, "The Master arrived first; this mountain was occupied first. The Master said, "I do not know.
Yunmen said, "Why do you not know? The Master said, "I did not come for the sake of humans or devas.
Yunmen said, "What principle did the Master realize to dwell on this mountain? The Master said, "I saw two earthen oxen fighting and entering the sea, continuing until—"

"Since there is no news at present," Shishuang asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "I have not gone out of my door for many years. Shishuang asked, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Green mountains shrouded by white clouds. Shishuang asked, "How far apart are the guest and the host? The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the long river. Shishuang asked, "When the guest and the host meet, what words are spoken? The Master said, "The blue heavens are clear and vast; the sun and moon shine brightly. Shishuang said, "I have understood. The Master said, "Have you understood, or have you not? Shishuang said, "I have understood. The Master said, "If you have understood, why do you say you have understood? If you have not understood, why do you say you have understood? Lǎn'ān spent thirty years at Míshān, yet he achieved nothing more than becoming a man who eats.
The Buddha who ate excrement and filth; and thirty years later, he was reborn as Lingshu of the Great Sui.
Those two calves—how could they have failed the mountains, rivers, heaven, and earth?

The Zen Master Shenzan of Guling in Fuzhou was a disciple who had received his formal training under [Master] Shi. Shi asked him, "While you were away from me, what work or practice did you undertake? The master replied, "I had no particular work or practice.
Thereupon, Shi sent him to perform manual labor. One day, while bathing, Shi ordered the master to remove the grime from his back. The master then patted his back and said, "Excellent!"
There was a Buddha hall, yet the Buddha therein was not sacred. The master turned his head and looked at it, saying, "Though he is not sacred, he nevertheless emits light.
One day, while the master was reading a sutra by the window, a fly struck the paper and sought to escape.
The Master looked at him and said, "The world is this vast, yet you are merely drilling through old scraps of paper; when will you ever get out?
Setting aside the scriptures, he asked, 'Whom have you encountered during your travels? I have observed that your speech has been extraordinary from the very beginning.'"
The Master said, "I have received from Venerable Baizhang the instruction on a place of rest, and now I wish to repay his compassionate virtue.

His teacher then informed the assembly that a vegetarian feast was being held and requested the Master to preach the Dharma. When he ascended the seat and began his discourse, it was entirely in the style of Baizhang’s school.

He then said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters. The nature of mind is without..."
Defilement is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected; one need only depart from delusive conditions to be a Buddha of Suchness. His teacher, having attained awakening upon these words, exclaimed:
"Who would have expected that, in my advanced years, I would hear of the ultimate reality!"
Baotan said: "Guling lightly borrowed the power of the ancient Buddha to fully unleash the dynamic potential (*ji*) of his master.

Once he was commanded to propagate the Dharma, everything he expounded was the profound essence of Baizhang. It was truly magnificent that he did not pride himself on the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, yet was able to fully realize the filial debt owed to his father.
How could those of later generations—people whose eyes look outward while their internal strength is empty—possibly fathom this?"
It was for the sake of a fine Buddha hall; though its dust, dregs, and chaff remain, it still serves to mold and forge practitioners.
Even now, one can hear the myriad phenomena of the "silent samādhi" at its final stage. To bring this story to completion, it is as if Guling has returned once more.
When a person asked Master He’antong of Guangzhou, “Are you a Chan master? the Master replied, “I, a poor monk, have never studied Chan.
After a long silence, he called to the man, who responded, “Yes. The Master pointed to a *tāla* tree and the man was speechless. Yangshan acted as a sandalwood tree.
After some time, the Master called out, "Ji-zi, bring me the bench over here. When Yangshan brought it, the Master said, "Return it to its original place.
He then asked Ji-zi, "What is that on the other side of the bench? Yangshan replied, "Nothing. The Master said:
"Over here," [the Master] said. Yang replied, "There is nothing. The Master called out again, "Jizi! Yang responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Go. Baotan remarked:
"From those of keen faculties and superior wisdom down to others, the ancient masters were all alike in their simple and robust endowment;
their reception of the Way was not far apart, and their application of it was likewise so. For instance, regarding 'not speaking,' they were all in accord."
From the masters of the Dà'ān era onwards, they have personally emerged from the furnace of Bǎizhàng;
like refined gold that has been smelted until it is free of all dross, they merely manifest for a time in accordance with the capacity of their audience.
To test their vital strength against one another and to grind their sharpness and dullness together—who other than true brothers of this house would dare to lightly provoke them?
Formerly, Chan Master Bāochè of Mágǔ Mountain in Púzhōu succeeded the Dharma of the Master Lángsuì of Shòuzhōu.
When the Master first visited Mágǔ, Mágǔ called out, "Lángsuì! The Master responded. This was repeated three times, and he responded each time in the same manner.
He assented. Gu said, "This dull-witted monk. Only then did the Master realize his error and say, "Master, do not deceive me.
If Liang-sui had not come to pay his respects, you would have spent your entire life being misled by the sutras and treatises. Ma-gu approved of this.
Baotan said: "Liangsui’s meeting with Magu can serve as a model for those who would become abbots of the realm; this is the method for those practicing Chan.
Jia Shan’s meeting with Huian (the Boatman) can serve as a model for those who would become spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of a region; this is the method for those returning for further study.
Yet the *Chuan Deng Lu* omits these accounts and records them with errors and omissions. One does not realize that it was due to the original records of Daoyuan that such [corruptions] came to pass."
Is it so? Or is it that they have been edited and abridged? One must not fail to clarify their similarities and differences.
When Liangshui went to visit Magu, as soon as Magu saw him approaching, he took up a hoe and entered the vegetable garden. Liangshui followed him into the garden. Magu then suddenly—
He returned to the abbot’s quarters and closed the door. The following day, he went back to the abbot’s quarters and knocked on the door.
Magu asked, "Who is it? Su replied, "Liangsui. As soon as he uttered his name, he suddenly attained awakening.
He immediately told Magu, "Master, do not deceive Liangsui. Had I not come to pay my respects, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises."
Upon returning from his travels to engage in lecturing and study, he immediately told his disciples: "What all of you know, Liang-sui knows entirely;
what Liang-sui knows, none of you know. Were it not for this one true word, how could one distinguish the ultimate point?"
Chan Master Huaiyun of Changjing Temple in Jingzhao was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Hongbian of Dajianfu Temple in Jingzhao.

When Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty summoned him for an audience and asked why the Chan school had come to be known by the names "Northern" and "Southern," the Master replied: "The Chan gate..."

Originally, there was no distinction between north and south. In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa, and it was transmitted in succession down to the twenty-eighth patriarch.

Bodhidharma came to this land as the first patriarch. When the fifth patriarch, the Great Master Hongren, was propagating the Dharma at Mount Dongshan in Qizhou, he had two disciples. One was named Huineng; he received the robe and the Dharma and resided there.
Lingnan was the domain of the Sixth Patriarch, whose name was Shenxiu; he propagated the teachings in the northern regions.

Later, his disciple Pujì established his master as the Seventh Patriarch and claimed himself to be the Seventh Patriarch. Although the Dharma they attained was one and the same, there were differences in their methods of guidance and awakening—namely, the sudden and the gradual.
Thus it is said: "The South is Sudden, the North is Gradual. It is not that the Southern school originally possessed [a different] Chan lineage.

This was the title of the Northern [King]. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'precept' (śīla)? He replied, "To guard against what is wrong and cease from evil is called precept. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'concentration' (samādhi)?
He replied, "When the six sense faculties encounter objects, the mind does not follow after conditions; this is called concentration. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'wisdom' (prajñā)?
He replied, "When both mind and objects are empty, and one perceives clearly without delusion, this is called wisdom. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'expedient means' (upāya)? He replied—

It is said: "Expedient means (upāya) is that which conceals the true mark (dharmatā) and covers the gateways of skillful artifice. To receive and guide those of middling and inferior capacities by applying teachings in a manner suited to them is called expedient means.
Even if one were to address those of the highest faculties by saying that expedient means should be abandoned and only the unsurpassed path taught, this too would be a discourse on expedient means.
Indeed, even the profound words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—which forget all achievement and sever all designations—do not transcend expedient means."
The Emperor asked, "What is the Buddha-mind? He replied, "Buddha is a term from the Western Heaven; in the language of Tang, it means 'Awakened.

It refers to the fact that when a person possesses wisdom and the power of illuminating awareness, this constitutes the Buddha-mind. 'Mind' is an alternative name for the Buddha, which has hundreds of thousands of different designations."
Its essence is solely one; fundamentally it has no shape and is not characterized by blue, yellow, red, or white, nor by male or female.
In heaven it is not a celestial being, and among humans it is not a human; yet it manifests as a celestial being and manifests as a human, and can appear as male or female.

It has neither beginning nor end, and is without birth or extinction; therefore, it is termed the "Naturally Awakened Nature. Your Majesty’s daily response to the myriad affairs of state is precisely this: Your Majesty is the Buddha.
"Even if a thousand Buddhas were to transmit it together, the mind would not think that there is anything else to be attained. The Emperor asked, "How is it when one now recollects the Buddha?
He replied, "The Tathāgata appeared in the world as a teacher of gods and humans and a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). He preached the Dharma according to their faculties.

For those of superior capacity, he opened the way to the Supreme Vehicle for the sudden realization of the ultimate principle; for those of middling or inferior capacity who could not yet understand it suddenly,"
For this reason, the Buddha provisionally opened the sixteen gates of contemplation for Vaidehī, enabling her to attain birth in Sukhāvatī through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus the sutra says: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha; outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no mind. The Emperor asked:

"If there are people who recite the sutras and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, or who seek the Buddha by reciting mantras, how do these compare? He replied: "The Tathāgata has provided various means of instruction..."

All praises are for the sake of the Supreme Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Just as the myriad currents of a hundred rivers do not fail to flow toward and merge into the ocean, so too do all these various distinctions and enumerations return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience). The Emperor asked:

"Since the Patriarch has already realized the seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*), how is it that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of the 'Dharma of non-attainment'? He replied: "In the Buddha’s entire dispensation, there is truly not a single dharma to be given."
To people, he merely showed that the individual self-nature of each person is identical to the single treasure-store of the Dharma.
At that time, when Śākyamuni was sealed by Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata with his own fundamental Dharma and attained nothing, he finally accorded with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span; this Dharma is equal. Cultivate all wholesome dharmas, yet do not dwell [in them]."
Regarding this matter, the Emperor asked, "Since the Chan Master has realized the meaning of the Patriarchs, do you still prostrate to the Buddha and study the sutras?
He replied, "That śramaṇas and sons of Śākya prostrate to the Buddha and study the sutras is the constant law of maintaining the tradition, which yields four kinds of retribution.

Nevertheless, relying on the Buddha's precepts to cultivate the self, seeking out spiritual friends, gradually practicing the Brahma-faring, and treading the path traversed by the Tathāgata—this is our way. The Emperor said:

"What is meant by 'sudden realization' (*tun-jian*)? What is meant by 'gradual cultivation' (*jian-xiu*)? He replied: "Sudden realization means clearly understanding that one's own Buddha-nature is identical to that of the Buddhas.
However, because there are defiled habits from beginningless time, one must employ gradual cultivation as an antidote to cause the nature to give rise to its functioning in accordance with it.
It is like a person eating rice: they do not become full in a single mouthful. This day’s discourse concluded when seven *ke* (a unit of time) had passed after sunset.
Baotan said: "The ruler who employs the net to encompass all under heaven has not failed to enfold the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Questions concerning the intent of the Patriarchs and the mind of the Buddha; questions concerning the study of precepts, concentration, and wisdom;

and questions concerning sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation—all these are the essentials for the ancients entering the Way, as well as the provisions for beginners in their studies. They are neither existent nor non-existent."
The Master’s wisdom was attained through spontaneity; how could he possibly have known such systematic principles, like a master physician of long standing?
Master Bian’s response accorded with both fact and principle, like the thread of a honeybee weaving through with exquisite clarity, unimpeded by the substance of the pearls.
Truly, this was a fortunate convergence of teacher and disciple, ruler and minister, at that time. Of the Buddha—
This "entrustment" (付囑) refers precisely to this. Later generations of those with deviant learning have recklessly criticized ministers and sovereigns for being sycophants of the Buddha;
they utterly fail to realize that where the Way resides, the governance of the world follows it.
When a sovereign who governs the world presides over a people who study the Way, his actions are unsurpassed—how can one offer such reckless criticism?

When Chan Master Zhizhen of Guishan in Fuzhou first visited Master Yunwen, Yunwen asked, "From where have you come? The Master replied, "I have come to where there is nowhere to go; I have arrived from where there is nowhere to come.
Although Yunwen remained silent, Zhizhen also attained realization for himself. Subsequently, he traveled to Wuxie Mountain in Wuzhou, where he met Master Zhengjue.
The Chan Master Yuan was traveling to Jianyang together with [his companions] in the second year of the Changqing era. While residing at Mount Gui, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Even blinking one's eyes does not depart from the person of the present moment; a single thought of pure mind is fundamentally the Buddha. He then spoke this verse:

"The mind is fundamentally free from dust, so what need is there to wash it? Within the body there is no illness, so why seek a physician? If you wish to know the state that is neither body nor Buddha, Look into the clear mirror."

While his lofty presence had not yet shone upon the world, he later encountered the era of Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of Buddhism. He presented two verses to the assembly, saying: "The bright moon divides its form, ever new in every place;
How could a layperson (baiyi) fall from being one who understands emptiness? Who says that being in the secular world hinders the path of cultivation?
Kanakamuni once took birth as the body of an elder. The second verse says: "When the Immortal of Patience sat in meditation beneath the forest trees, He was once..."

"The King of Singers had his limbs severed; how much more so in our Sage Dynasty, where such things do not occur? To merely command him to cease his practice of the Way—what cause for grief is there? Baotan said:
"The Way of the Buddha pervades the world, like the primal qi (*yuanqi*) that exists within heaven and earth.
Before heaven and earth existed, this primal qi never ceased for a single day. Once heaven and earth and the myriad things came into being, [it remained ever-present]."
Heaven and earth give birth to and nourish the myriad things; they are that which proclaims and distributes the primal qi.
The Buddha is like heaven and earth; the Way is like the primal qi; the disciples of the Buddha are like the myriad things.

If there were no Buddha and no heaven and earth, who would be the true sovereign of the Way and the primal qi? And if there were no myriad things and no disciples of the Buddha, then what [would exist]?
How lamentable! The Way and the primal qi (*yuanqi*) are such that they are like felling a tree: one chapter is felled today, yet another chapter grows tomorrow;
this is the inevitability of principle. My strength may come to an end, but the principle by which it is regenerated is inexhaustible.
How great is the primal qi! This was the situation for Chan Master Liu during the purge of the Buddhist clergy under Emperor Wuzong.
In his later years, he composed two gāthās in which he aspired to be like an ancient seer; their diction was dignified and composed, showing no sign of anxiety or urgency.
He was truly a man of the Way. If all things possess the capacity to firmly protect the primal qi so that it neither leaks nor is diminished, they are indeed numinous beings.
To advance from this state to become a True Ruler (Zhenzai) would not be difficult. Furthermore, there were those from the Chen and Shen clans...
Chan practice is of a similar nature.
One day, Master Cao of Jinzhou invited Master Mi for a meal but did not arrange any seating. As soon as Master Mi arrived, he spread out his sitting mat and prostrated.
The Master descended from his meditation seat. Baizhang then took the Master’s place and sat upon it. The Master withdrew and sat on the ground. When the meal was finished, Baizhang departed.
A attendant informed the Master, saying, "The Master is revered by all people; today your seat has been usurped by another.
The Master said, "If he returns within three days, he will still be saved. Indeed, Baizhang returned after three days.
[The Master] said, "The other day I encountered bandits.
Baotan remarked, "The hook was set in a place of non-suspicion; this is a skillful way to fish.
Just as the fine scales were leaping against the waves, they fell into my bait, yet I stirred not a single ripple nor harmed a single scale, obtaining them with dignified composure."
If he were an ordinary person, he would certainly already be in a dried-up carriage rut, beyond the possibility of remedy.
Since you, Master, have come personally from the Eastern Sea, it is hoped that you will leap through the Dragon Gate.
When Chan Master Huaizheng of Dongyi in Langzhou was visited by Yangshan for an audience, he asked, "Where are you from? Yangshan replied, "I am a man from Guangnan.
The Master said, "Is there a 'Bright Pearl that Subdues the Sea' in Guangnan or not? Yangshan replied, "There is. The Master asked, "What is the shape of this pearl? Yangshan—
[The Master] said, "In the bright fortnight it appears; in the dark fortnight it is hidden. The Master asked, "Can you bring it here?
Mount [Shan] said, "I can bring it here. The Master said, "Why do you not present it to this old monk? Mount said, "Yesterday I went to Mt. Wei and also sought this pearl from Huiji.
It left me with no words to respond and no principle to proffer. The Master said, "A true lion cub indeed! He acts as a great..."
The Lion’s Roar. Baotan said:
"Yangshan is like the bright moon-jewel. Those who pray to this jewel find it immediately manifest;
in the bright fortnight it appears, and in the dark fortnight it hides. This is the radiance of the jewel; there are no words with which to respond, and no principle by which to explain it."
"It can be extended; this is the substance of the pearl. Will you bring it here? You shall bring it to the eastern district, whereupon it will manifest within the pearl.
A true lion cub lets out a great lion’s roar; thus the pearl manifests again in the hand of one from the eastern district.
In future generations, such a pearl will not be absent. Question: "When this pearl is worn, it points south as north. What is its shape? Answer: "It is like a barbarian (hú)."
When it comes, why does it manifest? When the Han comes, the Han manifests. Why do you not present this to the old monk?
[He] drew a circle and performed a woman’s bow. This is a pit of filth! To take this up and show it to people—would it not make them retch? Alas!
Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan succeeded Chan Master Jingcen of Changsha in Hunan. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"If I were to exclusively promote the teachings and the school, the grass before the Dharma Hall would grow ten feet deep. I...
Having no other recourse, I spoke thus to the people: "The entirety of the worlds in the ten directions is the single eye of the śramaṇa;
the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions is the whole body of the śramaṇa; the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions is one's own radiance;
the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions exists within one's own radiance; throughout the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions, there is not a single thing [that is not so]."
A person is not a self. I have always told you all: the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm are the light of Mahāprajñā.
Before this light has yet been emitted, where could people possibly have full comprehension? Before the light has been emitted, there is as yet no news of either Buddha or sentient beings;
from where could mountains, rivers, and the great earth have come? [Monk: *Note: The original text contains a fragmentary ending ("僧"), indicating the speaker was likely addressing a monk.*
Question: "Who are the Buddhas? The Master said: "Since beginningless kalpas, who has been providing you with shelter and protection?
A monk asked: "Before there were any Buddhas, what was it like? The Master said: "When Luzu opened the hall, he too spoke of this and that with the monks."
The Master sent a monk to ask the Reverend Tongcan Hui, saying, "After you met Nanquan, what was it like?
Hui remained silent. The monk said, "Before you had met Nanquan, how was it? Hui replied, "It cannot be anything other than this.
The monk returned and reported this to the Master, who then presented a verse, saying: "The person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole..."

"However, having attained entry is not yet the ultimate reality. One must advance further from the tip of the hundred-foot pole; only then does one manifest the entire body throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
A monk asked, "But how does one advance from the tip of the hundred-foot pole? The Master said, "The mountains of Langzhou; the waters of Lishui."

The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Within the civilizing influence of the sovereign, across the four seas and five lakes, there was a scholar reading the *Sutra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*.
He asked, 'I have heard the names of the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, but I wonder in what lands they dwell.

The Master said, 'After Cui Hao inscribed his verse on the Yellow Crane Tower, did you, scholar, ever compose one yourself? He replied, 'I have not. The Master said, 'When there is nothing to do, then compose one.'"
One passage is excellent. A monk asked, "Nanquan said, 'When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? Master, what did you say?

The Master said, "He becomes a donkey for the eastern neighbor and a horse for the western neighbor. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "If you want to ride it, then ride it."
When it is time to descend, one simply descends. While the Master was with Yangshan enjoying the moon, Yangshan said, "Everyone possesses this very thing, yet they simply cannot use it.
The Master said, "That is exactly why I am borrowing you to use it. Yangshan asked, "How will you use it?
The Master gave him a kick straight to the chest, knocking him down. As Yangshan rose, he said, "You are nothing less than a great tiger!"
Baotan said: Changsha remarked, "If I were to expound the religious teachings, the grass in the Dharma Hall would have grown ten feet deep.
When this old man was surrounded by hundreds or thousands of followers at other times, he spoke horizontally and vertically until no further dharma remained;

how could all of this have been merely the secondary meaning? I dare ask those of all quarters: what constitutes the religious teachings? If you say it is that which existed before one's parents were born—
To take what has been transmitted before as the religious teaching is a realization born within the ghost caves beneath Black Mountain.
To take great capacity and great function as the religious teaching is a realization born amidst sparks from flint and flashes of lightning.
To take Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma as the religious teaching is the realization of a novice monk. Do not hold any of these views at all. Period.
In the end, what constitutes this religious teaching? When Luzu opened the hall, he spoke of things here and there for the sake of others—is that this religious teaching?
"The mountains of Langzhou, the waters of Lingshou; the four seas and five lakes are within the imperial transformation"—is that this religious teaching?
"Cui Hao inscribed the Yellow Crane Tower; when I have leisure, I shall compose a poem"—is that this religious teaching?
"Does the Eastern house becoming a donkey and the Western house becoming a horse belong to this religious tradition? Does trampling down Yangshan belong to this religious tradition?
Since then, he has been called 'Great Tiger Cen' by all quarters; he is an old lynx within this religious tradition.
His patterns are so variegated that all other beasts cower before him. I have always regretted his choice of conduct."

His character has not been seen in the world for some time, leaving us without a model to admire. An old man of long standing, observing alone his words that convey the Way, finds them brilliantly radiant.
His mastery of the terminology of the sutras and treatises is thorough and penetrating.
Is he not the one who will restore the Way of Mount Nanyue? Is he not the one? Is he not the one?
Chan Master Tanzhao of Baima in Jingnan used to say constantly, "How happy!
How happy! Yet, when his end approached, he cried out, "Alas! Alas! The Old Man of Yama has come to take me!
When the monastery director asked him, "Master, previously you were thrown into the water by the Regional Inspector; your countenance remained—"
[The Master] moved. "How can you be like this now? The Master picked up his pillow and said, "Tell me, was it so at that time, or is it so now?
The head of the monastery had no reply.
Baotan said: "To be joyful when alive and to cry out in suffering at death—this would surely leave all the monks in the world in doubt.
Yet, if you wish now to see that teacher, his joy is certainly not suffering, and his suffering is certainly not joy.
Those who have not yet penetrated birth and death need not harbor such doubts."
When National Teacher Shizu of Yunji Temple on Mount Zhongnan was with Nanquan, he asked:
"The mani jewel people do not recognize; it is personally held within the Tathāgatagarbha."
"What is the treasury? Nanquan said, "That which comes and goes with you. The Master asked, "What about that which does not come and go?
Nanquan said, "It is not the treasury. He further asked, "What is the pearl? Nanquan called out, "Master Zu!
The Master responded, "Yes. Nanquan said, "Go. You do not understand my words. From this, the Master attained awakening.
Baotan said: "The ancients removed the disease but did not remove the Dharma; for this disease was a cataract obscuring the Dharma, hence there was the question of the Master and Patriarch.
The Dharma is the medicine for the disease; hence there was Nanquan’s response. When both medicine and disease are cast aside, the pearl manifests of itself.
Since the pearl is not inherently a pearl, it borrows the treasury to clarify the pearl. Since the treasury is not inherently a treasury,"
Borrowing a pearl to illuminate the treasury. Alas! This hand that plays with a lump of mud puts Master Yongjia to shame.
Zen Master Yiduan of Xiangyan Monastery in Dengzhou addressed the assembly, saying:
"If you wish to attain accord, be reverent; do not allow even a hair’s breadth of lingering attachment. Be as direct as—"
"Only empty space has a slight degree of correspondence [with this]. It has no locks and no walls; it is formless and without eyes or mind.
He further said, "Speech is slander; silence is deception. There is a matter beyond this. This old monk’s mouth is too narrow; I cannot explain it for you.
The monk asked, "Precisely because of what is there no matter? The Master said, "I have never paused. He also said:
Even if one were to strip it away layer by layer until it is completely exhausted with nothing remaining, such a temporary provision is merely a skillful means for guiding people.
If this were the ultimate reality itself, it would be impossible.
Baotán said: "Speech and silence are one and the same path. People nowadays merely think it means neither speaking nor remaining silent;
if one interprets it thus, how can one avoid deceiving oneself? Master Duān’s ‘Vajra Ring’ is naturally difficult to penetrate.
If you wish to understand it easily, simply let everything be completely purified and serene, yet do not linger even upon that 'completeness. It is like being directly beneath [the ring]."
Space—space itself does not even stand. This is called "bringing the present moment to completion.
As soon as one speaks of the "present moment," there is already an empty kalpa, and furthermore, man and grass have both departed.

When Chan Master Congshen of Zhaozhou Guanyuan first visited Nanquan, he encountered Nanquan while the latter was reclining. Nanquan asked, "Where have you recently come from? The Master replied, "Ruixiang.
Nanquan asked, "Did you see the Ruixiang [Statue]? The Master said, "I did not see the Ruixiang; I saw the Reclining Tathāgata. Nanquan—
He rose abruptly and asked with a startled expression, "Are you a novice with a master, or a novice without a master?
The Master replied, "I am a novice with a master. Nanquan asked, "Where is your master? The Master said, "It is the bitter cold of mid-winter;
I humbly wish the Master good health and every blessing in your daily life. Nanquan granted him entry into his inner circle. One day, he asked Nanquan, "What is the Way?"
Zhuanzi said, "The ordinary mind is the Way. The Master asked, "Can one still direct oneself toward it? Zhuanzi said, "To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate from it.
The Master asked, "When there is no intention, how can one know it is the Way? Zhuanzi said, "The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing."
"To know this as deluded cognition is not to know it as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one truly penetrates it, it is the Way beyond doubt, like the great void.
How could one forcibly impose right or wrong upon that which is vast, empty, and open? At these words, the Master attained realization;
he looked about with a hesitant gaze, his eyes flashing like lightning, and asked Nanquan, "Where does a person who knows 'it exists' find rest? Nanquan—
Nanquan said, "The ox went down the mountain. The Master said, "Thank you for the instruction. Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window.
