There was no one in the assembly to respond. Later, while he was ascending the tower with his subordinates, several monks were walking past.
One official said, "Those coming are all traveling monks. The Shangshu (Minister) said, "They are not. The official asked, "How do you know they are not?
The Shangshu replied, "Wait until they come closer and I shall question them. As the monks passed by the tower one after another, the Shangshu suddenly—

He called out, "Venerable One! and the monks all turned their heads to look. The Minister said to the assembly of officials, "You do not believe the Way. He then offered a verse for the Chan practitioner:

"The Chan practitioner possesses a profound mechanism; That mechanism is profound—is it then 'is' or 'is not'? If you wish to understand the intent prior to the mechanism, All will find themselves at odds with the words."
Baotan said: "When scholars and officials practice Chan, they aim solely at seeing the fundamental root clearly.

Whether the Great Dharma is thoroughly penetrated or not is naturally like water reaching the channel once it has reached its course. This is not the same as the case among the monks' community, where even a hair's breadth of doubt renders one unfit to be a vessel for the teachings.
For this reason, there are those who act with leniency or severity toward good spiritual friends. Thus it is said.

One knows that Chen Cao of Muzhou was one who employed the hand of a patch-robed monk (naseng). His physical bearing was quite similar [to Muzhou’s], though his strength was slight and his stature small.
When he interrogated the monks from atop the tower, was it not just like the events at Muzhou at that time?
Fortunately, he encountered no "lion cubs" (disciples); had there been any, he would have had to rescue the Minister first before he could succeed.
Chan Master Xinghua Cunjian of Weifeng succeeded Chan Master Ruyong Yong of Baoying in Ruizhou.
The Master ascended the hall and said: "Upon this mass of flesh, there is a towering precipice ten thousand fathoms high. At that time, a monk asked: "Upon this mass of flesh..."

"Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high—is this not what the Master said? The monk replied, "Yes. The monk then overturned the meditation seat. The Master said, "You blind donkey! and struck him.
The Master then asked another monk, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "From Changshui. The Master said, "Does it flow east or west?
He replied, "It is not like that at all. The Master said, "How then? The monk then said, "Zhenzhong (take care). The Master [nodded].
He then struck him and drove him out of the Dharma Hall. Another monk came to pay his respects; the Master raised his whisk, and the monk said, "Today you have failed.
The Master lowered the whisk, and the monk said, "There is still this one remaining. The Master then struck him. The Master asked the monk, "Where have you recently come from?
He replied, "I have recently come from Xiangzhou. The Master asked, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master."
The Master said, "It happens that Old Baoying is not here. The monk then gave a shout.
The Master said, "I told you he was not here; why do you shout again? The monk shouted once more, whereupon the Master struck him.

The monk bowed, and the Master said, "This staff was originally meant for you to strike me, but I shall strike you three or five times instead, so that these words may spread far and wide. This was Master Xingming.

Before he had moved to the Western Hall, after paying his respects, Ming bowed and said, "I have no other fine things to offer, but I have purchased a Jiangxi razor from Xuzhou as a token of my service and present it to the Master. The Master said, "You came from Xuzhou;
where did you get a Jiangxi razor? Ming firmly grasped the Master’s hand and pinched it once. The Master said, "Attendant, take it away. Ming [did so].

He brushed out his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "A-la-la! The Master ascended the hall and said, "In various quarters, people possess only the 'eye' for the simultaneous moment of the chick pecking and the hen hatching;
they do not possess the 'function' of that simultaneous moment. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the function of the simultaneous moment of pecking and hatching?
The Master said, "An adept does not peck or hatch; at the very moment of pecking and hatching, one loses it. The monk said, "This is still not it."

The monk asked, "At the place where I questioned you, Master, how did you respond? The Master said, "How was it at the place where you questioned me? The monk said, "I lost it. The Master then struck him. The monk was dissatisfied with this.
Later, while in the assembly of Yunmen, he heard another monk cite these words and finally realized the essential meaning.
He returned to seek further instruction, but the Master had already passed away. He then paid his respects to Venerable Fengxue, who asked, "At that time, you..."
Regarding the story of the former master’s “sipping and pecking,” is there still a point for realization later on?
A monk said, “I have already seen the principle. The Master asked, “How so? The monk said, “At that time, I was walking in the shadow of a lamp; when I looked back, nothing could be seen.
Fengxue said, “You understand.”
Baotán said: "The gentleman embraces his grandson and not his son, because [the grandson] can serve as the representative (shī) for his grandfather at the ancestral sacrifice.

My view is that if the person performing the sacrifice is not the right one, the spirits will not accept the offering. Therefore, the gentleman is careful regarding the transmission [of the teachings].

Thus, there are things transmitted because they were seen, and there are also things transmitted because they were heard. Between father, grandfather, son, and grandson, what is heard and what is seen may be vastly different. What I have seen..."

The second transmission was indeed difficult. From Linji, it passed once to Xinghua, and the second transmission reached Nanyuan. His towering excellence and transcendent mastery were as if one were seeing Linji himself;
he truly did not fail his lineage. Upon this bare flesh-ball, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, there is already the intent to transcend Buddhas and patriarchs.
A master does not merely wait for the "cracking" and "pecking"; he cracks and pecks simultaneously.
Simultaneously losing [all attachments], there arises the intent to issue commands to all directions. When a monk asks, "Where have the sages of antiquity gone?
[the response is]: "Not ascending to heaven, they enter directly into hell. Thus, there arises the hand that lashes and strikes Buddhas and patriarchs.
These three matters can be visualized through contemplation. Furthermore, this person has great utility. What would it be like when he does not encounter others?
"The rooster and goose dance on a separate path; he leads one into a thousand peaks. In every instance of his application, it is exactly like this.
Truly, he does not disgrace himself as a direct descendant of Linji.
Formerly, Chan Master Yong of Nan’uan in Ru Prefecture received the Dharma from Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue in Ru Prefecture.
While at Huayan Monastery in Xiangzhou, he encountered Shoukuo, an attendant of Nan’uan, and secretly investigated the essential principles of Nan’uan’s school.
He then went directly to Nanyuan. Upon first seeing him, he did not prostrate but asked: "Entering the gate, one must discern the master; please, Teacher, distinguish them for me.
Nanyuan struck his knee with his left hand; the Master shouted. Nanyuan struck his knee with his right hand; the Master shouted again.
Nanyuan raised his left hand and said, "This one follows you, Dharma brother. He then raised his right hand and said, "This one..."
"Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, "Blind! As Nan-yuan was about to pick up his staff, the Master said, "What are you doing?

He snatched the staff away and struck him, saying, "Old monk, do not say I did not warn you. Nan-yuan said, "I have been the abbot for thirty years, yet today I am being prosecuted at my own door by this yellow-faced Zhejiang man.
The Master said, "The Master is much like one who cannot manage to hold his own alms bowl."
[Zhaodu] said, "I am not hungry. Nan'uan asked, "When did you ever come to Nan'uan before? The Master replied, "What kind of talk is this? Nan'uan said, "I am asking you for certain.
The Master said, "In that case, I cannot let you off the hook. Nan'uan said, "Sit and drink tea for now. Only then did the Master perform the rites of teacher and disciple.
Thereafter, he responded to the prediction made by [Master Daowu] of Mount Miao-yang regarding his emergence in the world.
Tuonan. The Dharma-way of Nan’uan flourished greatly. He ascended the hall and said: “The patriarchs’ seal of mind resembles the mechanism of an iron ox:
when it moves away, it is sealed; when it stays still, it is broken. Now, as for neither moving nor staying—does it consist in being sealed, or does it consist in not being sealed?
Is there anyone among you who can say? At that time, the Elder Lupi came forward and asked: “A student...”

"You possess the mechanism of the iron ox; I request that you do not apply the seal. The Master said, "I am accustomed to hooking whales and leviathans in the vast depths, yet I sigh at the snail’s pace as it crawls through the mud and sand.
As Lupei was about to offer a word in response, the Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk and said:
"Do you remember my previous words? Lupi replied, "I remember them. The Master said, "Try reciting them for me. As Lupi was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again with his whisk.
Addressing the assembly in the hall, he said: "As for the eyes of those who study the Way, when facing a critical moment, you must employ the great function directly before you.
Do not confine yourselves to minor details. Even if one attains realization prior to words, it is still being stuck in the shell."

The Master said, "At the two meal times, when ascending to the hall, you must not bite through even a single grain of rice. Seeing Zun Punuo washing a Buddha statue, the Master asked, "This one you are washing—from this, can you wash that one?
Zun said, "Bring me that one, and I will wash it. The Master [replied], "That one cannot be brought forth."
Thereupon he stopped. The Master ordered the steward to go and ask the practitioner Gan-zhi, "Where have you come from?
The monk said, "From Mount Yao. Gan asked, "What is your purpose in coming? The monk said, "To convert you. Gan asked, "Have you brought any medicine with you?
The monk said, "What illness do you have, practitioner? Gan then gave him two ingots of silver, saying, "If there is anyone [who needs it], return these to them."
"Come. When the monk returned immediately, the Master was surprised. The monk said, "The Buddha-dharma was consistent; I obtained two bars of silver. The Master ordered him to repeat those words.
After he had repeated them, the Master told the monk to quickly return the silver to the practitioner's house.

When the practitioner saw that the monk had returned, he said, "You have come back," and subsequently added more silver as an offering. Li Ao, the Regional Inspector of Langzhou, entered the mountains to visit [the Master].

The Master happened to be holding a scripture and did not look up. An attendant informed him, "The Governor is here. Hào, being of a narrow and impetuous temperament, remarked, "Seeing the person is not as good as hearing of their reputation.
The Master called out, "Governor! Hào responded, "Yes? The Master said, "How can you hold the ears noble while degrading the eyes?
Hào folded his hands in apology and asked, "What is the Way? The Master pointed upward with his finger.
The Master asked, "Do you understand? Xu Ao replied, "I do not. The Master said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the pitcher.

Xu Ao was filled with joy and satisfaction, prostrated himself, and composed this verse: My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane; Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture.
"I have come to ask about the Way; there is nothing else. "The clouds are in the blue sky; the water is in the pitcher. Hao asked again, "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom?
The Master said, "In my place, there are no such idle furnishings. Hao could not fathom the profound meaning. The Master said:
The Prefect wished to obtain a guarantee for this matter. One must simply stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor.
If one cannot relinquish the things of the inner chambers, it constitutes a leakage. One night, the Master practiced walking meditation while ascending the mountain;
suddenly, the clouds parted and he beheld the moon. He let out a great laugh, and the residents ninety li to the east of Liyang all said that the sun was rising.
At home, they questioned one another in turn until the morning, when the disciples of Yaoshan said, "Last night, the Master laughed loudly on the mountain peak.
Li Ao then presented another poem, saying: "Having chosen this secluded dwelling to satisfy my rustic sentiments, All year long there is neither parting nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend directly to the solitary peak; Under the moon, I strip away the clouds and let out a laugh."
Baotan said: "I do not believe that descendants are not of the same vital essence (*qifen*) as their ancestors. Human beings take what they have received as their vital essence;
Buddhas and patriarchs take what they have transmitted as their vital essence. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also says, 'receiving the vital essence of the Buddha,' which is precisely this.
Furthermore, observe how Baizhang was the patriarch, Huangbo was the father, and Linji was the son—this is one such category."
This refers to the "lineage of spirit" (*qifen*). Furthermore, Baizhang is the patriarch, Guishan is the father, and Yangshan is the son;
thus, from the time they shared the same ancestral source but had different fathers, the Guishan-Yangshan father-and-son pair constitute one class of "lineage of spirit.
Moreover, Yaoshan is the patriarch, Yunyan is the father, and Dongshan is the son; as these were the direct descendants of Shitou, they thereby established the Yunyan-Dongshan lineage.
This is a portion of the same essential energy. Let us set aside what is distant and take up what is near;
let us speak of the portion of energy that arises within the body of a single person, such as when Yaoshan met Shitou. His natural disposition was already transcendent;
yet, in his encounters with Boyan and Daowu, he established the dharma-methods of an entire generation. He sat down and subdued Ganji, leveling him out.
Li Ao was like one who had fallen into decrepitude and old age, offering no benefit to the world. Yet he let out a great laugh that was heard ninety li away;
this shows that even in old age, he remained increasingly eminent. Is this not because the vital energy (*qi*) of a single person’s life varies from beginning to end?

The *Zhuangzi* says: "One year of incense and one year of rancid herbs will still leave a foul odor after ten years. If this is true for material things, how much more so for the human spirit! As for Guan... [text ends].
He was indeed one of the greatest among those of the mind-dharma.
Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun of Jingzhou succeeded to the Dharma of Chan Master Chongxin of Longtan in Liuzhou.
The Master was originally the son of a man who sold cakes at Zhugong. His family had lived for generations in the lane of Tiantai Temple.

[The donor] would regularly provide ten cakes, which Huiguang accepted and ate. At the end, he presented one cake to his son, saying, "I bestow this upon you so that it may provide shade and protection for your descendants.
The Master thought to himself, "These cakes were brought by me; why does he instead give them back to me? Is there another meaning to this? He went to him and asked.

Wu said, "This was brought by you; returning it to you—what fault is there in that? Upon hearing this principle, the Master attained immediate enlightenment and subsequently left the household life to serve him with diligent devotion at his side.
One day he asked, "Since I arrived here, I have not received instruction on the essential point of the mind. Wu said:
"Ever since you arrived, I have never failed to point out the essential meaning of the mind. The Master asked, "Where did you point it out?
Wuzhuo said, "When you brought me tea, I received it for you; when you brought me food, I accepted it for you; and when you performed your obeisance..."
I then bowed my head. Where else could the essential point of the mind not be indicated? Master Wuxue lowered his head and remained so for a long while.
Huizhao said, "If you see, see directly; if you deliberate, you are already mistaken. At that moment, the Master attained realization. He then asked again, "How does one maintain this?
Wuxue said, "Roam freely according to your nature; let go as circumstances arise. Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no other superior understanding. Afterwards...
He went to the Dragon Pool in Liyang and settled there. A monk asked, "Who can obtain the pearl within the topknot?
The Master said, "One who does not gaze upon it obtains it. The monk asked, "Where is it placed? The Master said, "It has a place.
He then added, "If it has a place, tell me where. A group of nuns asked, "How can one become a monk? The Master said, "How long has it been since you came as nuns? The nuns replied, "Indeed..."
When the monk was present, [Nanquan] asked, "Is there? The master said, "What is this right now? The nun said, "I am clearly in the body of a nun;
how could I not recognize it? The master said, "Who recognizes you? Li Ao asked, "What is true suchness and prajñā? The master said, "I have no true suchness or prajñā.
Li Ao said, "It is fortunate to have met the Master. The master said, "This is still beyond the ordinary."
Deshan asked, "I have long heard of Longtan; yet now that I have arrived, neither the pond nor the dragon is to be seen.
The Master said, "You have come directly to Longtan yourself. Deshan then desisted.
Baotán said: "Generally, when any creature accumulates a thousand years, it becomes a dragon; even a single *zhōng* of water can contain it. Thus, dragons may be treated with familiarity and served.
In the time of Gaoxin, there was the Clan of Dragon-Feeders (*huàlóngshì*). Yet, a True Lord (*zhēnzǎi*) presides over them;
in years of drought, he sends down rain, and the suffering is boundless. There are even times when they transform back into ordinary creatures, as small as fine grains of millet."
Wherever the thunderclaps roll over, there is nowhere to escape; such is called being at odds with the natural order, and one is not a true dragon.

In the time of the Buddha, there was one named Sāgara, who resided in a jeweled palace throughout his successive lives. Though his resources were both abundant and lacking, he served the Buddha with devotion equal to that of the devas.
There is also the one named Subhakūṭarāja (Floating Banner King). From the summit of his palace, Sāgara, two streams of water emerge daily.
For this reason, the tides of the great ocean do not miss their appointed time; he can also raise vast clouds and pour down refreshing rain to moisten all living beings.
This is a Bodhisattva-dragon; the Dragon Pond must belong to this class. When compared with the deeds of Emperor Tenno...

Then his lips were like pearls in a deep pool. His earnestness in seeking the Way was such that he bore the image of one who "is active and vigilant all day long, and remains alert as if in peril at evening.
When he finally received the seal of approval, there arose the sense of clouds and mist gathering together in profusion.
At this point, they were like father and son; he gave birth to one like Deshan, who revitalized the orthodox lineage of Caoxi. How could it be anything less?
Water merely flows from the crown of the palace; the ocean of his compassionate clouds and vows has continued to circulate until the present day.
Although even Bodhisattvas and dragons must eventually vacate their abodes, Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Liuzhou inherited the Dharma.

After Chan Master Decheng of Huating was enlightened by seeing through Yaoshan, he thereafter transcended all categories and left the mundane behind. He alone drifted in a small boat upon the Wujiang River at Huating;
amidst clear mists and bright moons, as the ripples shimmered like leaping gold, he found his own joy. Thus, he was known as the Boatman Monk.
A fellow practitioner said to Dao-wu, "In the future, there will be a sharp and intelligent presiding abbot who will come seeking you.
Later, Dao-wu encouraged the Monk of Jingkou to go and pay his respects to the Master. When he arrived, the Master asked him, "Abbot, which monastery do you reside at?"
Zhaozhou said, "If it resembles [it], it does not abide; if it abides, it does not resemble. The Master asked, "If it neither resembles nor does not resemble, what is it that it resembles?
Zhaozhou said, "It is not a dharma of the present moment. The Master asked, "Where did you learn this? Zhaozhou said, "It is not something reached by the ears or the eyes.
The Master said, "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. He also said, "Dangling a line a thousand feet long..."
"The fish was in a deep pool, three inches away from the hook. Why did you not speak? As Huai would have opened his mouth, the Master split him with his oar and struck him into the water.
He urgently called out, "Speak! Speak! Just as Huai was about to speak, the Master struck him again. At that moment, Huai attained great enlightenment.
Baotan said: "Jiashan was like one ascending the Dragon Gate; Chuangzi was the thunderclap that scorched his tail.
I have observed that when Wujou examined Xuanshao and Huangbo received Linji, they both employed this very mechanism.
Chuangzi used his empty hands as the hook and the Great Dharma as the bait; though there were those with great mouths and slender scales, he had no regard for them—only shrimp and crabs."
What concern is this of mine? It is simply because there was a father like Yaoshan, a friend like Daowu, and a son like Jiashan.
To abandon the boat and rush toward the bright moon—what regret could there be in that? Were it not for the power of my friends, what else could I have hoped for?
When Chan Master Baiyan Mingzhe of Ezhou went to pay his respects, he arrived with Master Dongshan and his senior companion, Master Mi. The Master asked, "Where have you recently come from, Ācārya?"
Dongshan said, "I have recently left Hunan. The Master asked, "What is the surname of the Military Governor? Dongshan said, "He has no surname.
The Master asked, "What is his given name? Dongshan said, "He has no name. The Master asked, "Does he still attend to official affairs?
Dongshan said, "There are still the corridors and offices. The Master asked, "Does he not go in and out [of them]? Dongshan then shook his sleeves and departed. The Master—
The next day, upon entering the Sangha hall, [Dongshan] said: "Yesterday, in response to you two *jialuo*, one of your turns of phrase was not stable. I now ask you both to speak it.
If you can speak it, I, this old monk, will open the rice gruel and meals so that we may spend the summer retreat together. "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Dongshan said. "It is too noble a birth.
Thereupon, the Master opened the rice gruel and meals, and they spent the summer together.
Baotan said: "The lineage of Dongshan has reached this point, becoming increasingly aged yet flourishing.
Now, in establishing the Dharma for an era, one must first attend to father, son, and brother before reaching out to others; even the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is no different.

Thus, if there is even a hair’s breadth of something not yet forgotten, sleep and food are both neglected. This is not merely the result of the efforts of a single family; it is truly the work of Heaven."
This is because they were driven by the conditions of future generations. Dongshan regarded Baiyan as merely his uncle;
how could he not have come and gone? He simply shook out his sleeves and left. If it had been Deshan or Linji, what would they have cared about an uncle?
They would have said, "I have promised to stay for the summer retreat to share this rice gruel with you," waiting to deliberate upon their own family heritage. What a truly noble personage!
Chan Master Decheng of Huating Ship was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Shanhui of Jia Mountain in Lishui.
While he was presiding over Zhulin Temple in Jingkou, he ascended the hall for a discourse. A monk asked, "What is the Dharmakāya? The Master said:
“The Dharma-body is without marks. Question: “What is the Dharma-eye? The Master said: “The Dharma-eye is without flaw. At that time, Daowu was sitting among the guests.
Upon hearing these words, he could not help but laugh out loud. When the Master descended from his seat, he invited Daowu for tea and asked:

“Just now, when I responded to this monk’s question, there must have been something incorrect, which caused you, Venerable Sir, to laugh. I hope you will not withhold your compassion and explain it to me.”
"Truly pitiful," I said. "The Master is one who has transcended the world, yet you have no teacher. The Master asked, "In what way am I not right?
I hope you will explain it for me. I said, "I shall certainly not say anything. You should go and study under the Master Huating Chuanzi.
The Master asked, "What is this man like? I said, "This man has not a single tile to cover his head above, nor..."
"A place where even the point of a锥 (chui) cannot be stuck. [The monk] thought it best to change his attire; the Master then dispersed the assembly, changed his clothes, and went straight to Huating.

Upon seeing the Master arrive, he asked, "In what monastery do you reside, Venerable Sir? The Master replied, "If it were like residing, I would not be residing; if I were residing, it would not be like residing."
Cheng said, "It does not resemble anything; what, then, does it not resemble? The Master said, "It is not the dharma before one's eyes. Cheng said, "Where did you learn this?
The Master said, "It is not something reached by the ears or the eyes. Cheng said, "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.
He added, "The line hangs down a thousand feet, yet its intent lies in the deep pool; it is three inches away from the hook—what do you say to this?"

“Not yet. As the Master was about to open his mouth, Xuecheng took up his staff and struck him across the back, knocking him into the water. Just as the Master stepped onto the boat, Xuecheng hurriedly called out, “Speak!
Speak! As the Master was about to open his mouth again, Xuecheng struck him once more. At that moment, the Master attained a great awakening; he nodded his head three times.
Xuecheng said, “The silk line on the tip of the pole is for you to handle as you wish; without disturbing the clear waves, the meaning is naturally distinct. The Master—
He then asked, "Master, what is your intention in casting the line and throwing the hook? Cheng said, "The thread hangs in the green water; floating, it signifies both existence and non-existence.
The Master said, "The words carry the profound yet there is no path; the tongue speaks, yet it does not speak.

Cheng said, "Having fished through the waves of the river, only then is the golden-scaled fish encountered. The Master then covered his ears. Cheng said, "So it is, so it is! You must truly conceal your body."
Where there is no trace, do not hide your body where there is no trace. Later, after [the Master] had settled in, a monk asked:

"Regarding the meaning established by the patriarchs of old and the meaning of the teachings, why does the Master say they do not exist here? The Master said: "If one does not eat for three years, there will be no hungry people on the day before.
The monk asked: "Why is it that I do not awaken? The Master said: "It is precisely because of awakening that you have become deluded, O *śrāmaṇera*."

The verse says: "Brilliantly clear, there is no dharma to be awakened to; The dharma of awakening, instead, deludes people. Stretching out both legs and sleeping— Without falsehood, there is also no truth.

Lepu was at a loss for a reply. The Master struck him. Lepu then devoted himself to the Master for several years. A monk asked, "What is the fundamental reality? The Master said, "Drink."

Water does not lose its source. A question was asked: "What was the purpose of the ancients spreading their hair to cover the mud? The Master said: "The nine suns have been shot down, yet one shadow still remains;
once an arrow falls to the ground, the world is no longer dark. A question was asked: "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?"
He said: "The wind blows upon the lotus leaves, filling the pond with green; travelers for ten *li* find their journey shortened by one stage.
When the Chief Seat of Xichuan arrived at Baima while traveling, he cited a passage from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and asked: "When a single mote of dust contains the infinite Dharma-realm, what then?
Baima replied: "It is like the two wings of a bird, or the two wheels of a chariot. The Chief Seat said: "I thought the Chan school was something different!"

There was a remarkable matter. Originally, [the Master] had not departed from the teachings of the scriptures. He then returned to his own quarters and, following the direction [of the inquiry], sent a junior monk to deliver the previous message to ask about it.
The Master said: "To carve sand is not the talk of one who polishes jade; to speak in mere words is to deviate from the contemplation of a man of the Way.
When the junior monk returned and reported this, the Head Seat said: "I had thought that the meaning of the Chan gate was no different from that of the scriptural teachings."
"Truly, there is something extraordinary here. [A monk] asked, "What is the realm of Jia Shan? The Master said, "Monkeys carry their young back into the green peaks;
birds hold flowers in their beaks before the azure cliffs. It has been twelve years since he reopened the profound pivot of the Dharma.
Baotán said: "There is no dharma before one's eyes; the meaning lies right before one's eyes.
It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is beyond the reach of ears and eyes. These were the words with which he was ridiculed by Dàowū while in Jīngǒu.
These were the words with which he was reviled by Chuánzǐ upon arriving at Huátíng. This is based on the toppling of the staff and whisk at Jiāshān’s summit.
"Come. These were his words. Not a single word was ever altered, yet success or failure followed accordingly from beginning to end.

Thus we know that delusion and enlightenment reside in the person, not in the Dharma. Observe how, after the two oars had been pulled down and away, he was never for a moment in accord with his teacher;
yet how his spirit of transcending the past and surpassing the crowd closely resembled that of his master! Great!
To briefly indicate the human condition as it is at its great point of differentiation: at first, it might be exhausted by a single cup, and its emergence would not extend beyond a few feet.
Yet, once waves and billows begin to rise and fall, there arises a momentum that swallows the heavens and kicks away the sun.
When the sun overflows the eyes, everyone is universally bathed in its light. Regarding the "Story of the Realm" of Jia Shan, only Fa Yan alone perceived the true person; such was that person.

It is difficult to know; its Dharma is likewise difficult to know. When the sun blazes before one's eyes and illuminates ten thousand *li*, the Buddha-sun turns back the tide to bring joy to all—this is accomplished by this very hand. Should one not stand in awe?
Formerly, Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Langzhou received the Dharma from Chan Master Quanhuo of Yantou in Ezhou.
These three masters—Yantou, Xuefeng, and Qinshan—were close friends. From Dayu Peak in Hanyang, they traveled in succession until they reached Linji.
Ji Shun entered the world and first visited Yangshan. As soon as he stepped through the gate, he held up his sitting cloth and called out, “Master!

Yangshan took up his whisk, intending to raise it, but the Master said, “Not bad, a skilled hand. Later, he went to visit Deshan. Holding his sitting cloth, he ascended the Dharma hall and gazed about.
Deshan asked, “What are you doing? The Master gave him a shout. Deshan said, “Where does my old monk’s fault lie?”
[The Master asked: "Where [did you learn this]? The Master said, "A double case. He then went down to attend the hall.
Deshan said, "This master is somewhat like a true traveler. On the following day, when [the Master] came to inquire after him, Deshan said, "Venerable brother, were you the one who arrived yesterday?
[The Master] said, "I was. Deshan said, "Where did you learn such empty pretension? The Master said, "From Quanhuo."
He never deceived himself. Deshan said, "In the future, you must not let me down. One day, [Zhaozhou] went to pay his respects.
As Deshan entered the abbot’s quarters, Zhaozhou turned his body sideways and asked, "Is this a saint or an ordinary person? Deshan gave a shout. Zhaozhou bowed.
Someone reported this to Dongshan, who said, "Had it not been for Upasaka Huo, it would have been very difficult to handle. When Zhaozhou heard this, he remarked:
The old man Dongshan did not recognize good from bad; he wrongly established these names and phrases. At that time, I would have used one hand to lift him up and the other to press him down.
When Xuefeng was serving as the head cook at Deshan, one day the meal was late, and Deshan went down from the Dharma Hall holding his alms bowl.
Xuefeng then said, "The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded; where is the Old Monk going with his alms bowl?
Deshan returned to his quarters. Hearing this from within the hall, the Master clapped his hands and said, "Great Deshan has not yet realized the final word.
When Deshan heard of this, he summoned an attendant and ordered him to call the Master up to question him, saying, "You do not approve of me."
The Master secretly conveyed his intention to him. On the following day, when Deshan ascended the hall to preach, his discourse was different from his usual style.
When the Master arrived before the Sangha Hall, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "I am glad that the old man at the head of the hall has understood the 'final word.
Hereafter, no one in the world will be able to do anything with him. Nevertheless, he shall live for only three years. Indeed, after three years, he passed away.
One day, while he was conversing with Xuefeng and Qinshan, the three of them were gathered together. Xuefeng suddenly pointed to a bowl of water.
Qinshan said, "The water is clear; the fish appears. Xuefeng said, "The water is clear; the fish does not appear. The Master kicked over the bowl of water and departed.
From this point on, [Yunyan] succeeded Dongshan; Cunen and Huan both succeeded Deshan. The Master and Xuefeng took their leave of Deshan together.
Deshan asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going down the mountain for a short visit to bid farewell to the Master.
Deshan said, "What will you do after that? The Master said, "I shall not forget this. Deshan said, "On what basis do you make such a statement? The Master said, "Is it not so?"

"One only transmits the teacher's teaching after hearing wisdom that surpasses the teacher's. Should one's wisdom be equal to the teacher's, it is feared that hereafter one might diminish the teacher's virtue by half.
The teacher said, "So it is, so it is. You must maintain this well. The teacher and Xuefeng both performed a prostration and withdrew. Cunen resided at Xianggu in Min;
the teacher established a hermitage on Sleeping Dragon Mountain at Dongting. A monk asked, "If there is no teacher, is there still a way out?"
[The monk] asked, "Is there anything at all? The Master said, "Before the sound, ancient cloth has rotted away. [The monk] asked, "How is it when one comes forth with such majestic presence?
The Master said, "It pierces the eye. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's intent? The Master said, "Bring Mount Lu here, and I will tell you."

One day, the Master ascended the hall and said to his disciples, "I once studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for seven or eight years and perceived three points of meaning that seemed like the talk of a patch-robed monk.
He then added, "Enough! Enough! At that time, a monk prostrated and requested the Master to provide an illustration. The Master said:
The intent of my teaching is like the three dots of the character *i*. The first dot is placed toward the east; it opens the eyes of all bodhisattvas.
The second dot is placed toward the west; it sustains the life-force of all bodhisattvas. The third dot is placed toward the zenith;
it seals the crown of the heads of all bodhisattvas. This is the meaning of the first section. Furthermore, it is said: "My teaching..."
"The intent is like that of Maheśvara, who splits open his face and raises one eye. This is the meaning of the second section. Furthermore, it is said:
'The intent of my teaching is like a poison-smeared drum; when struck once, all who hear it, whether far or near, perish—this is called 'all dying together.
This is the meaning of the third section. At that time, the Venerable Xiaoyan asked: 'What is the poison-smeared drum?'"
Gum. The Master pressed both hands against his knees, leaned forward, and said, "This is how Han Xin presided over the court.

A monk asked, "In the midst of vast dust and turmoil, how does one discern the master? The Master said, "A copper bowl filled to the brim with oil. He asked, "How is it before the ancient sail has been raised?
The Master said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass. From that time on, whether he was asked about the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Way, [he responded in this manner].
When asked about meditation, the Master would always make a sound like a sigh and say to the assembly, "When this old man departs, I shall depart with a great roar.
After the Guangqi era, bandits rose up in the Central Plains; indeed, this was proven true.
Baotan said: "The realization of Yantou should have been recorded in his writings, yet this alone was not written down;
thus it is understandable that people came to claim this old man was one who knew by birth. This fails to illuminate the underlying principle:
while the mind of a true spiritual friend has indeed transcended the realms of birth and death, the body of the spiritual friend still remains within those realms of birth and death."
As soon as you emerge from the state of ignorance, you must awaken. For once you fall into the realm of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the dust of birth and death defiles you;
it is like muddy water flowing in a stagnant pool—it cannot be avoided that one must wash away the filth.
Even the Elder Śākyamuni, while residing in Tuṣita Heaven, could not avoid the single encounter with the staff on the mountain of Perfect Enlightenment. This is what I mean by "one."
This is what is meant by "knowing by birth. Only when the Buddha-dharma reaches its ultimate virtue does it act like thunder and lightning rolling forth in midsummer.
Upon reaching this point, it strikes the sea monsters and shatters the pillars, further manifesting its majesty.
It makes no distinction between father and teacher; encountering the startling, it startles, and encountering the shaking, it shakes—just as at Mount Neng and Mount Kong.

This is an example of such things. Some may doubt this, wondering whether Heaven possesses private intent when it reveals its will secretly or after a long silence, and might ask if Heaven, too, has partiality.
I say: not so. The secret revelation is like thunder; the long silence is like lightning. Any failure to understand this is merely the fault of those who are ignorant.
How could this be the fault of Heaven? The sounds of antiquity have crumbled and decayed; how can one distinguish the master amidst the dust?
As for the three turns of speech when the ancient sail had not yet been hoisted, and the three sections of meaning from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—these are all like a stroke of lightning.
Finally, within the great governing principle of the essential school, there are over one hundred and fifty phrases and nine hundred and sixty-odd characters.
Every word and every phrase is capable of penetrating to the very marrow of the learner’s bones. This book, however, has been omitted and not included;
I have therefore taken it up to complete it, hoping thereby to obtain even a partial glimpse of its entirety.
Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Fuzhou was a disciple who went up to Dongshan nine times and visited Touzi three times. Later, he attained enlightenment at Aoshan Inn.

When Guantong asked him to ascend Mount Xianggu, he took the high seat and held up his whisk, saying, "This is for those of middle and lower capacity. A monk then asked, "What about those of the highest capacity?"
When a monk approached, the Master raised his whisk. The monk said, "This is for those of middling or inferior capacity. The Master struck him.
The Master was asked, "What was the meaning of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant? The Master immediately rose and entered the abbot’s quarters.

Once, while the Master was on a work assignment at a village estate, he encountered a macaque on the road. The Master said, "This beast carries an ancient mirror on its back; let it pick me up, monk!"
[The monk] asked about "rice seedlings. The Master said, "For kalpas without name, why is it established as the 'ancient mirror'?
The monk said, "A flaw has arisen. The Master said, "Why do you not even recognize this dead, urgent *huatou*? The monk said, "It is the old monk’s fault.
The Master asked Changqing Ling, "The ancients said, 'Three before, three after. What is the meaning of this? Ling then went out.
One day he asked, "Regarding the single path transmitted by all the sages of antiquity, when Shigong Xuefeng was instructed to point it out, he remained silent and Ling bowed and withdrew.

Xuefeng smiled broadly. On another day, he said to Ling, 'I have often told the assembly of monks that there is a turtle-nosed snake on the South Mountain; you all must look at it very carefully. Ling said:"
"Today, there are many in this hall who have lost their bodies and forfeited their lives. The Master approved of this. Ling went up to the Abbot’s quarters to visit the Master again.
The Master asked, "What is it? Ling said, "Today the weather is clear; it is a good day for communal labor (*pǔqǐng*).
One day the Master asked, "Who among the assembly is the Venerable Beidhūta? A monk said, "I truly do not dare deceive anyone. On another day, the Master summoned him.
[The Master] said, "Bei Toudou, why do you not go to seek instruction everywhere? Bei replied, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land;

the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. The Master approved of this. Later, when the Master ascended the hall, he said: "To understand this matter is like an ancient mirror set upon its stand."
"When a Hu comes, a Hu appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears. Sand asked, "What if one suddenly encounters the arrival of a bright mirror?

The Master said, "Both Hu and Han are hidden. Sand said, "The old monk’s heels have not yet touched the ground. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "I left Mount Míngzhào.
I once asked him, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Míngzhào [replied by] leaning against..."
[The monk] took his seat. The Master said, "Do you accept him? The monk replied, "I do not accept him. The Master said, "You are a descendant of the ancient Buddha Muzhou;
go quickly to pay your respects and repent! Xuansha said, "That old fellow on the mountain has missed the point regarding Muzhou's matter.
The Master said to Jingqing, "In the past, the venerable elders would lead officials on a tour of the hall, saying, 'This entire assembly consists entirely of students...'"
"Buddha, Dharma, Sangha. The official said, "Though gold dust is precious, what then? The old master had no reply.

Jingqing remarked, "This has been a case of throwing a brick to draw out a jade gem. Fayan offered a different interpretation, saying, "How can you, official, value the ears while deprecating the eyes?
A teacher from Min presented a silver bedstead. A monk asked, "The Master receives such offerings from the Great King; with what will you repay them?"
The Master pressed his hand against the ground and said, "Strike me lightly. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "If I speak of east and west, you will follow my words and pursue my phrases.
But if I were like a langur monkey hanging from a horn, where would you go to search for me?"
Baotan said: "In the history of the Way, there has been but one person since antiquity for whom the path was so arduous—Xuefeng was such a man.
The ancients examined themselves until they reached ultimate penetration. It is like drilling for fire: first there is warmth, then smoke arises from within."
Finally, the fire blazes; the cooking is successfully completed to offer the sacrifice to the Supreme Deity (Shangdi), and only then do the fire-related rites conclude.
This is not yet the "swan among swans" (*hongjian zhong zhi hongjian*) of gradual progress. At Xuefeng’s place, he attained entry—this was the first emergence of warmth.
At Dongshan’s place, his realization blossomed—this was the smoke rising within. At Deshan’s place, he attained penetration.
"Leaving" refers to the finality of the fire burning; "the Tortoise Mountain attaining the Way" refers to the completion of the work of cooking.
When he first went up to Touzi three times and visited Dongshan nine times, honoring Master Huo and befriending Master Sui, it was as if not a single day passed without a teacher or a friend.
This serves as a model for scholars throughout the world: carrying a ladle upon one's back while walking.
Throughout the four seas, he claimed that his seventeen hundred spiritual friends were all scooped up from the tip of a ladle;
this is the method for teaching those throughout the world who act as teachers. In raising disciples, he was like Changqing, Xuansha, Jingqing, and Yunmen—all great pillars of the Dharma;
this is the method for teaching those throughout the world to "cook" Buddhas and "cook" patriarchs.
This Dharma has never for a single day been absent from the world.
It is simply that there are no such capacities, no such whetstones, and no such furnaces. What can I do with such people?
Master Waguan of Quanzhou was asked by Deshan, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not understand. Deshan said, "It is well that you hold fast to this 'not understanding.
The Master said, "If I do not understand, what is there to hold fast to? Deshan said, "You are truly great..."
"It is like an iron stake. The Master then tucked up his robes.
Baotán said, "The ancients let go more fiercely than they held fast; one who knows there is a hand that binds tigers will certainly not let you go.
The proverb says: 'In raising a child, there is no need for instruction; once the trap is set, he will naturally understand. Thus it was with Linji."
Regarding Yuepo and Deguan at Deshan—both these elders were like this. Jia Shan and Xuefeng employed this remaining intent to bring their two disciples to life.
Alas! Jia Shan can truly be said not to have failed An. It is a pity that Xuefeng annotated and broke through [the case of] Waguan, yet did not act as fully for Deshan as he had for Yuepo.
The former Chan Master Shanhui of Jia Mountain in Lizhou succeeded in the Dharma to Chan Master Yuan'an of Lebu Mountain in Lizhou.
This master had studied under Linji, who often praised him before the assembly, saying: "A single arrow from the gate of Linji—dare anyone [dodge it]?"
When he reached the front lines of the assembly, the Master granted him permission. He considered himself sufficient and went to Mount Jia-shan to pitch a hermitage.

Later, upon seeing and reading a letter of instruction from Jia-shan, he was struck with a sudden sense of awe. He then abandoned his hut and went to Jia-shan, where he prostrated and stood with his body upright.
Jiashan said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix’s nest is not of its kind; get out! The Master said, "I have traveled from afar to seek the Way;
I request the Master to grant me an audience. Jiashan said, "Before my eyes there is no you; here there is no old monk. The Master said, "Wrong!"
Jiashan said, "Wait, wait, Ācārya! Do not be so hasty or precipitate. The streams and mountains differ, yet the clouds and moon are the same.
It may be that you, Ācārya, have silenced the tongues of all people under heaven, but how can you make those who have no tongues speak?"
The Master was at a loss for a reply. Jiashan then struck him. The Master remained devoted to his teachings for several years.

One day, the Master asked Jiashan, "How does one realize the place where neither Buddha nor demons reach? Jiashan replied, "A candle illuminates images for a thousand li; in a dark room, even an old monk is lost.
He asked again, "When the morning sun has already risen, why does the night moon not appear? Jiashan replied, "The dragon..."
The fish swimming through the pearls in their mouths do not look back. As Jiashan was about to pass away, he spoke these words: "The branch of Shitou—look, it is about to perish!
The Master replied, "Not so. Jiashan asked, "Why? The Master said, "There are still green mountains that remain."
Jiashan said, "If it is thus, then my Way shall not fall into ruin. When Jiashan passed away, the Master arrived at Cenyang and met an old acquaintance.
While discussing matters concerning Wuling, the acquaintance asked, "In the blink of an eye several years have passed; where have you been escaping calamity?
The Master replied, "I have been right in the midst of the marketplace, yet people do not even recognize me. The acquaintance was unable to fathom this. He asked again, "I have heard of the West..."
"From the twenty-eight patriarchs in the heavens down to this land, it has been one person transmitting it to another. Now, what if neither side were to condescend?
" The Master said, "An old countryman does not speak of court affairs at his gate. Question: "What matters should he discuss?
The Master said, "Until I meet someone else, I shall never open my fist. [The questioner] said, "There was once someone who did not come from the court; when we met—"
"Did you understand? The Master said, "The capacity beyond measure is merely a vain exertion of self-striking. The monk had no reply.
As for Great Master Furi’s meeting with Yunju and subsequently meeting Jiaoshan, the account is found in the chapter on Jiaoshan.
Baotan said: "Because Le Pu had seen Linji, Jia Shan exhausted himself with the style of Linji;
because Furi had seen Yunju, Jia Shan enriched himself with the style of Yunju. It was not that there was only one Jia Shan who could emulate both Linji and Yunju;
it was like using the 'Hanging Jade' and the 'Qushan Chariots' to take a detour through Yu in order to attack the two neighboring states."
This is the title [of this work]. When the Buddha-sun arrives, it permits those who have traveled afar to come forth like a dark tide;

Lo Pu was unaware of it, yet both the channels and the harbors were filled. They swam as they would in the August tide of Qiantang, with thunder crashing and lightning rushing—a sight that had surely never been seen before.
Chan Master Liang-jia of Dongshan in Yuanzhou was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Wen-sui of Qingshan in Liuzhou.
In his youth, he relied upon Chan Master Huanzhong of Hangzhou, where Yan-tou and Xue-feng were also present. Together, they traveled to various regions to study.
An old karmic affinity. Although Deshan had each received a seal of transmission, the Master repeatedly encountered his vigorous challenges and remained ultimately stuck in doubt and stagnation.
One day he asked Deshan, "Tianhuang spoke thus; Longtan spoke thus. I wonder, how would Deshan speak?
Deshan said, "Try bringing forth what Tianhuang and Longtan said, and I will see. Only then did the Master...
As he was about to speak, Deshan struck him with his staff and had him carried into the Nirvana Hall.
The Master said, "That is true; you have struck me quite severely. Later, when the Master visited Dongshan, Dongshan asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "From Daci. Dongshan asked, "Did you see Daci? The Master replied, "I saw him. Dongshan asked, "Did you see him before his form, or after his form?"
[The Master] saw him. The Master said, "Seeing is neither before nor after. Dongshan remained silent. The Master said, "You left your teacher too early;
you have not fully realized your teacher’s intent. At twenty-seven years of age, he resided at Mount Qin. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Liang Gong’s bent red [beard]; Master Zhi’s scissors. [The monk] asked, "All the dharmas of the Buddhas all issue forth from this sutra."
"What is this sutra? The Master said, "I have asked about it before; I do not yet know what is said within the sutra. [The monk] said, "If you have doubts, please ask me.
[The Master] asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "An embroidered pouch and a silver incense bag; the wind blows their fragrance along the road.
Once, while traveling through Jiangxi with Xuefeng and Yantou, the Master stopped at a tea shop to drink tea. The Master...
[The Master] said, "One who does not know how to turn their body and pass through the breath shall not be granted tea today.
Xuefeng said, "I am the same. The Master said, "Both old fellows do not understand the language. Yantou said, "Where have you gone?
The Master said, "An old crow in a cloth bag—though alive, it is as if dead. Yantou said, "Step back! Step back!"
[The Master] said, "Zhuo! The Master said, "Brother Huo, set that aside for a moment; how about Cunkong? Xuefeng drew a circle with his hand. The Master said, "I cannot help but ask.
Yantou laughed heartily and said, "It is far too distant. The Master said, "Though one has a mouth, one cannot speak;
those who drink tea are many. Both Yantou and Xuefeng were speechless. A monk came to visit; the Master raised his fist.
The Master said, "If you open it to form a palm, the five fingers will be uneven; if you now make a fist, there will certainly be no high or low.
Tell me, does Qingshan’s way allow for deliberation, or does it not? The monk stepped forward, raised his fist, and withdrew.
The Master said, "To act just like that is simply to be a fellow who knows nothing of opening or closing. The monk asked, "I do not know how you, Master, would receive him?"

The monk said, "If I were to receive people, I would do so just as you do. The Master said, "If you have come specifically for this purpose, I must reveal the essence of our school. The monk said, "Then please do so. The Master then struck him;
the monk was speechless. The Master said, "Like one who waits by a stump for a rabbit—you are wasting your mental energy in vain."
Baotan said: Qingshan, with his youthful and transcendent bearing, encountered the right teachers and friends at a fortunate juncture, yet he was unable to emerge as a preeminent figure of his time.
When he spoke, it was like a startled deer or a fleeing rabbit—uncontainable and impossible to restrain.
Thus, he was subjected to rigorous testing for a long time; nevertheless, he could not ultimately die at the hands of Deshan, but instead returned to Dongshan, his true master.
How could the conditions and opportunities for spiritual resources not have their own measure?

Generally speaking, among those who study the Way, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, the depth or shallowness of their practice, and the speed or slowness of their realization.

As for Qinshan’s following Yantou and Xuefeng—considering that at that time these two elders were the greatest masters under heaven—their state of hardship and toil was such that, even in later generations, this...
That they did not lose their ease and leisure in old age allows us to know the flourishing or decline of the Buddha-Dharma at this time.
The critical points of Dongshan’s teaching were dense and intricate; father and son each maintained their own family tradition.
In his later years, Qingshan thrust his arm into their midst, leaving nothing whatsoever upon which to rely. How could this have been the result of these two elders’ spiritual transformation?
Is it by power?
Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Fuzhou received the Dharma from Chan Master Jiaoran of Changsheng Mountain in Fuzhou.
While the Master was at Xuefeng, he was cutting down a tree with a monk. Xuefeng said, "When you reach the heart, stop. The Master said, "Cut it away!
Xuefeng said, "The ancients transmitted mind-to-mind; why do you say 'cut it away'?
The Master threw down his axe and said, "Transmitted. Xuefeng struck him with a staff and departed. A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is..."
Regarding the first phrase: Xuefeng remained silent for a long time. A monk reported this to the Master, who said, "This is the second phrase.
Xuefeng then sent the same monk back to ask, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven!

Later, while Xuefeng was working together with the community to carry firewood, he asked the Master, "An ancient said, 'Who would have known that beneath the official hat is still the person of former sorrows'?"
"What was the intention of the ancients? The Master, wearing his bamboo hat tilted to one side, said, "Whose words are these?
Xuefeng asked the Master, "A bearer of the scriptures can carry the Tathāgata on their shoulders; what is it to carry the Tathāgata on one's shoulders?
The Master then took Xuefeng up in his arms and placed him upon the meditation seat. When Xuefeng returned from the communal labor, he carried a bundle of rattan himself along the road.
He encountered a monk who set down his bamboo staff and stood with his hands clasped. As the monk approached to pick it up, Xuefeng stepped on him.
The monk retreated, and upon returning, he reported the incident to the Master, saying, "Today I stepped on that monk; how swift he was!
The Master replied, "The Master has merely caused that monk to enter the Nirvana Hall. The Master once visited a hermitage keeper.
The Master said, "Recently, a monk asked me about the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West. I then raised my whisk to show him.
I do not know whether he understood it or not. The Teacher said, "How would one dare say whether he understood it or not?
If someone asks the Hermitage Master, 'In this matter, some people guarantee its attainment,' it is like a tiger’s head wearing horns. If someone rejects it, it is not worth a single coin. This.
"Why is it that praise and blame differ regarding this matter? Please try to discern it for me. Deyin said, "What occurred just now was merely accidental;
how could one possibly discern it? The Master said, "If you act like this, you shall not be fit to guide others in the future.
Xuefeng asked, "When both light and objects have vanished, what is it then? Deyin said, "Let Jiaoran pass by; who would dare to deliberate upon it? Xuefeng said, [and remained silent].
"I grant you passage; how do you deliberate upon this? The Master said, "I clearly grant the Abbot passage as well. Xuefeng deeply approved of him.
Upon arriving at Lingyun’s place, he asked about the koan of the undifferentiated primordial chaos (*hundun*), which is recorded in the chapter on Lingyun.

The Master stayed at Changsheng Mountain to propagate the Dharma. A monk asked, "How should one proclaim the fundamental vehicle of the ancestors? The Master said, "It cannot be done for you, O *jia* (Venerable)."
Liyang had cleared away Changsheng Mountain. A monk asked, "The ancients said that ignorance is itself Buddha-nature and that afflictions need not be eliminated.
What is meant by 'ignorance is itself Buddha-nature'? The Master’s expression turned stern; raising his fist, he scolded him, saying, "Today, this monk is being beaten!
The monk asked, "What is meant by 'afflictions need not be eliminated'? The Master placed his hand upon the monk's head.
[The Master] said: "This monk creates such karmic entanglements for people. [A student] asked: "When meeting a person who has attained the Way, one does not respond with speech or silence;
I wonder, what then should one use to respond? The Master said: "What can the ink on this paper possibly do?"
Baotan said: "The gate of Xuefeng obtained such a man; indeed, the world has long held the title of 'the soaring falcon that cleaves the void.
Yet, while he may ascend with a sudden burst and reach the point of striking down his prey, there will inevitably be instances of gain and loss therein.
In my view, this is not equal to 'seeing their colors and taking flight,' 'circling before settling'—a state where one is ten thousand times free from even a single failure."
This is strategy. Changsheng, while at Xuefeng and Lingyun, employed the skill of soaring and gathering;
yet when it came to seizing sparrows and swallows, he employed the mechanism of striking and pouncing. How could one find students like these two masters? I see in them the perfection of their art.
Chan Master Shanzhao of Taizi Monastery in Fenzhou was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Shouzhi of Cuoyan on Mount Xishan in Nanchang.

When Master Shouzhi heard that [Master] Fenyang had appeared in the world, he harbored doubts and went to observe him. Upon finding his spiritual resonance, he entered the inner chamber, where [Fenyang] specifically bestowed his seal of approval upon him. South.

While traveling and residing at Gao’an, Dayu ascended the seat, opened the meditation mat, and said: “If you come with clarity, I will join you in clarity; if you come in obscurity, I will join you in obscurity.
If you can speak thus, you may roam freely throughout the world; if you cannot, then simply fold the mat back up.

A monk asked, “All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows. I pray that the Master will manifest the true reality. The Master said, “I do not understand. The monk [remained silent].

[The questioner] asked, "How so? The Master said, "When the autumnal notes of the lyrics have ceased, the melodic resonance is born anew. Among the great assembly of monks and laypeople, there are all manner of extraordinary individuals.
In our own dynasty, Yang Dainian composed a verse that says: "The eight-cornered millstone runs through the void; The golden-maned lion transforms into a dog.
If you wish to hide your body within the Northern Dipper, You must join your palms before the Southern Star."
Do you understand? A single verse spreads throughout all quarters, blocking the mouths of the patch-robed monks. It is also said: When a monk visited Luzu, Luzu simply faced the wall.
Nanquan said, "I usually tell the teachers and monks: 'Realize it before you were even conceived in the womb.'"
He could not even find one person, let alone half a person. Daoyu was not like this; he realized it before even being conceived in the womb.
[The Master] once said, "Today we have gathered to eat some mustard greens. If you call them 'a stalk of mustard greens,' you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow.
He descended from the seat without further words. At that time, Yunfeng Yue heard this being cited.
Greatly startled, he went to the Master’s chamber that night. The Master asked, "What do you seek by coming here? He replied, "I seek the Buddha-mind Dharma.

The Master said, "The wheel of the Dharma has not yet turned, but the wheel of food must turn first. You are a person of later birth with physical strength; why do you not go begging for alms for the community?
I am too busy enduring death to have the leisure to preach the Dharma for you. Xue immediately did as instructed. When the Master moved his residence to Cui...
Yuan Yue went along with him again. That night, they went to the Master’s quarters. The Master said, "Do you wish to seek the Buddha-mind Dharma once more?
You do not consider that I have only recently taken charge of this monastery; the walls and roof are drafty and leaking, and moreover, it is cold and snowy.

Day and night I have been looking for you to beg for charcoal for the sake of the assembly. How can I endure the cold and preach the Dharma for you? Yuan Yue did so again. Just as he was returning, the *weina* (steward) arrived.
That vacancy remained unfilled. One night, Yue visited the Master’s quarters. The Master said, "The Buddha-dharma does not fear being let to rot.
I shall now trouble you with the office of Hall Superintendent. Yue was unable to respond and departed. The next day, he returned to the Hall Superintendent's post;

however, he harbored resentment that the Master had not explained the Dharma of the Mind-Ground to him. While sitting on the back rack, a broken bucket bound beneath the rack fell from the shelf to the floor.
He leaped up. Suddenly he attained enlightenment. He immediately saw that his former applications were merely running in circles. He put on his *kāṣāya* and went to the dormitory hall.

The Master (Fenyang) welcomed him with a smile and said, "Venerable Vinaya Master, I am glad that the Great Matter is now completed. Yue bowed twice, perspiring profusely, yet unable to utter a single word.
Furthermore, [the Master] pointed out the "Ten Wisdoms of the Same Reality" of Fenyang. Later, he said, "The former Master only wanted you to recognize..."

This is not something to be seen with the physical eyes; it is too effortless. Yet those of later generations and junior students thrust their heads into the words and phrases, greedily clinging to their conceptual flavors, like a donkey licking where it has been urinated upon—no matter how many times they are struck with the staff, they will not turn back.

This is because they do not seek extensively for true knowledge, nor do they travel through various lineages; instead, having obtained but a single word or half-phrase, they nod their heads and swallow their own saliva, claiming that they have already attained full realization.
The Senior Elder still has points that are not yet settled. Our late Master had a "Song of the Styles of the Fifteen Houses," titled "Extensive Wisdom" (*Guangzhi*).
Its verses say: "The Great Way does not speak of high or low; How could True Emptiness (*zhēnkōng*) venture into separation or subtlety?

The great ocean swallows all streams, sharing in their increase and decrease; The wondrous peak towers aloft, supporting them all. Ten thousand currents and a thousand rivulets are all the Bohai Sea."
The seven golden mountains and five peaks all reach to Mount Sumeru; after the golden *ūrṇā* hair transmits the lamp, the second, third, fourth, and seventh generations are universally known.

The grace of the robe of faith extensively opens up one’s cognitive wisdom; the elders of all quarters may act as they please. To recognize the mind as the source is what is taught from the very beginning;
to lose the mind by chasing external objects, however, gives rise to doubt. The Master said: "This describes the fundamental principle (*zongzhi*). It may be a direct pointing, or..."

Skillfully applied is the resolution: the guiding thread of the Way emerges before, while the responsive capacity follows behind. Its essential purport is as clear and distinct as a mirror; those who are blind and lack the eye of wisdom cannot perceive it.
A man of clear vision perceives its subtle essence; he does not speak of victory or defeat, nor fall into folly. In every thing, he meets with the flowing water of wisdom.
Following the tradition of this school, he directly reveals the lineage of the Patriarchs: "The Buddha is the mind; the Buddha is not the mind. This has been clearly manifest through the ages.
There is no separate entity; this very true mind is my own mind. My own mind still emerges through skillful means (*upāya*). The Master said: "This describes the ancestral lineage of Mazu.
Whether as the Five Ranks (*wuwei*) or the Three Paths (*sanlu*), these arrangements are skillfully interwoven according to the capacities of beings.

Not touching upon the present moment is the fundamental school. Extending the hand to penetrate the mystery—there is neither Buddha nor Patriarch. The Master said: "This describes the Dongshan school."

[The lineage] extends to ministers and subjects, fathers and sons; whether the vessels are square or round, there is no distinction between self and other. From commoners and nobles to dukes and marquises, all follow the same path of equanimity.
Whether foolish or wise, humble or eminent, the gradual stages are made clear. The Master said: "This describes the lineage of Shishuang. Sometimes he struck [the board], sometimes he sang;

responding to questions according to people's capacities, his discourse was always precise and appropriate. In his reception of others, how could he ever have lost propriety? This is a shallow interpretation.

Those of such a sort, however, give rise to slander. Sometimes both [aspects] are clarified; sometimes only one is spoken. It simply requires sharp spiritual acumen and the joy of Chan. Revealing the provisional is not for the sake of competing for cleverness;
shedding light is only to distinguish the worthy and the wise. There are circular signs (*maṇḍala*) and there are silent discourses.

Bringing them from a thousand miles away, one meets them with a blink of the eye; though there be ten thousand kinds of ingenuity, they are all but a single empty circle. Śākyamuni’s eye penetrates through faith—thus spoke the Master.
[The interlocutor] says: "This describes the lineage of the Miu-yang (Shitou and Yangshan) school. Sometimes the whole is presented; sometimes the whole is employed.

The myriad phenomena in their dense array are truly not shared [by others]; the green mountains do not obstruct the flying white clouds. Faintly upon the dais, the golden phoenix penetrates through. The Master says:
"This describes the lineage of the Shitou and Yaoshan schools. The mirror of Xianggu; the moon of Dizang; the illumination of Xuansha and Chongshou is without flaw. Because..."
The Duke posed a question regarding the ultimate source. The meaning and intent were clear and pure to those who came. The Master said, "This describes the lineage of Xuefeng and Dizang.
Whether it is called 'lifting' or 'picking up,' a monk of true substance must strike it out with vigor. To clarify the human matter within a phrase is most refined;
a skilled hand is like using one wedge to drive out another. Whether it is raising up for recommendation or extending the hand in grace, the essential point lies in the mind."

It is easy to open one's mouth when speaking of emptiness, yet few recognize that their ancestors gave rise to Great Compassion. Those who merely hold a candle walk through the streets illuminating it. The Master said:
"This describes the Yunmen lineage. Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout uniquely emerge from heaven and earth to sweep across all things."
From the very beginning, who would dare to make arbitrary distinctions? Even a garrulous master cannot speak of it. Seizing the opportunity; taking it away at the opportune moment.
His swift and sharp wit flashes like lightning; heaven and earth are held within the palm of his hand. The spirits of the bamboo and wood have their skulls split open.
Whether as guest or host, whether discerning or selecting, he fully unfolds the Zen school’s eye of correct discernment; the Three Mysteries and Three Uses must be employed.

The pivot: the four propositions and the hundred negations are all swept away at once. I urge my fellow practitioners not to force an understanding; otherwise, even those who are somewhat clever will remain obstructed.
If you do not know the lineage, do not be reckless; you will sink forever into the ocean of birth and death. It is difficult to encounter, difficult to meet, and difficult to hear.
With a fierce and resolute mind, quickly attain thorough liberation. The Master said: "This describes the lineages of Deshan and Linji."
Ciming had an excellent attendant named Mingyan Su, who delighted in his master’s style. From Shishuang he went to Dayu, where he entered the master’s room.
The master kicked out a single sandal; Mingyan stepped back and stood there. As the master stooped to pick up the sandal, Mingyan suddenly tripped it over.
The master rose and faced the wall, drawing three lines on the wall with his finger one after another. Mingyan stood behind him with wide-open eyes. The master—
He whirled it around and struck him with his boot, then went to the Dharma Hall. Nanquan said, "To teach people in this way is to blind the eyes of the entire city.
A monk who was lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* asked, "If one has such faith and understanding, how can there be the arising of the marks of dharmas?
At that time, a dog was lying beneath the meditation platform. The Master kicked it and said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If..."

Upon understanding, the characteristics of arising phenomena are immediately perceived. He composes a verse: "It is a pitiable matter that there is no oil within sand; Cuiyan chews his rice and feeds it to an infant.
Once one knows the ultimate point of good and evil, One realizes for the first time that one's face was previously covered in ash."
The eulogy says: "The whole assembly gathers to eat a stalk of mustard relish. If you call it 'a single stalk of mustard relish,' you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
This is the shedding of one who was moved by wind and thunder; he is of dragon lineage and knows his destination, yet has not yet undergone transformation.
Once he fell into the hands of this old man, he was cast into the ordinary ditches and canals. Thunder!
The movement of wind and the passage of time do not require the incantations of the *guoluo* and *mangling* insects; let them transform of their own accord.
