[The Master said: "And yet, why are you dozing off right now? The monk said, "Just so, just so. The Master said, "What did you say? The monk said, "Not so, not so.
The Master struck him twice with his staff and said, "One blow strikes you for being 'just so'; one blow strikes you for being 'not so.
The monk requested further instruction, saying, "I do not know where I shall go when I die. The Master said, "You..."
"Is this person now alive or dead? The monk said, "If he were alive, I would not say; if he were dead, I would not say.
The Master said, "You have acted as a servant to Jianyuan. The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him. Another monk came forward, and the Master said, "Just now that monk suffered a defeat;
do you know it? The monk said, "I know. The Master struck him again. The monk then requested further instruction.
In the territory of Jia Shan, before the monk had even finished speaking, the Master gave a shout. The monk was bewildered. The Master asked, "What were you asking?

As the monk prepared to speak, the Master struck him repeatedly with shouts and drove him out. Another monk requested further instruction, saying, "I have been practicing Chan but cannot attain realization;
where does my illness lie? The Master said, "The illness lies right here. The monk asked, "Why is it that I cannot realize it? The Master said, "With eyes wide open..."
"You bed-wetting brat! I’ll beat you! He addressed the assembly, saying: "I have no method to give to people here;
I simply settle the case according to the facts. It is just as if you were to bring a crystal bottle here—why would you cherish it so?
As soon as I see it, I break it for you. And suppose you bring a *maṇi* jewel; I will likewise [break it] for you."
[He] seized [it]. I was waiting for you to come just like this, so I have cut off both your hands as well.
Therefore, Master Linji said: "When encountering a Buddha, kill the Buddha; when encountering a Patriarch, kill the Patriarch; when encountering an Arhat, kill the Arhat.
Since you are called a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend), why must you kill people? Tell me, what is the principle here? This is the Master’s discourse on the Dharma.

He was extremely prolific; the *Zhengfayan zang* and the *Wuku* were both produced by his hand. Because he composed a verse on the "Divine Arm Bow" (*shenbi gong*), he incurred the taboos of his time and was twice censured by the authorities.
He subsequently presided over Mount Jing and passed away there.
The eulogy says: From Linji, the Dharma was transmitted through twelve generations until it reached Dahui, whose Way flourished even more than before.
My own thought was that after several generations, it would decline; unfortunately, after one transmission from Dahui, all his disciples died young.
Once the "seeds of fire" were extinguished, those who were empty, foolish, and deceitful rushed forth like a collapsing dam, usurping the name and emblems of the Buddha-Dharma.
Frivolous words have been unleashed at will, causing the single school of Linji to degenerate into mere sophistry.
This has deceived scholars and caused them to fall into the darkness; even wailing and shedding tears would not suffice to convey my grief.

The Way of Dahui is like the sun in the midst of the sky, yet it is now obscured by high crags and deep valleys, by smoke, clouds, dust, and mist, as if by the hands of an Asura or the gate of a Gandharva.
"Vaiśravaṇa’s City (Gandharvanagara). When this object first appeared as it was being constructed, it served to obscure the sun; yet the sun remained exactly as it was.
Can one call such things as lofty crags, deep valleys, mist, clouds, dust, or fog, or the hand of an Asura, or a Gandharva-city, 'the sun'?
They are soon to be swept away by whirling winds and transformed into drifting dust, vanishing in an instant. Although...
Even if the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were to dance together in harmony, it would still not suffice to satisfy my heart. Mahāmati’s realization was vast and expansive;
he did not merely dwell beneath the cliffs of Yaṇtóu or Xuěfēng. His wisdom and eloquence sprang forth with the vigor of a steed, like that of Dàzhū of Nányáng.
In his mastery of killing and giving life, and his strategic release and capture, he was no different from Shǒushān and Fēngxué. A student such as this should, for themselves, [realize...]
I have sought [this account]. Were it not for his shaking up the ancestral legacy and sustaining the family estate, it could not be fully recounted in a single word. Alas!

As the sages of former times withered away and later generations lacked those who heard their teachings, may these words never be forgotten, so that those with a sincere heart may find guidance therein.
The End of the Lower Volume of the *Dàguāngmíngzàng* (Great Treasury of Radiant Light).

Jiyin once composed the *Sēngbǎozhuàn* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha); however, it merely records their origins and the points where masters and disciples struck a chord of mutual resonance.
It rarely touches upon the "interlocking patterns" and "knotted corners" [of Chan discourse]. Recently, I encountered Master Jian at Nanguo in Siming.
He compiled them in this manner, tracing back to the profound mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and then addressed them, saying:
"Can the direct, authentic transmission from antiquity truly be expressed through written words and language? Gong rebuked him, saying: "You rely on the teachings of the current King Yù;
you see only a single corner and are vulgarly caught in a net. You have never heard the discourse of the Great Way for those who study later."

Using this discourse on transcendence, I have extolled the wondrous points of our Patriarchs; yet all of it is in accord with the examination of their essential school, without a single hair’s breadth of addition or subtraction.
Should anyone be able to read this, it will fit together like two halves of a tally. My wish-king is thus established.

Through practice and realization, this lineage was further extended. It is certain that in future generations there will be one like Yang Xiong.

This "Epilogue by Tianmu Shi Qiao Wenli" for the *Guangmingzang*, written in the summer of the Xinchou year of the Chunyou era, is a record compiled by the monk Tan Juzhou. Upon reading it, I find the various ancestral lineages clearly delineated. Furthermore...
I cherish its phrasing for not venturing into the strange or the absurd; it is truly what is called "prajñā in written form.
Therefore, I have had it carved for circulation, so that from one lamp within the Inexhaustible Treasury, there may arise ten thousand lamps, illuminating the entire Dharma-realm. How excellent!
Written on the day of the summer solstice in the first year of the Xiachun era, the year of Yichou, by Zhao Mengfu of the former Bianjing.
